translated_text:
Thus, both a human being’s animal nature and his rationality include something shared with other animals and something peculiar to him alone. The same applies to the formation of his bodily constitution. Although his growth and nourishment have something in common with those of plants, they are not identical to them. For he feeds on what gives him pleasure and delights his soul, and he grows as his sensation, movement, intent, and work develop. Plants are not like this. The same applies to the various classes and individuals within a species. Thus, the rationality of the Arabs, manifested in the discernment of their hearts and the eloquence of their tongues, is more perfect than that of others. Indeed, some human beings fall below beasts in rationality and discernment, while others reach heights whose limits cannot be fathomed.

All this shows that when individuals within a class, classes within a species, species within a genus, and lower genera share the designation of a higher genus, this does not entail that the common meaning is present in them equally. Likewise, there is no single entity shared by externally existing realities. Rather, the mind grasps a meaning found in one thing, whose counterpart is found in another. It has already become clear that this is a counterpart by way of resemblance, not sameness, and that the reality of this common meaning in one differs from its reality in the other. This is where those who employ comparative reasoning go wrong: they attend to the common meaning that unites things, but not to the difference that distinguishes them.

And the Arabs, among the various peoples, and the Muslims, among the adherents of religions, are the foremost of people

in perceiving differences and distinguishing shared features.

This is evident in their intellects, languages, sciences, and judgments. Thus, when the Arab theologians of Islam debated these Sabian theologians—the non-Arab Romans—and explained the superiority of their own reasoning and discourse over those of their opponents, the superiority of the Muslim theologians’ discourse became apparent. This is what Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-Bāqillānī did in his Book of Subtleties, in which he refuted many of the philosophers’ corrupt doctrines concerning celestial spheres, stars, intellects, souls, the Necessary Existent, and other matters. He discussed their logic and their classification of existing things, such as their division of being into substance and accident, followed by their division of accidents into the nine categories. He also presented the Muslim theologians’ classification, which distinguishes, groups, and differentiates things in ways absent from those philosophers’ discourse.

This is because Allah taught man clear expression, as He, Exalted is He, says:

“The Most Merciful,
Taught the Quran,
Created man,
Taught him eloquence.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“And He taught Adam all the names.”

And He says:

“Taught man what he did not know.”

Clarity belongs to both the heart and the tongue, just as blindness and muteness may affect both the heart and the tongue. As He, Exalted is He, says:

“Deaf, mute, and blind, so they do not return.”

And He says:

“Deaf, mute, and blind, so they do not understand.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Why did they not ask when they did not know? The only cure for ignorance is to ask.”

A transmitted report states:

“Incapacity lies in the heart, not in the tongue.”

Or he said:

“The worst incapacity is that of the heart.”

Ibn Masʿūd used to say:

“You live in a time whose scholars are many and whose orators are few. A time will come upon you whose scholars are few and whose orators are many.”

Yet on close examination, you find them evenly matched, or nearly so, with neither having any clear advantage over the other. Thus, either all their definitions should be accepted, all rejected, or accepted in one respect and rejected in another.

This applies to definitions that alike distinguish the thing defined and set it apart from everything else. But when one person includes in a definition what another excludes, or vice versa, discussing this yields knowledge of the term’s definition and the breadth or narrowness of its scope. Examples include discussing the definition of khamr (wine): is it fermented grape juice, or every intoxicant? The same applies to the definition of backbiting and similar matters. This is what scholars discuss, as when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked:

“What is backbiting?”

He replied, “Your mentioning your brother in a way he dislikes”—the hadith continues.

Likewise, he said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr.”

And ʿUmar said from the pulpit:

“Khamr is whatever clouds the mind.”

Similarly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.”

A man asked him, “O Messenger of Allah, a man likes his shoes and clothing to look good. Is that arrogance?”

He replied, “No. Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.”

This also includes interpreting speech, explaining it and clarifying it. Anyone who explains another person’s words, interprets them and clarifies their meaning must therefore know the definitions of the terms they contain.

translated_text:
Thus, any definition expressed in words is merely a definition of a term, akin to translation and explanation. Sometimes it is purely verbal, when the person addressed already knows what is being defined. At other times, its meaning needs to be explained and clarified, when the person addressed does not know what the term denotes. This is done by giving an example or combining descriptions. Yet this does not convey a conception of the thing’s essence to someone who has not conceived it through something other than words. Let this be understood. As for what they call defining a thing, defining it according to its essence, or defining essences, it distinguishes the thing only by mentioning some of its attributes, as explained above. It also contains confusion, some of which we have already pointed out.

As for “the question of syllogistic reasoning,” it is to be discussed in two respects. The first concerns syllogistic reasoning in general, which they have made the standard for the sciences and have precisely formulated in logic. The second concerns the kinds of syllogisms they employ in the sciences.

Regarding the first, we say: there is no dispute that when two premises are known to be true and are properly combined, this yields knowledge of the conclusion.

A narration in Sahīh Muslim, traced back to the Prophet, states:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden.”

However, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say this to argue against an opponent disputing with him. Rather, the combination of statements here is like what he also said

translated_text:
in the Sahīh:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden.”

He intended to explain to them that all intoxicants fall within the meaning of khamr, which Allah has forbidden. This explains the meaning of khamr; they already knew that Allah had forbidden khamr. They used to ask him about drinks made from grape juice, as related in the two Sahīhs from Abū Mūsā:

“He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a drink made from sorghum called mizr and a drink made from honey called bitʿ. He had been endowed with concise, comprehensive speech, so he said: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

Through this comprehensive statement—a universal proposition—he intended to explain to them that every intoxicant is khamr. He then added what they already knew, that “every khamr is forbidden,” to establish firmly in their hearts that intoxicants are forbidden, as he explicitly stated in his words: “Every intoxicant is forbidden.” Had he confined himself to saying, “Every intoxicant is forbidden,” someone might have interpreted this as referring to the final cup, as some indeed did.

For this reason, Ahmad said: “His statement, ‘Every intoxicant is khamr,’ is more emphatic.” For they do not call the final cup khamr. Had he merely said, “Every intoxicant is khamr,” some might have interpreted this to mean that it resembles khamr in being forbidden. But when he added, “And every khamr is forbidden,” it became clear that he intended to include it within the designation khamr, which Allah has forbidden.

The point here is that this form of syllogism is innate and requires no instruction. Rather, it is as familiar to people as arithmetic. Yet these men make their formulations lengthy and obscure.

translated_text:
The same applies to dividing a premise—called a “proposition,” meaning a declarative sentence—into particular and universal, negative and affirmative, and the like; to the statements that a true proposition has a true converse and contrapositive, that its negation is false, and that its formulation varies; and to similar matters. Likewise, they divide syllogisms into simple categorical syllogisms, conditional syllogisms based on implication or mutual exclusion, and other types. Even if most of this is sound, it contains some falsehood.

Even the truth it contains involves needless length and multiplication of words, poor expression and inarticulate explanation, and abandoning the straight, short path for a distant, circuitous route. This is not the place to explain all that. Its useful truths are innate and do not require this discipline; whatever does require it offers no benefit beyond learning their terminology and method, or their errors.

Such is the case with everyone who espouses a false doctrine: acquaintance with his discourse is indispensable to understanding his terminology and misguidance. It is therefore needed to expose his misguidance, through which those endowed with certainty recognize his true condition. It also makes clear to them what Allah has explained concerning His judgment, both in recompense and in His commands, and that these people fall under the censure directed at those who strain to produce speech that conveys nothing and multiply words to no benefit.

The purpose here is to set out several points:

original_text:
الْوَجْهُ الْأَوَّلُ:

 لَكِنَّ الْفَرْقَ:
 أَنَّ التَّجْرِبَةَ تَتَعَلَّقُ بِفِعْلِ الْمُجَرِّبِ كَالْأَطْعِمَةِ وَالْأَشْرِبَةِ وَالْأَدْوِيَةِ
translated_text:
The first point:

The syllogism in question yields knowledge only through a universal affirmative proposition. Every syllogism must therefore contain an established, comprehensive universal proposition. This, too, is acknowledged and agreed upon.

Hence their statement: “No syllogism can be formed from two negative premises or from two particular premises.” Accordingly, universal truths—comprehensive statements—must constitute the starting points of syllogisms and proofs, and the foundations on which they are built and upon which they depend.

They further state that the starting points of demonstrative syllogisms consist of certain knowledge: internal and external sensory perceptions, rational truths, self-evident truths, mass-transmitted reports, and findings established through experience. Some also add intuitive truths.

Yet neither internal nor external sensory perceptions contain universal propositions, since internal and external sensation apprehend only particular things, which are established only when the reporter has perceived through the senses what he reports; they are therefore dependent on sensory perceptions. Likewise, experience concerns only particular, perceptible things. The intellect judges similar cases by comparing them, which is reasoning by analogy. Intuitive truths—according to those among them who recognize them—are of the same kind as findings established through experience.

The difference, however, is that experience involves the experimenter’s own actions, as with foods, drinks, and medicines

original_text: وَالْحَدْسُ يَتَعَلَّقُ بِغَيْرِ فِعْلٍ كَاخْتِلَافِ أَشْكَالِ الْقَمَرِ عِنْدَ اخْتِلَافِ مُقَابَلَتِهِ لِلشَّمْسِ. وَهُوَ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ تَجْرِبَةٌ عِلْمِيَّةٌ بِلَا عَمَلٍ فَالْمُسْتَفَادُ بِهِ أَيْضًا أُمُورٌ مُعَيَّنَةٌ جُزْئِيَّةٌ لَا تَصِيرُ عَامَّةً إلَّا بِوَاسِطَةِ قِيَاسِ التَّمْثِيلِ. وَأَمَّا الْبَدِيهِيَّاتُ - وَهِيَ الْعُلُومُ الْأَوَّلِيَّةُ الَّتِي يَجْعَلُهَا اللَّهُ فِي النُّفُوسِ ابْتِدَاءً بِلَا وَاسِطَةٍ مِثْلُ الْحِسَابِ وَهِيَ كَالْعِلْمِ بِأَنَّ الْوَاحِدَ نِصْفُ الِاثْنَيْنِ - فَإِنَّهَا لَا تُفِيدُ الْعِلْمَ بِشَيْءِ مُعَيَّنٍ مَوْجُودٍ فِي الْخَارِجِ مِثْلُ الْحُكْمِ عَلَى الْعَدَدِ الْمُطْلَقِ وَالْمِقْدَارِ الْمُطْلَقِ وَكَالْعِلْمِ بِأَنَّ الْأَشْيَاءَ الْمُسَاوِيَةَ لِشَيْءِ وَاحِدٍ هِيَ مُتَسَاوِيَةٌ فِي أَنْفُسِهَا. فَإِنَّك إذَا حَكَمْت عَلَى مَوْجُودٍ فِي الْخَارِجِ لَمْ يَكُنْ إلَّا بِوَاسِطَةِ الْحِسِّ مِثْلُ الْعَقْلِ. فَإِنَّ الْعَقْلَ إنَّمَا هُوَ عَقْلُ مَا عَلِمْته بِالْإِحْسَاسِ الْبَاطِنِ أَوْ الظَّاهِرِ بِعَقْلِ الْمَعَانِي الْعَامَّةِ أَوْ الْخَاصَّةِ. فَأَمَّا أَنَّ الْعَقْلَ الَّذِي هُوَ عَقْلُ الْأُمُورِ الْعَامَّةِ الَّتِي أَفْرَادُهَا مَوْجُودَةٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ يَحْصُلُ بِغَيْرِ حِسٍّ فَهَذَا لَا يُتَصَوَّرُ. وَإِذَا رَجَعَ الْإِنْسَانُ إلَى نَفْسِهِ وَجَدَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَعْقِلُ ذَلِكَ مُسْتَغْنِيًا عَنْ الْحِسِّ الْبَاطِنِ وَالظَّاهِرِ لِكُلِّيَّاتِ مُقَدَّرَةٍ فِي نَفْسِهِ مِثْلُ الْوَاحِدِ وَالِاثْنَيْنِ وَالْمُسْتَقِيمِ وَالْمُنْحَنَى وَالْمُثَلَّثِ وَالْمُرَبَّعِ وَالْوَاجِبِ وَالْمُمْكِنِ وَالْمُمْتَنِعِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَفْرِضُهُ هُوَ وَيُقَدِّرُهُ. فَأَمَّا الْعِلْمُ بِمُطَابَقَةِ ذَلِكَ الْمُقَدَّرِ لِلْمَوْجُودِ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَالْعِلْمُ بِالْحَقَائِقِ الْخَارِجِيَّةِ فَلَا بُدَّ فِيهِ مِنْ الْحِسِّ الْبَاطِنِ أَوْ الظَّاهِرِ. فَإِذَا اجْتَمَعَ الْحِسُّ وَالْعَقْلُ - كَاجْتِمَاعِ الْبَصَرِ وَالْعَقْلِ - أَمْكَنَ أَنْ يُدْرِكَ الْحَقَائِقَ الْمَوْجُودَةَ الْمَعْنِيَّةَ وَيَعْقِلَ حُكْمَهَا الْعَامَّ
translated_text:
whereas intuition concerns what does not involve one’s own action, such as the changing shapes of the moon as its position relative to the sun changes. In reality, it is a purely cognitive experience involving no action. What it yields, too, consists of particular, individual matters, which become general only through reasoning by analogy.

As for self-evident truths—the primary knowledge that Allah places directly in souls, without any intermediary, such as arithmetic, including the knowledge that one is half of two—they do not yield knowledge of any particular thing existing outside the mind. Examples include judgments concerning number and magnitude in the abstract, and the knowledge that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. Whenever you make a judgment about something existing outside the mind, this can only be through sensory perception, just as with intellectual apprehension. For intellectual apprehension consists in understanding what you have learned through internal or external sensation, by apprehending general or particular meanings. As for apprehending universals whose individual instances exist outside the mind without any sensory perception, this is inconceivable.

When a person examines himself, he finds that he does not apprehend this independently of internal and external sensation with regard to universals conceived in his mind, such as one and two, the straight and the curved, the triangle and the square, the necessary, the possible, and the impossible, and other such things that he himself supposes and conceives. But knowing that what is thus conceived corresponds to something existing outside the mind, and knowing external realities, necessarily requires internal or external sensory perception.

When sensory perception and intellect work together—as when sight and intellect work together—it becomes possible to apprehend the existing realities in question and understand the universal judgment that applies to them

original_text:
الَّذِي يَنْدَرِجُ فِيهِ أَمْثَالُهَا لَا أَضْدَادُهَا وَيُعْلَمُ الْجَمْعُ وَالْفَرْقُ. وَهَذَا هُوَ اعْتِبَارُ الْعَقْلِ وَقِيَاسُهُ. وَإِذَا انْفَرَدَ الْإِحْسَاسُ الْبَاطِنُ أَوْ الظَّاهِرُ أَدْرَكَ وُجُودَ الْمَوْجُودِ الْمُعَيَّنِ. وَإِذَا انْفَرَدَ الْمَعْقُولُ الْمُجَرَّدُ عَلِمَ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ الْمُقَدَّرَةَ فِيهِ الَّتِي قَدْ يَكُونُ لَهَا وُجُودٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَقَدْ لَا يَكُونُ وَلَا يُعْلَمُ وُجُودُ أَعْيَانِهَا وَعَدَمُ وُجُودِ أَعْيَانِهَا إلَّا بِإِحْسَاسِ بَاطِنٍ أَوْ ظَاهِرٍ.
 فَإِنَّك إذَا قُلْت:
 مَوْجُودٌ أَنَّ الْمِائَةَ عُشْرُ الْأَلْفِ لَمْ تَحْكُمْ عَلَى شَيْءٍ فِي الْخَارِجِ؛
 بَلْ لَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي الْعَالَمِ مَا يَعُدُّ بِالْمِائَةِ وَالْأَلْفِ لَكُنْت عَالِمًا بِأَنَّ الْمِائَةَ الْمُقَدَّرَةَ فِي عَقْلِك عُشْرُ الْأَلْفِ وَلَكِنْ إذَا أَحْسَسْت بِالرِّجَالِ وَالدَّوَابِّ وَالذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَأَحْسَسْت بِحِسِّك أَوْ بِخَبَرِ مَنْ أَحَسَّ أَنَّ هُنَاكَ مِائَةَ رَجُلٍ أَوْ دِرْهَمٍ وَهُنَاكَ أَلْفٌ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ:
 حَكَمْت عَلَى أَحَدِ الْمَعْدُودَيْنِ بِأَنَّهُ عُشْرُ الْآخَرِ. فَأَمَّا الْمَعْدُودَاتُ فَلَا تُدْرَكُ إلَّا بِالْحِسِّ. وَالْعَدَدُ الْمُجَرَّدُ يُعْقَلُ بِالْقَلْبِ وَبِعَقْلِ الْقَلْبِ وَالْحِسِّ يُعْلَمُ الْعَدَدُ وَالْمَعْدُودُ جَمِيعًا وَكَذَلِكَ الْمَقَادِيرُ الْهَنْدَسِيَّةُ هِيَ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ. فَالْعُلُومُ الْأَوَّلِيَّةُ الْبَدِيهِيَّةُ الْعَقْلِيَّةُ الْمَحْضَةُ لَيْسَتْ إلَّا فِي الْمُقَدَّرَاتِ الذِّهْنِيَّةِ كَالْعَدَدِ وَالْمِقْدَارِ لَا فِي الْأُمُورِ الْخَارِجِيَّةِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ.
translated_text:
under which similar things, but not their opposites, fall, and to recognize similarities and differences. This is the intellect’s comparative and analogical reasoning. When internal or external sensation operates alone, it apprehends the existence of a particular thing. When abstract thought operates alone, it knows the universals conceived within it, which may or may not exist outside the mind. Whether their individual instances exist or not can be known only through internal or external sensation.

For when you say, “It is a fact that one hundred is one-tenth of one thousand,” you are not making a judgment about anything outside the mind. Indeed, even if nothing in the world could be counted in hundreds or thousands, you would still know that the hundred conceived in your mind is one-tenth of the thousand. But when you perceive men, animals, gold, and silver, and ascertain—through your own senses or the report of someone who has perceived them—that there are one hundred men or dirhams in one place and one thousand in another, or the like, you judge that one of the two quantities counted is one-tenth of the other.

The things counted can be apprehended only through sensory perception, whereas abstract number is apprehended by the heart. Through the heart’s understanding and sensory perception together, both number and the things counted are known. Geometrical magnitudes likewise belong to this category. Thus, primary, self-evident, purely intellectual knowledge concerns only things conceived in the mind, such as number and magnitude, not things actually existing outside it.

original_text: فَإِذَا كَانَتْ مَوَادُّ الْقِيَاسِ الْبُرْهَانِيِّ لَا يُدْرَكُ بِعَامَّتِهَا إلَّا أُمُورٌ مُعَيَّنَةٌ لَيْسَتْ كُلِّيَّةً وَهِيَ الْحِسُّ الْبَاطِنُ وَالظَّاهِرُ وَالتَّوَاتُرُ وَالتَّجْرِبَةُ وَالْحَدْسُ وَاَلَّذِي يُدْرِكُ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ الْبَدِيهِيَّةَ الْأَوَّلِيَّةَ إنَّمَا يُدْرِكُ أُمُورًا مُقَدَّرَةً ذِهْنِيَّةً لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي مَبَادِئِ الْبُرْهَانِ وَمُقَدِّمَاتِهِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ مَا يُعْلَمُ بِهِ قَضِيَّةٌ كُلِّيَّةٌ عَامَّةٌ لِلْأُمُورِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَالْقِيَاسُ لَا يُفِيدُ الْعِلْمَ إلَّا بِوَاسِطَةِ قَضِيَّةٍ كُلِّيَّةٍ. فَامْتَنَعَ حِينَئِذٍ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِيمَا ذَكَرُوهُ مِنْ صُورَةِ الْقِيَاسِ وَمَادَّتِهِ حُصُولُ عِلْمٍ يَقِينِيٍّ. وَهَذَا بَيِّنٌ لِمَنْ تَأَمَّلَهُ. وَبِتَحْرِيرِهِ وَجَوْدَةِ تَصَوُّرِهِ تَنْفَتِحُ عُلُومٌ عَظِيمَةٌ وَمَعَارِفُ. وَسَنُبَيِّنُ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنْ أَيِّ وَجْهٍ وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِمْ اللَّبْسُ. فَتَدَبَّرْ هَذَا فَإِنَّهُ مِنْ أَسْرَارِ عَظَائِمِ الْعُلُومِ الَّتِي يَظْهَرُ لَك بِهِ مَا يَجِلُّ عَنْ الْوَصْفِ مِنْ الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الطَّرِيقَةِ الْفِطْرِيَّةِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ السَّمْعِيَّةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ الْإِيمَانِيَّةِ وَبَيْنَ الطَّرِيقَةِ الْقِيَاسِيَّةِ الْمَنْطِقِيَّةِ الْكَلَامِيَّةِ. وَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ لَك بِإِجْمَاعِهِمْ وَبِالْعَقْلِ أَنَّ الْقِيَاسَ الْمَنْطِقِيَّ لَا يُفِيدُ إلَّا بِوَاسِطَةِ قَضِيَّةٍ وَتَبَيَّنَ لَك أَنَّ الْقَضَايَا الَّتِي هِيَ عِنْدَهُمْ مَوَادُّ الْبُرْهَانِ وَأُصُولُهُ لَيْسَ فِيهَا قَضِيَّةٌ كُلِّيَّةٌ لِلْأُمُورِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ وَلَيْسَ فِيهَا مَا تُعْلَمُ بِهِ الْقَضِيَّةُ الْكُلِّيَّةُ إلَّا الْعَقْلُ الْمُجَرَّدُ الَّذِي يَعْقِلُ الْمُقَدَّرَاتِ الذِّهْنِيَّةَ وَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي أُصُولِ بُرْهَانِهِمْ عِلْمٌ بِقَضِيَّةِ عَامَّةٍ لِلْأُمُورِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي ذَلِكَ عِلْمٌ.
translated_text:
Since most of the sources supplying the premises of demonstrative syllogisms—internal and external sensation, mass transmission, experience, and intuitive apprehension—yield knowledge only of particulars, not universals, while the faculty that apprehends primary, self-evident universals apprehends only things conceived in the mind, none of the aforementioned principles and premises of demonstration provides knowledge of a universal proposition applicable to things actually existing outside the mind. Yet a syllogism yields knowledge only through a universal proposition. It is therefore impossible to obtain certain knowledge through what they describe as the form and material of the syllogism.

This is clear to anyone who reflects upon it. Precisely formulating it and conceiving it clearly opens up vast fields of knowledge and understanding. We shall explain, Allah willing, how their confusion arose. Reflect carefully on this, for it is one of the secrets of the greatest branches of knowledge. Through it, you will perceive an indescribably great difference between the way grounded in innate disposition, reason, transmitted revelation, the revealed Law, and faith, and the way of syllogisms, logic, and speculative theology.

It has become clear to you, both from their unanimous agreement and through reason, that the logical syllogism yields knowledge only through a proposition. It has also become clear that the propositions they regard as the material and foundations of demonstration contain no universal proposition applicable to existing things. Nor do they contain any means of knowing a universal proposition other than abstract reason, which apprehends things conceived in the mind. If, then, the foundations of their demonstration contain no knowledge of a general proposition applicable to existing things, this furnishes no knowledge.

original_text:
وَلَيْسَ فِيمَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ مَا يُمْكِنُ النِّزَاعُ فِيهِ إلَّا الْقَضَايَا الْبَدِيهِيَّةُ فَإِنَّ فِيهَا عُمُومًا وَقَدْ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ بِهِ تَعَلُّمَ الْأُمُورِ الْخَارِجَةِ فَيَفْرِضُ أَنَّهَا تُفِيدُ الْعُلُومَ الْكُلِّيَّةَ. لَكِنَّ بَقِيَّةَ الْمَبَادِئِ لَيْسَ فِيهَا عِلْمٌ كُلِّيٌّ. فَكَانَ الْوَاجِبُ أَنْ لَا يَجْعَلَ مُقَدِّمَةَ الْبُرْهَانِ إلَّا الْقَضَايَا الْعَقْلِيَّةَ الْبَدِيهِيَّةَ الْمَحْضَةَ. إذْ هِيَ الْكُلِّيَّةُ. وَأَمَّا بَقِيَّةُ الْقَضَايَا فَهِيَ جُزْئِيَّةٌ فَكَيْفَ يَصْلُحُ أَنْ تُجْعَلَ مِنْ مُقَدِّمَاتِ الْبُرْهَانِ؟
 إلَّا أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 تُعْلَمُ بِهَا أُمُورٌ جُزْئِيَّةٌ وَبِالْعَقْلِ أُمُورٌ كُلِّيَّةٌ فَبِمَجْمُوعِهِمَا يَتِمُّ الْبُرْهَانُ كَمَا يُعْلَمُ بِالْحِسِّ أَنَّ مَعَ هَذَا أَلْفَ دِرْهَمٍ وَمَعَ هَذَا أَلْفَانِ وَيُعْلَمُ بِالْعَقْلِ أَنَّ الِاثْنَيْنِ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ الْوَاحِدِ فَيُعْلَمُ أَنَّ مَالَ هَذَا أَكْثَرُ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 هَذَا صَحِيحٌ؛ لَكِنَّ هَذَا إنَّمَا يُفِيدُ قَضِيَّةً جُزْئِيَّةً مُعَيَّنَةً. وَهُوَ كَوْنُ مَالِ هَذَا أَكْثَرَ مِنْ مَالِ هَذَا. وَالْأُمُورُ الْجُزْئِيَّةُ الْمُعَيَّنَةُ لَا تَحْتَاجُ فِي مَعْرِفَتِهَا إلَى قِيَاسٍ. بَلْ قَدْ تُعْلَمُ بِلَا قِيَاسٍ وَتُعْلَمُ بِقِيَاسِ التَّمْثِيلِ وَتُعْلَمُ بِالْقِيَاسِ عَنْ جُزْئِيَّتَيْنِ. فَإِنَّك تَعْلَمُ بِالْحِسِّ أَنَّ هَذَا مِثْلُ هَذَا وَتَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا مِنْ نَعْتِهِ كَيْت وَكَيْت فَتَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْآخَرَ مِثْلُهُ وَتَعْلَمُ أَنَّ حُكْمَ الشَّيْءِ حُكْمُ مِثْلِهِ. وَكَذَلِكَ قَدْ يُعْلَمُ أَنَّ زَيْدًا أَكْبَرُ مِنْ عَمْرٍو وَعَمْرًا أَكْبَرُ مِنْ خَالِدٍ وَأَمْثَالُ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ الَّتِي تُعْلَمُ بِدُونِ قِيَاسِ الشُّمُولِ الَّذِي اشْتَرَطُوا فِيهِ مَا اشْتَرَطُوا.
translated_text:
Nothing in what we have mentioned is open to dispute except the self-evident propositions, for these possess generality. One might think that this generality provides knowledge of things outside the mind, and thus suppose that these propositions yield universal knowledge. But the remaining principles contain no universal knowledge. Only purely rational, self-evident propositions should therefore serve as premises of demonstration, since these alone are universal. The remaining propositions are particular, so how can they properly serve as premises of demonstration?

Unless it is argued:

Through these propositions, particulars are known, while through reason, universals are known; together, they complete the demonstration. For example, sensory perception establishes that one man has a thousand dirhams and another two thousand, while reason establishes that two is greater than one. It is thus known that the latter has more wealth.

The reply is:

This is correct, but it yields only a specific, particular proposition: that one man’s wealth exceeds the other’s. Knowledge of specific particulars does not require a syllogism. They may be known without a syllogism, through analogical inference, or through inference from two particular propositions. For you know through sensory perception that this thing is like that thing, and you know that this thing has such-and-such attributes; you therefore know that the other is like it, and that what holds true of a thing holds true of its like. Likewise, it may be known that Zayd is older than Amr and that Amr is older than Khālid, along with similar specific matters that can be known without the subsumptive syllogism for which they have laid down their stipulated conditions.

" أَهْلَ كَلَامٍ "

translated_text:
It has thus become clear that this rational, logical syllogism which they have devised and defined cannot, by itself, yield any universal knowledge concerning external reality. Their claim is therefore invalid:

“It is the standard by which universal demonstrative knowledge is measured.”

It does, however, yield knowledge of specific, individual particulars, but these can be known better through other means.

This brings us to the second point. We say: Things that actually exist are known through inward and outward perception, through analogical inference, and through inference containing no universal proposition, subsumption, or generalization. Rather, its three terms—the minor, middle, and major—are individual particulars, and its two premises and conclusion are particular propositions. Knowledge of these specific things through such methods is sounder, clearer, and more complete.

Someone who sees Zayd with his own eyes in one place and Amr in another has no need to infer this from the principle that a single body cannot occupy two places. Likewise, someone who weighs quantities of dirhams, each amounting to a thousand dirhams, has no need to draw an inference about a thousand of those dirhams on the grounds that they equal the standard weight, that this is one and the same object, and that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. There are many similar examples.

This is why these people are called “men of talk”: they have supplied no knowledge that was not already known. They have merely added further talk that may serve no purpose: the syllogisms they have formulated to clarify what is already known through sensory perception. Although this

translated_text:
syllogism and others like it can be useful in another context and when dealing with those who deny sensory perception, as we shall explain, Allah willing.

Likewise, someone may know that this dinar is like that one, this dirham is like that one, and these quantities of wheat and barley are like their counterparts. If he then knows some of the attributes of one member of a pair and what holds true of it—whether by nature, such as its nourishing and beneficial effects; by convention, such as its value and price; or under revealed law, such as its permissibility or prohibition—he knows that the same holds true of the other. Analogical inferences thus undoubtedly yield greater certainty than subsumptive syllogisms. Once the likeness is known, there is no need to construct a subsumptive syllogism for the two cases; doing so merely adds something superfluous. In this way, particular propositions are known through analogical inference.

Whoever says that this occurs through a subsumptive syllogism formed in the mind—namely, that if this were coincidental, it would not occur in most cases—has spoken falsely. This does not occur to people who know things through their own experience. Rather, merely knowing that the cases are alike, they immediately judge them alike, because knowledge of their likeness itself entails this as a self-evident truth of reason. Just as it is known through self-evident reason that one is half of two, so it is known through it that what holds true of a thing

translated_text:
holds true of its like, and that one is like one, just as it is known that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. Likeness and difference in quality or quantity may be known through internal and external sense perception, while the knowledge that two like things are equal, and that what is more numerous and larger is greater and weightier, is self-evident to reason.

The same applies to an inference composed of propositions about particulars: for example, knowing that Zayd is Amr’s brother and Amr is Bakr’s brother, and therefore Zayd is Bakr’s brother. Likewise, knowing that Abū Bakr is superior to Umar, and Umar is superior to Uthmān and Alī, and therefore Abū Bakr is superior to Uthmān and Alī. Or that Medina is superior to Jerusalem, and pilgrimage to Medina is not obligatory, so no pilgrimage is made to Jerusalem. Or that the Messenger’s grave—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is the finest of graves, yet touching or kissing it is not prescribed; therefore, touching or kissing the graves of so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so is not prescribed.

The world abounds in such inferences. This is more effective in establishing what holds true of a particular than mentioning the general. A specific name identifies a particular more effectively than a general name does, even though the general name encompasses other things that the specific name does not.

It is thus clear that far more particulars are known through sensory perception, analogical inference, and inferences involving particulars than are known through subsumptive syllogisms. Thus, if the subsumptive syllogism—as they have formulated it—does not yield knowledge of universals, as explained above, and is not needed for knowledge of particulars

Their discussion of the syllogism they have formulated thus becomes like their discussion of definitions. The two amount to the same thing. Reflect on this, for it is of immense importance.

The third argument:

If a syllogism must contain a universal proposition, while the senses do not apprehend universals, which are apprehended only by reason, and that proposition cannot be known through another syllogism because this would entail circularity or an infinite regress, then there must be universal propositions apprehended without syllogism, such as those they classify as self-evident.

We therefore say: Since it must be acknowledged that some rational knowledge of universals arises directly in the mind and presents itself as self-evident without syllogism, it must be firmly accepted that rational knowledge of universals can dispense with syllogism.

This is something they themselves, along with all humanity, acknowledge: some conceptions and judgments are self-evident and need not be acquired through definition or syllogism. Otherwise, circularity or an infinite regress would necessarily follow.

Every universal truth can be known without logical syllogism. It is therefore unjustifiable to judge any universal knowledge to depend on it.

This becomes clear through the fourth argument:

We say: Granted that the form and matter of logical syllogism yield universal knowledge, on what grounds is it known that universal knowledge is otherwise unattainable? How, then, can these pretentious men, who follow that of which they have no knowledge—along with their imitators among the adherents of religious communities and their scholars—declare: “Conceptions and judgments that are not self-evident can be known only through definition and syllogism”?

Lack of knowledge is not knowledge of absence. Whoever makes such a claim has not examined his own mental experience. Had he done so, he would have found that he possesses universal knowledge without logical syllogism and many conceptions without definition. Even if he knows this to be true of himself or his fellows, how can he know that all the children of Adam—with their differing natural dispositions, knowledge, and gifts bestowed upon them by the True One—are just like him, and that Allah grants no one knowledge except through a logical syllogism formed in his mind?

These men even claim that the prophets were likewise. Indeed, they have extended their claim to the Lord of all worlds, asserting that His knowledge of the affairs of His creation comes only through logical syllogism. This is further clarified by the fifth argument:

The aforementioned principles that they regard as yielding certainty—namely, internal and external sensory perceptions, self-evident truths, findings established through experience, and intuitive apprehensions—undoubtedly yield sensory certainty. But on what grounds do they claim that certainty cannot be attained through anything else?

They must provide evidence for this negation before their statement, “Certainty cannot be attained without them,” can be valid. This is correct, but it is not what their leading authorities say. Undoubtedly, anyone possessed of reason and faith must oppose them in their denial of truths attained outside this method. It was through this that those among them who succumbed to hypocrisy became hypocrites and heretics.

Thus, sensible people, whether adherents of religious communities or others, came to regard logic as liable to foster denial of the truth, obstinacy, heresy, and hypocrisy. Someone even related to us that a non-Arab man came to study logic under one of their teachers. After studying a portion of it, he asked, “Master, which chapter deals with abandoning prayer?” They laughed at him.

translated_text:
Observation bears this out: whoever thinks highly of logic and its practitioners, unless he has a foundation in religion and reason through which to acquire beneficial truth, will suffer corruption in both his reason and his religion. Thus, disbelief, hypocrisy, ignorance, misguidance, and corrupt words and deeds are found among them to an extent apparent to any observer. This is why the first person to mix logic with the principles of jurisprudence and similar Islamic sciences was beset by considerable confusion.

Many distinguished Muslims and scholars used to say:

“Logic is like arithmetic and similar disciplines: it cannot demonstrate the truth or falsehood of Islam, nor establish or refute it.”

Such words come from someone who has seen only its outward aspect: its discussion of simple elements, both expressions and meanings; then their combination into propositions, together with their contradictories, simple converses, and contrapositives; then their arrangement in definitions and syllogisms, and the content of syllogisms. In reality, however, logic contains many unsound notions and false claims that cannot be exhaustively discussed here. And Allah knows best.

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bestow blessings and peace upon His servant and Messenger Muhammad, who calls to guidance and right conduct, and upon his family and those who follow his guidance.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—also said:

To proceed:

I had always known that an intelligent person has no need of Greek logic and that a dull-witted person gains no benefit from it. Yet I used to think its propositions were true, since we had found many of them to be true. Later, however, it became clear to me that some of its propositions were erroneous, and I wrote something on the subject.

While I was in Alexandria, someone met with me whom I found extolling the philosophers through exaggeration and blind imitation. I explained to him some of the grounds on which they deserved to be judged ignorant and misguided. This prompted me to write down some remarks on logic in a single sitting between the noon and afternoon prayers, recording them there and then. This was not, however, my main concern; my attention was devoted to what I had written against them on “metaphysics.” It became clear to me that much of what they had stated about logic lay at the root of their erroneous views on metaphysics,

such as their account of essences as composed of attributes they called essential, and their restriction of the paths to knowledge to the definitions and demonstrative syllogisms they described—indeed, their account of the definitions through which conceptions are acquired, and even their account of the forms of syllogism and its certain premises.

Someone then wished to copy the remarks I had written at that time criticizing their views on logic. I permitted this because it opens the way to knowing the truth, although the scope for refuting them thus opened could accommodate many times as much as I had written.

Know, then, that they based “logic” on the discussion of definition and the like, and demonstrative syllogism and the like. They said: “This is because knowledge is either conception or assent. The means by which conception is attained is definition, and the means by which assent is attained is syllogism.”

We say: The discussion concerns “four points”: two negative and two affirmative. The first of the two negative points concerns their claim that the conception sought can be attained only through definition; the second, that the assent sought can be attained only through syllogism. The other two concern their claims that definition yields knowledge of conceptions, and that syllogism—or demonstration as they describe it—yields knowledge of assents.

translated_text:
The first point concerns their statement:

“Conception can be attained only through definition.”

This may be examined from several angles.

First: There is no doubt that one who denies a claim must provide evidence, just as one who affirms it must. A proposition, whether negative or affirmative, requires evidence unless it is self-evident. Negation without knowledge is simply speaking without knowledge. Their statement that conceptions can be attained only through definition is a negative proposition, and it is not self-evident. What, then, is their evidence for it? If this is a statement made without knowledge, yet it is the very first foundation they laid, how can speaking without knowledge serve as the foundation for the criterion of knowledge and for what they claim is a rule-governed instrument whose observance safeguards the mind against error in thought?

Second: It may be said that “definition” can mean the thing defined itself, but this is not what they intend here. It can also mean a statement indicating the essence of the thing defined, which is what they intend here. It sets out in detail what the name indicates in general. We therefore say: If a definition is a statement made by the definer, then the definer must have identified the thing defined either through a definition or without one.

If the former, the same question applies to the second definition as to the first, necessarily resulting in circularity or an infinite regress. If the latter, their negative claim is invalidated—namely, their statement that it can be known only through definition.

We find none of the leading authorities in the sciences employing these definitions: neither the authorities on jurisprudence, grammar, medicine or arithmetic, nor practitioners of the crafts. Yet they conceive the individual concepts of their disciplines. It is therefore clear that conception has no need of these definitions.

(Fourth: To this day, no definition is known that is sound according to their principles. Indeed, the most obvious of things is the human being, yet its definition as a “rational animal” is subject to the well-known objections. The same applies to the definition of the sun and similar things. Even the grammarians, when their later scholars ventured into definitions, offered twenty-odd definitions of the noun, all of which are open to objections according to their principles. Scholars of legal theory likewise offered twenty-odd definitions of analogical reasoning, all of which are also open to objections. Most definitions mentioned in the books of philosophers, physicians, grammarians, scholars of legal theory and speculative theologians are open to objections; only a few have escaped them. If conceiving things depended on definitions, people would not, to this day, have conceived any of these things. Assent depends on conception, so where no conception is attained, no assent is attained. Humanity would therefore possess no knowledge in most of its disciplines. This is sophistry of the highest order.

(Fifth: According to them, conception of an essence is attained only through a real definition composed of shared and distinguishing essential attributes—that is, one composed of genus and differentia. (Sixth: According to them, definitions apply only to composite essences: species possessing a genus and a differentia. As for what is not composite—that which does not fall under a genus together with anything else, exemplified by some of them by the intellect—it has no definition. Yet they have defined it, and its conception is among those they seek to acquire. It is therefore clear that conception has no need of definition. Indeed, if this can be known without a definition, those species can all the more readily be known, since they are closer to the genus and their individual instances are familiar.

They say that assent does not depend on the complete conception attained through a real definition. Rather, even a minimal conception suffices, if only through a distinctive property. The conception of the intellect belongs to this category. This is an admission on their part that conception as such does not depend on a real definition.

Seventh: Unless someone hearing a definition already knows its individual terms and how they signify their respective meanings, he cannot understand the statement. Knowing that a term signifies a meaning and has been assigned to it presupposes a conception of that meaning. If he already conceives what the term designates and means before hearing it, it cannot be said that he conceives it only by hearing it.

(Ninth: A person conceives existing things either through his external senses, as with taste, colour, smell, and the bodies possessing these attributes, or through his internal senses, as with hunger, love, hatred, joy, sorrow, pleasure, pain, volition, aversion, and the like. None of these requires a definition.

(Tenth: They say that an objector may challenge a definition by presenting counterexamples to its applicability or exclusiveness, or by opposing it with another definition. If someone hearing a definition can invalidate it, sometimes through counterexamples and sometimes through a competing definition—and it is well known that neither is possible without first conceiving what is being defined—then it follows that what is being defined can be conceived without the definition. This is precisely what we seek to establish.

(Eleventh: They acknowledge that some conceptions are self-evident and require no definition. It may then be said that whether knowledge is self-evident or inferential is a relative matter. What requires inference for one person may be self-evident to another because he has acquired it through such means as direct observation, mass transmission, or corroborating indications. People’s powers of apprehension vary beyond any fixed measure. Thus, what is self-evident to one person but not another may likewise become self-evident to the latter through means like those available to the former, without any need for a definition.

The Second Point: “A Definition Yields a Conception of Things”

We say: Discerning scholars of rational inquiry hold that the function of a definition, like that of a name, is to distinguish what is defined from everything else—not to convey a conception of it or make its reality known. This latter claim is made only by the Greek logicians, the followers of Aristotle, and those among Muslim thinkers and others who follow their path in imitation of them. The great majority of those engaged in rational inquiry and theology, whether Muslims or others, hold the contrary view.

This view was introduced only by those who discussed the foundations of religion and jurisprudence after Abū Hāmid, towards the end of the fifth century AH. They were the ones who treated definitions according to the method of Greek logic. Other scholars of rational inquiry, from all the various schools—the Ash'arīs, Mu'tazilīs, Karrāmīs, Shi'a, and others—hold that a definition serves only to distinguish what is defined from everything else. This is well known in the works of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī, Judge Abū Bakr, Abū Ishāq, Ibn Fūrak, Judge Abū Ya'lā, Ibn 'Aqīl, Imām al-Haramayn, al-Nasafī, Abū 'Alī, Abū Hāshim, 'Abd al-Jabbār, al-Tūsī, Muhammad ibn al-Haysam, and others.

Furthermore, there is no doubt that the art of definition described by the logicians is a convention of their own devising. Nations before them knew the realities of things without this convention, and the great majority of nations

Yet they claimed that this art makes the realities of things known, and that these realities cannot be known except through it. Both claims are mistaken.

When they sought to achieve this, they had to distinguish between certain attributes and others. Since they made conception depend on what they deemed essential, they necessarily had to distinguish between what they regarded as essential and what they did not. This led them to distinguish between things that are alike, treating one attribute as essential but not another, although the two were equal or closely similar. Finding a distinction between things that are alike is impossible, and between closely similar things is difficult. What they seek is therefore either impossible or difficult to attain. If it is impossible, their undertaking fails altogether. If it is difficult, then even once attained, it adds nothing to what was already known before attaining it.

Thus, either they cannot meet the condition they have stipulated, or they meet it without achieving their intended aim. In either case, the definition they have devised is not a means of producing a conception of realities in the mind of someone who cannot conceive of them without a definition, although it may serve to distinguish what is defined in the same way that names do.

Fakhr al-Rāzī recognized the position held by the leading scholars of theology and established in his al-Muhassal (Compendium) and elsewhere that conceptions cannot be acquired. This is precisely what we mean when we say that a definition does not yield a conception of what is defined. There are several arguments showing that definitions do not convey conceptions of realities.

First:

A definition is merely the statement and claim of the person framing it. His statement, for example, “The definition of man is a rational animal,” is a declarative proposition and a mere claim unsupported by any proof. Either the listener knows it to be true independently of this statement, or he does not. In the first case, it is established that he did not acquire this knowledge through the definition. In the second case, merely stating something without supporting evidence does not impart knowledge to him. How could it, when he knows that the speaker is not infallible in what he says? Thus, on either assumption, a definition does not impart knowledge of definitions.

If it is said:

“It gives him only a conception of what the term designates, without judging whether this is, for example, the very thing being asked about or something else.”

We reply:

“In that case, it is merely like a single term signifying its meaning—that is, a name signifying what it names.”

This confirms what we have said: a definition signifies in the same way that a name does. A mere name does not give someone a conception of what it names unless he has already conceived it independently of that name. This is undisputed, and the same applies to a definition.

The reply is:

If the person framing the definition has provided no proof of its soundness, the listener cannot come to know what is defined through it, since the person framing it may be mistaken. For if the listener does not know from the speaker’s statement that the definition is sound, and that statement may be true or false, he cannot come to know what is defined through that statement.

It is astonishing that these people claim that these are rational methods yielding certainty. They make knowledge of the simple the foundation of knowledge of the composite, yet place their reliance here on a definition that is merely the unsupported statement of the person framing it. It is a report from a single individual concerning a rational matter, not a sensory one, and admits of correctness and error, truth and falsehood. Then they criticize those who, in matters known through transmission, rely on a single transmitter’s report accompanied by contextual evidence that gives certain knowledge to a listener acquainted with it. They claim that a single transmitter’s report does not impart knowledge. Yet even if such a report does not impart knowledge, this is precisely what their own account of definition amounts to: it is a report from a single individual, with no proof of its truth. Indeed, according to them, no proof of its truth can even be established.

Thus, the definition does not convey a conception of what is defined. If, however, the listener has conceived what is defined before hearing the definition, or conceives it while hearing it or afterwards, independently of the definition, and knows that this is its definition, he knows that the person framing it has defined it truthfully. In that case, the definition has not conveyed the conception. This is clear.

In summary, conceiving what is defined through a definition is impossible without knowing that the statement of the person framing it is true. The truth of his statement cannot be known merely from his assertion. Hence, what is defined cannot be known through the definition.

It is therefore impossible to know the thing defined before knowing that its definition is sound. Yet knowledge of the definition’s soundness can be attained only after knowing what is defined. For a definition is a report about a subject [of the report] (1), namely, what is defined. It is impossible to know that a report is sound and true before conceiving its subject, without uncritically accepting the report and taking the reporter at his word concerning something of which both the reporter and the recipient have knowledge. This is not a case of reporting matters beyond one’s observation.

Fourth:

They define a thing through attributes that they call essential and accidental. They call these the parts of the definition, the parts of the essence, its constitutive elements, those included within it, and similar expressions. If the listener does not know that the thing defined possesses those attributes, he cannot conceive it. If he knows that it possesses them, he has already conceived it without the definition. Thus, in either case, he has not conceived it through the definition. This is clear.

For when it is said, “A human being is a rational animal,” someone who does not know that this is a human being needs to know this relationship. If he has not conceived what “rational animal” denotes, he needs two things: to conceive it and to know the relationship just mentioned. If he knows this, he has already conceived a human being without the definition.

Admittedly, a definition may bring the conception of what is defined to mind, just as a name does. The mind may be inattentive to something; upon hearing its name alone, a person turns his mind towards the thing indicated by the name or definition and conceives it. Thus, the benefit of a definition is of the same kind as that of a name, and definitions of species through their attributes are like boundaries

translated_text:
of individual things by reference to their directions.

For example, when it is said, “The boundary of the land on the side facing the qiblah is such-and-such, and on the eastern side such-and-such,” the land is distinguished by its name and its boundaries. The boundaries of the land are needed when there is a risk of including more or less than the name denotes. They serve to include everything within those boundaries and exclude whatever does not belong, just as the name does. The same applies to the definition of a species. This is achieved sometimes through verbal definitions and sometimes through definitions established by designation. In both cases, a definition merely explains what the name denotes and distinguishes what is defined from other things; it does not produce a conception of what is defined.

Since the purpose of a definition is to explain what a name denotes, and naming is a matter of linguistic convention, reference must be made to the intention and language of the person assigning the name. Hence the jurists say that some names have their limits determined by revealed law, while others have their limits determined by customary usage.

“Interpreting and explaining speech” also belongs here. If this means clarifying the speaker’s intention, it rests on knowing the limits of meaning in his words. If it means demonstrating and establishing the correctness of his words, it requires knowledge of evidence for their correctness.

The former involves clarifying the conception conveyed by his words, or conveying a conception of his words so as to convey, through translation, a conception of what the names denote. Sometimes this is for someone who has already conceived what is named but does not know that this is its name; at other times, it is for someone who has not yet conceived what is named. In that case, what is named is indicated as far as possible, either by pointing to the thing itself or to something analogous to it.

Hence it is said that a definition is sometimes of the name and sometimes of what is named. The leading authors who write on the art of definition according to the method of the logicians acknowledge, upon

translated_text:
closer examination, that definitions serve the same kind of purpose as names and amount to rendering one expression by another. Al-Ghazālī states this in al-Mi‘yār (The Criterion), which he composed on logic; it is likewise found in the writings of Ibn Sīnā, al-Rāzī, al-Suhrawardī, and others.

Explaining unfamiliar vocabulary in the Quran, hadith, and other texts belongs to this category. Indeed, interpreting the Quran and other forms of discourse belongs, at its most basic level, to this category, since the purpose is to explain what the speaker intends by those terms and that discourse. They agree that this kind of definition is a verbal definition. Yet this is precisely what is needed when teaching the sciences set out in written works—indeed, when reading any book, and in every kind of communication. Anyone reading books on grammar, medicine, or other subjects must know what their authors intend by those terms and by the statements composed of them. The same applies to anyone reading books on jurisprudence, speculative theology, philosophy, or other subjects.

Knowing these definitions is a matter of religion with respect to every expression found in the Book of Allah Most High and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Such knowledge may be an individual obligation or a collective obligation. Hence Allah Most High censures those who do not know these limits of meaning, saying:

“The Bedouins are stronger in disbelief and hypocrisy and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.”

What He revealed to His Messenger includes terms that may be “unfamiliar” to the listener, such as dīzā (unfair), qaswarah (a lion or hunters), ‘as‘asa (to fall or recede, of night), and similar expressions. A term may also be “familiar,” yet its precise limits remain unknown, while its meaning is understood only in general terms—as with the terms prayer, zakat, fasting, and Hajj.

translated_text:
Thus it is clear that a thing can be made known only through acquaintance with the thing itself or something resembling it. Whoever knows the thing itself has no need of a definition to know it. Whoever does not know it can come to know it through a definition only if he knows something resembling it, even if only in certain respects. Similar attributes shared by it and other things are then combined for him in a way that uniquely identifies the thing being defined. Whoever examines this closely will recognize its truth and understand how people know what they have been told about the unseen: the angels, the Last Day, and the various kinds of bliss and torment in Paradise and Hell. Their account of definition is thereby invalidated.

(Fifth: Simple conceptions cannot be sought and therefore cannot be acquired through definition. For if the mind is already aware of them, seeking them is impossible, since acquiring what has already been acquired is impossible. If it is unaware of them, the soul cannot seek that of which it is unaware, for seeking and intending presuppose awareness.

If it is said: “Yet a person seeks to conceive of angels, jinn, the spirit, and many other things of which he is unaware.”

The reply is: He has heard these names and seeks to conceive of what they denote, just as someone who hears expressions whose meanings he does not understand seeks to conceive of their meanings. When he conceives of what these names denote, he must also know that it is designated by the corresponding name. For if he conceived of a reality without that name being included in the conception, he would not have conceived of what he sought. Here, then, what is conceived is an entity together with the fact that it is designated by such-and-such a name. This is not a conception of the meaning alone, but of both the meaning and its name. There is no doubt that this can be sought. It does not follow, however, that the meaning taken on its own can be sought.

translated_text:
Moreover, what is sought here cannot be attained through definition alone. Rather, the thing being defined must be made known by pointing to it or by some other means for which words alone do not suffice. Once it is established that simple conceptions cannot be sought, either a person already possesses them—in which case they are not acquired through definition, and definition therefore supplies no conception—or he does not possess them, in which case definition alone does not enable him to conceive of the things named when he does not know them. Whenever he has some awareness of them, he needs a definition for that awareness only in the same way that he needs a name. The point is to establish that a definition and a name serve the same purpose.

(Sixth): It may be said: According to them, what enables one to conceive of a reality is the general definition composed of essential, rather than accidental, attributes. This account rests on the distinction between the essential and the accidental. They say that the essential is what falls within the essence, while the accidental is what lies outside it. They divide the latter into what necessarily accompanies the essence and what necessarily accompanies its existence.

This account rests on two unsound principles: the distinction between an essence and its existence, and then the distinction between what is essential to it and what necessarily accompanies it.

(The first principle is their claim that an essence has an established reality outside the mind distinct from its existence. The truth is that all of this is established in the mind. What can be conceived in the mind is broader than what actually exists outside it. It exists and is established in the mind; it is not, in fact, devoid of both existence and established reality. Thus, distinguishing between existence and established reality, or between existence and essence, while claiming that both are outside the mind, is a grave error.

These people supposed that the realities of species, such as the reality of the human being, the horse, and the like, were established outside the mind, distinct from the individual entities existing there, and that they were without beginning and incapable of change. These are what are called “Platonic Forms.” Nor did they stop there: they also asserted the same concerning matter, essence, and place. They posited matter stripped of forms, established outside the mind: this is the prime matter on which they based their doctrine of the eternity of the world. The majority of rational thinkers judged them mistaken on this point.

The views of those who distinguish between existence and essence are discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is to draw attention to the fact that the distinction they make in logic between an essence and its existence outside the mind rests on this unsound principle. The proper distinction is that essence is the impression of a thing formed in the mind, whereas existence is what there is of that thing outside the mind,

The “second principle”—the distinction between what necessarily accompanies an essence and what is essential to it—has no basis in reality. For if an essence outside the mind is taken to be stripped of its inseparable attributes, then existence outside the mind can likewise be taken to be stripped of these inseparable attributes. If, on the other hand, this is taken to be the essence itself together with its inseparable attributes, that is equivalent to saying: this is “existence together with its inseparable attributes.” Both are invalid. Evenness and oddness in a number, for example, are like being an animal and being rational in a human being. In either case, when the subject is brought to mind together with its attribute, the subject cannot be conceived without that attribute.

The second ground:

Whether an attribute is essential to its subject is determined by the reality that makes that subject what it is, whether our minds conceive it or not. Thus, if one of two attributes is essential while the other is not, the difference between them must arise from their external reality, which exists independently of the mind. For there to be something among external realities whose reality consists solely in precedence or posteriority in the mind would be possible only if reality and essence were what is posited in the mind, rather than what exists outside it. That, however, depends on what the individual mind supposes. The substance of this argument would then amount to things posited in minds that have no external reality: groundless imaginings and suppositions. This is common in their fundamental principles.

If they do, they must include all the attributes. If they do not, and deem the proximate genus alone sufficient, this is sheer arbitrariness. Tenth:

Disputes arise among them in this field that cannot be resolved on this basis. Whatever entails an equal balance of opposing proofs is false.

Section

Their statement, “No propositional judgment can be known except through the syllogism”—the one whose form and matter they have described—is a negative proposition that is not self-evidently known. They have offered no proof whatsoever for it. They have thus asserted what they have not established and spoken without knowledge. Indeed, knowledge of this negation is unattainable on their own principles. How, then, do they know that no human being can know any propositional judgment that they do not regard as self-evident except through the logical syllogism based on subsumption whose matter and form they have described?

translated_text:
Moreover, they acknowledge what must necessarily be admitted: some propositional judgments are self-evident, while others are inferential. They cannot all be inferential, since inferential knowledge depends on what is self-evident. The point previously made concerning conceptions therefore applies here: the distinction between the two is relative, depending on the person. What requires inference for one person may be self-evident to another.

A self-evident propositional judgment is one in which conceiving its two terms—its subject and predicate—is sufficient to assent to it. It does not depend on anything mediating between them, namely, the proof constituted by the middle term. This holds whether or not the conceptions of the two terms are themselves self-evident. It is well known that people differ in mental capacity far more than they differ in physical strength. Some attain such speed and precision in forming conceptions that they far surpass others. Such a person may conceive both terms so fully that this complete conception makes implications apparent which remain unclear to someone who has not conceived them in this way.

It is evident that, for certain propositions, some people may need the mediating term that constitutes the proof, while others do not. Many people know a proposition through sensory perception, experience, demonstration, or mass transmission, whereas someone else comes to know it only through reasoning and inference. Thus, many people need proof that the predicate holds of the subject not for themselves, but for others. They explain this to others using proofs they themselves do not need, even providing illustrative examples.

translated_text:
The logicians have stated that propositions known through mass transmission, experience, and the senses are confined to those who know them and do not constitute proof against anyone else, unlike other propositions, which are shared and may be used as proof against an opponent. This distinction is false and is one of the foundations of irreligion and disbelief. For, concerning miracles and other matters transmitted from the prophets through mass transmission, one of these people says, on the basis of this distinction: “This has not reached me through mass transmission, so it constitutes no binding proof against me.” Yet that is not a prerequisite.

This also includes the denial, by many adherents of religious innovation, speculative theology, and philosophy, of prophetic reports known to hadith scholars. They say, “These are not known to us,” just as some disbelievers say that the prophets’ miracles are not known to them. This is because they have not become acquainted with the means that necessarily yield knowledge of these matters. Nevertheless, the proof is binding upon them, whether or not these reports have reached them through mass transmission.

The philosophers who practise logic have embraced ignorant notions, such as their claim that the angels are the ten intellects, that they are eternal and without beginning, and that the intellect is the lord of everything other than itself. No Jew, Christian, or Arab polytheist has ever said anything like this. None has ever said that an angel is the lord of the entire world. They also say that the active intellect is the originator of everything beneath the lunar sphere. This, too, is disbelief that none of the disbelievers among the People of the Book or the Arab polytheists has ever reached.

They also say that the Lord does not act by His will and power, does not know particulars, and cannot change the world; rather, the world is an emanation that has flowed from Him without His will, power, or knowledge

 سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ حِسِّيَّةً ظَاهِرَةً أَوْ بَاطِنَةً وَهِيَ الَّتِي يُحِسُّهَا بِنَفْسِهِ أَوْ كَانَتْ مِنْ التَّجْرِيبِيَّاتِ أَوْ الْمُتَوَاتِرَاتِ أَوْ الْحَدْسِيَّاتِ عِنْدَ مَنْ يَجْعَلُ مِنْهَا مَا هُوَ مِنْ النَّفْسِيَّاتِ الْوَاجِبِ قَبُولُهَا مِثْلَ الْعِلْمِ بِكَوْنِ نُورِ الْقَمَرِ مُسْتَفَادًا مِنْ الشَّمْسِ إذَا رَأَى اخْتِلَافَ أَشْكَالِهِ عِنْدَ اخْتِلَافِ مُحَاذَاتِهِ لِلشَّمْسِ كَمَا يَخْتَلِفُ إذَا قَارَبَهَا بَعْدَ الِاجْتِمَاعِ كَمَا فِي لَيْلَةِ الْهِلَالِ وَإِذَا كَانَ لَيْلَةَ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ عِنْدَ الْإِبْدَارِ.
 وَهُمْ مُتَنَازِعُونَ:
 هَلْ الْحَدْسُ قَدْ يُفِيدُ الْيَقِينَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَمِثْلَ الْعَقْلِيَّاتِ الْمَحْضَةِ وَمِثْلَ قَوْلِنَا الْوَاحِدُ نِصْفُ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَالْكُلُّ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ الْجُزْءِ
original_footnote:

(التسلسل في المتوترات) تصحيف، والصواب: (التسلسل في المؤثرات) كما هو المعروف، وكما هو في الأصل (من الرد على المنطقيين) ١/ ١٢٠.
translated_text:
then the response is:

If everything they call a demonstration must contain a universal proposition, that universal proposition must be known—that is, its universality must be known. Otherwise, whenever it is admitted that it might be particular rather than universal, knowledge of what follows from it cannot be attained. An unquantified or unrestricted proposition whose wording permits either a universal or a particular interpretation has the force of a particular proposition.

If the knowledge obtained through the syllogism to which they reserve the name “demonstration” necessarily requires knowledge of a universal affirmative proposition, the response is this: if knowledge of that proposition is self-evident, then knowledge of each particular instance falling under it can, with even greater reason, be self-evident. If it is inferential, it requires self-evident knowledge, leading to intractable circularity or [an infinite regress in mass-transmitted reports] (*), both of which are invalid.

The same applies to all the other universal propositions they make the starting points of demonstration and call “those that must be accepted.” These may be propositions derived from external or internal sensation—the latter being what a person perceives within himself—or propositions based on experience, mass-transmitted reports, or intuition, according to those who count some intuitive propositions among the soul’s apprehensions that must be accepted. An example is knowing that the moon derives its light from the sun by observing how its phases change as its alignment with the sun changes: its appearance when it is close to the sun after conjunction, as on the night of the new crescent, differs from its appearance on the night of opposition, when it is full.

They disagree, however, over whether intuition can yield certainty.

The same applies to purely rational propositions, such as our statements that one is half of two and that the whole is greater than the part

“Al-tasalsul fī al-mutawattirāt” is a textual corruption. The correct reading is “al-tasalsul fī al-mu’aththirāt” (infinite regress of causes), as is well known and as found in the original text, al-Radd ‘alā al-mantiqiyyīn (Refutation of the Logicians), 1:120.

original_text: وَالْأَشْيَاءُ الْمُسَاوِيَةُ لِشَيْءِ وَاحِدٍ مُتَسَاوِيَةٌ وَالضِّدَّانِ لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ وَالنَّقِيضَانِ لَا يَرْتَفِعَانِ وَلَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ فَمَا مِنْ قَضِيَّةٍ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْقَضَايَا الْكُلِّيَّةِ تُجْعَلُ مُقَدِّمَةً فِي الْبُرْهَانِ إلَّا وَالْعِلْمُ بِالنَّتِيجَةِ مُمْكِنٌ بِدُونِ تَوَسُّطِ ذَلِكَ الْبُرْهَانِ بَلْ هُوَ الْوَاقِعُ كَثِيرًا. فَإِذَا عُلِمَ أَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ فَهُوَ نِصْفُ كُلِّ اثْنَيْنِ وَأَنَّ كُلَّ اثْنَيْنِ نِصْفُهُمْ وَاحِدٌ فَإِنَّهُ يُعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْوَاحِدَ نِصْفُ هَذَيْنَ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَهَلُمَّ جَرًّا فِي سَائِرِ الْقَضَايَا الْأُخَرِ مِنْ غَيْرِ اسْتِدْلَالٍ عَلَى ذَلِكَ بِالْقَضِيَّةِ الْكُلِّيَّةِ. وَكَذَلِكَ كُلُّ جُزْءٍ يُعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْكُلَّ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ جُزْئِهِ بِدُونِ تَوَسُّطِ الْقَضِيَّةِ الْكُلِّيَّةِ. وَكَذَلِكَ هَذَانِ النَّقِيضَانِ مَنْ تَصَوَّرَهُمَا نَقِيضَيْنِ فَإِنَّهُ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُمَا لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ. وَكُلُّ أَحَدٍ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْمُعَيَّنَ لَا يَكُونُ مَوْجُودًا مَعْدُومًا كَمَا يَعْلَمُ الْمُعَيَّنَ الْآخَرَ وَلَا يَحْتَاجُ ذَلِكَ إلَى أَنْ يُسْتَدَلَّ عَلَيْهِ بِأَنَّ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ لَا يَكُونُ مَوْجُودًا مَعْدُومًا مَعًا وَكَذَلِكَ الضِّدَّانِ فَإِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الشَّيْءَ لَا يَكُونُ أَسْوَدَ أَبْيَضَ وَلَا يَكُونُ مُتَحَرِّكًا سَاكِنًا كَمَا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْآخَرَ كَذَلِكَ. وَلَا يَحْتَاجُ فِي الْعِلْمِ بِذَلِكَ إلَى قَضِيَّةٍ كُلِّيَّةٍ بِأَنَّ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ لَا يَكُونُ أَسْوَدَ أَبْيَضَ وَلَا يَكُونُ مُتَحَرِّكًا سَاكِنًا. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي سَائِرِ مَا يَعْلَمُ تَضَادَّهُمَا فَإِنْ عَلِمَ تَضَادَّ الْمُعَيَّنَيْنِ عَلِمَ أَنَّهُمَا لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِالْقَضِيَّةِ الْكُلِّيَّةِ يُفِيدُ الْعِلْمَ بِالْمُقَدِّمَةِ الْكُبْرَى الْمُشْتَمِلَةِ عَلَى الْحَدِّ الْأَكْبَرِ. وَذَلِكَ لَا يُغْنِي دُونَ الْعِلْمِ بِالْمُقَدِّمَةِ الصُّغْرَى الْمُشْتَمِلَةِ عَلَى الْحَدِّ الْأَصْغَرِ وَالْعِلْمِ بِالنَّتِيجَةِ وَهُوَ أَنَّ هَذَيْنِ الْمَعْنَيَيْنِ ضِدَّانِ فَلَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ يُمْكِنُ بِدُونِ الْعِلْمِ
translated_text:
and that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another, that two contraries cannot coexist, and that two contradictories can neither both be false nor both be true. There is no universal proposition of this kind used as a premise in a demonstration whose conclusion cannot be known without that demonstration as an intermediary. Indeed, this frequently occurs.

Thus, if it is known that every unit is half of any two units, and that half of any two units is one unit, then it is known that this particular unit is half of these particular two units, without inferring this from the universal proposition. The same applies to all the other propositions. Likewise, with any part, one knows that this particular whole is greater than its part without recourse to the universal proposition. Similarly, whoever conceives of two particular contradictories as contradictories knows that they cannot coexist.

Everyone knows that this particular thing cannot both exist and not exist, just as he knows this of another particular thing. This does not require an inference from the proposition that nothing can both exist and not exist. The same applies to contraries: a person knows that this thing cannot be both black and white, or both moving and at rest, just as he knows the same of another thing. To know this, he does not need a universal proposition stating that nothing can be both black and white, or both moving and at rest.

The same applies to every other pair known to be contraries: if one knows that two particular things are contraries, one knows that they cannot coexist. Knowledge of the universal proposition yields knowledge of the major premise, which contains the major term. Yet this does not suffice without knowledge of the minor premise, which contains the minor term. Knowledge of the conclusion—that these two notions are contraries and therefore cannot coexist—is possible without knowledge of

original_text:
بِالْمُقَدِّمَةِ الْكُبْرَى:
 وَهُوَ أَنَّ كُلَّ ضِدَّيْنِ لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ. فَلَا يَفْتَقِرُ الْعِلْمُ بِذَلِكَ إلَى الْقِيَاسِ الَّذِي خَصُّوهُ بِاسْمِ الْبُرْهَانِ وَإِنْ كَانَ الْبُرْهَانُ فِي كَلَامِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَكَلَامِ سَائِرِ أَصْنَافِ الْعُلَمَاءِ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِمَا سَمَّوْهُ هُمْ الْبُرْهَانَ؛ وَإِنَّمَا خَصُّوا هُمْ لَفْظَ الْبُرْهَانِ بِمَا اشْتَمَلَ عَلَيْهِ الْقِيَاسُ الَّذِي خَصُّوا صُورَتَهُ وَمَادَّتَهُ بِمَا ذَكَرُوهُ.
 مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ:
 أَنَّهُ إذَا أُرِيدَ إبْطَالُ قَوْلِ مَنْ يُثْبِتُ الْأَحْوَالَ وَيَقُولُ: إنَّهَا لَا مَوْجُودَةٌ وَلَا مَعْدُومَةٌ فَقِيلَ: هَذَانِ نَقِيضَانِ وَكُلُّ نَقِيضَيْنِ لَا يَجْتَمِعَانِ وَلَا يَرْتَفِعَانِ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذَا جَعْلٌ لِلْوَاحِدِ لَا مَوْجُودًا وَلَا مَعْدُومًا وَلَا يُمْكِنُ جَعْلُ الْحَالِ لِلْوَاحِدِ لَا مَوْجُودَةً وَلَا مَعْدُومَةً كَانَ الْعِلْمُ بِأَنَّ هَذَا الْمُعَيَّنَ لَا يَكُونُ مَوْجُودًا مَعْدُومًا مُمْكِنًا بِدُونِ هَذِهِ الْقَضِيَّةِ الْكُلِّيَّةِ فَلَا يَفْتَقِرُ الْعِلْمُ بِالنَّتِيجَةِ إلَى الْبُرْهَانِ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قِيلَ:
 إنَّ هَذَا مُمْكِنٌ وَكُلُّ مُمْكِنٍ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُرَجِّحٍ لِوُجُودِهِ عَلَى عَدَمِهِ عَلَى أَصَحِّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ أَوْ لِأَحَدِ طَرَفَيْهِ عَلَى قَوْلِ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ.
 أَوْ قِيلَ:
 هَذَا مُحْدَثٌ وَكُلُّ مُحْدَثٍ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُحْدِثٍ فَتِلْكَ الْقَضِيَّةُ الْكُلِّيَّةُ وَهِيَ قَوْلُنَا: كُلُّ مُحْدَثٍ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُحْدِثٍ وَكُلُّ مُمْكِنٍ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُرَجِّحٍ يُمْكِنُ الْعِلْمُ بِأَفْرَادِهَا الْمَطْلُوبَةِ بِالْقِيَاسِ الْبُرْهَانِيِّ عِنْدَهُمْ بِدُونِ الْعِلْمِ
translated_text:
the major premise—namely, that no two contraries can coexist. Knowledge of this therefore does not require the syllogism to which they have reserved the name “demonstration.” Yet in the speech of Allah and His Messenger, and in the discourse of scholars of all kinds, demonstration is not restricted to what they call demonstration. Rather, they themselves have restricted the term to what is contained in a syllogism whose form and matter they have limited in the manner they describe.

For example, suppose one wishes to refute those who affirm states and say that they are neither existent nor nonexistent. One might argue: “These are two contradictories, and two contradictories can neither both be true nor both be false. This makes one and the same thing neither existent nor nonexistent, and the state of a single thing cannot be regarded as neither existent nor nonexistent.” It is nevertheless possible to know that this particular thing cannot be both existent and nonexistent without knowing this universal proposition. Knowledge of the conclusion therefore does not require demonstration.

Likewise, one might say: “This is contingent, and every contingent thing must have a factor determining its existence rather than its nonexistence, according to the sounder of the two views—or determining one of its two alternatives, according to some people.”

Or one might say: “This has come into existence, and whatever has come into existence must have an originator.” That universal proposition—namely, our statement that everything that has come into existence must have an originator, and that every contingent thing must have a determining factor—has particular instances which they seek to establish through demonstrative syllogism, although these can be known without knowledge of

original_text:
بِالْقَضِيَّةِ الْكُلِّيَّةِ الَّتِي لَا يَتِمُّ الْبُرْهَانُ عِنْدَهُمْ إلَّا بِهَا فَيُعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْحَدَثَ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُحْدِثٍ وَهَذَا الْمُمْكِنُ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُرَجِّحٍ؛ فَإِنْ شَكَّ عَقْلُهُ وَجَوَّزَ أَنْ يُحْدِثَ هُوَ بِلَا مُحْدَثٍ أَحْدَثَهُ أَوْ أَنْ يَكُونَ وَهُوَ مُمْكِنٌ - يَقْبَلُ الْوُجُودَ وَالْعَدَمَ - بِدُونِ مُرَجِّحٍ يُرَجِّحُ وُجُودَهُ جُوِّزَ ذَلِكَ فِي غَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْمُحْدَثَاتِ وَالْمُمْكِنَاتِ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى؛ وَإِنْ جَزَمَ بِذَلِكَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَمْ يَحْتَجْ عِلْمُهُ بِالنَّتِيجَةِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ -
 وَهُوَ قَوْلُنَا:
 وَهَذَا مُحْدَثٌ فَلَهُ مُحْدِثٌ أَوْ هَذَا مُمْكِنٌ فَلَهُ مُرَجِّحٌ - إلَى الْقِيَاسِ الْبُرْهَانِيِّ.
 وَمِمَّا يُوضِحُ هَذَا:
