 وَبَيَّنَّا تَخْطِئَةَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُقَلَاءِ لِمَنْ قَالَ:

Thus, one can know that this occurrence must have an originator and that this contingent thing must have a determining factor. If his reason doubts this and allows that he himself could come into being without an originator who brought him into being, or could exist—despite being contingent, admitting both existence and nonexistence—without a factor determining his existence, then the same possibility would apply all the more readily to other originated and contingent things. But if he is certain of this in his own case, his knowledge of the particular conclusion—namely, “This has come into existence, so it has an originator,” or “This is contingent, so it has a determining factor”—does not require a demonstrative syllogism.

This is further clarified by the following: you will find no human being seeking to establish a conclusion through reasoning and to prove it by a demonstrative syllogism whose validity he knows who could not know that conclusion without that logical demonstrative syllogism. Hence, among all other kinds of rational people, you will find no one who constructs his argument from two premises as these people do. Rather, they state the evidence that entails the conclusion. That evidence may consist of one premise, two premises, or three premises, according to the needs of the person reasoning and drawing the inference, for people’s needs differ. We have discussed this at length in our discussion of al-Muhassal.

We have also explained how the majority of rational people judge mistaken those who maintain that every instance of knowledge acquired through reasoning necessarily requires two premises, neither of which can be dispensed with, and that no more than two are needed. You should examine this using rational subject matter that is not established by the texts of the prophets, for this exposes the invalidity of their logic. the nabīdh (a steeped drink) whose ruling is disputed, saying: “Nabīdh is intoxicating, and every intoxicant is forbidden,” or: “It is wine, and all wine is forbidden.”

Our statement, “Intoxicating nabīdh is wine,” is known from the revealed text, namely the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every intoxicant is wine.”

Our statement, “All wine is forbidden,” is known from the revealed texts and scholarly consensus. There is no dispute about this; the dispute concerns only the minor premise. It is established in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and all wine is forbidden.”

Another wording reads:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Some people may suppose that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated this in the form prescribed by logic, to demonstrate the conclusion through two premises, as logicians do. Such a supposition betrays great ignorance. His standing, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is far above employing such a method to impart knowledge. Indeed, even those inferior in reason and knowledge to individual scholars of his community would not accept following the method of these logicians. Rather, they regard them as ignorant people proficient only in practical disciplines such as arithmetic, medicine, and the like. As for the universal demonstrative sciences that yield certainty, and the sciences concerning God, they were not qualified practitioners of them. Muslim scholars of rational inquiry have explained this in their books and discussed these people at length.

The point is that Muslims already know that all wine is forbidden, so they have no need to learn this through a syllogism. Some of them were uncertain only about particular kinds of intoxicating drinks, such as nabīdh made from honey, grains, and other ingredients, as reported in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Thus, he answered them, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with a universal proposition explaining that everything that intoxicates is forbidden. He also explained that everything that intoxicates is wine. These are two true, concordant universal propositions. Knowing either one entails knowing that every intoxicant is forbidden; knowing that every intoxicant is forbidden does not depend on knowing both propositions together.

For anyone who believes in the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and knows that he said, “Every intoxicant is forbidden,” knows that intoxicating nabīdh is forbidden. Doubt may nevertheless arise over whether he meant an intoxicating quantity or intoxicants as a category. This is uncertainty about the meaning of his statement. Once the person understands what he intended, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he knows the conclusion sought. The same applies if he knows that nabīdh is wine. Knowing this establishes its prohibition even more firmly, for those who permit the disputed nabīdh do not call it wine. Once a person knows from the revealed text that “Every intoxicant is wine,” this alone constitutes proof that every intoxicant is forbidden for believers who know that wine is forbidden.

As for someone who does not know that wine is forbidden because he does not believe in the Messenger, the Prophet’s words cannot serve as proof for him. If, however, he knows that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah but does not know that he prohibited wine, the statement “Every intoxicant is wine” does not benefit him. the Lawgiver. According to the majority of scholars, who prohibit every intoxicant, the two terms are coextensive in his usage, in both their general and particular applications. The purpose here is not to establish “the legal question,” but to draw attention to the example, for Muslim scholars who have written on logic frequently use it.

Logicians give examples using a form stripped of its subject matter, signifying nothing specific, so that knowledge of the example is not derived from a concrete instance. Thus they say:

Every A is B, and every B is C.
Therefore, every A is C.

Yet the aim is to obtain the knowledge sought concerning specific subject matter. When that subject matter is removed, someone may suppose that this procedure is necessary in particular cases. This is not so. Rather, when they are asked to establish knowledge of the two universal premises in all their rational inquiries not derived from those protected from error, you find them appealing to evidence that also makes it possible to know the particulars under investigation without knowing the universal proposition. Knowledge of those particulars therefore does not depend on demonstration.

Propositions conveyed by the prophets do not require the rational syllogism that they call demonstration. Nor does knowledge acquired through reason require their demonstrative syllogism. It is therefore needed neither in matters known through revelation nor in those known through reason. Hence, it cannot be maintained that knowledge is acquired only through the demonstrative syllogism they describe.

A further clarification is that propositions based on sense perception can only be particular. Through our senses, we have perceived only the burning caused by this fire and that fire; we have not perceived that every fire burns. If it is said:

“Knowledge of particular things is not what is intended, for demonstration yields only knowledge of a universal proposition. Conclusions known through demonstration can therefore only be universal, as they themselves maintain. Universals, however, are universal only in the mind, not in external reality.”

The reply is:

On this assumption, demonstration yields no knowledge of anything that exists, but only of things conceived in the mind whose realization in external reality is unknown. If demonstration provides no knowledge of anything that exists, it is of very little benefit—indeed, of no benefit at all. Yet they do not maintain this; rather, they use it to acquire knowledge of external and metaphysical realities. The truth of the matter, however, as we have explained elsewhere, is that inquiries in natural philosophy which concern not necessary universals but generalizations holding for the most part do not achieve the intended purpose of demonstration.

Then he said:

“Dependence is a negative attribute, so I am dying without having come to know anything.”

They also related a similar account to us about another of their distinguished scholars. Anyone familiar with them knows this, and knows that they are the most ignorant people on earth concerning the methods by which rational and transmitted knowledge are acquired—except those among them who have acquired knowledge through methods other than those of logic. Their knowledge comes from those other sources, not from their logical methods, despite all their toil over the demonstration by which they claim to assess knowledge. Whatever knowledge any of them has acquired did not come through what they have elaborated in logic.

Another point showing that certain knowledge, whether universal or particular, does not depend on their demonstration based on a universal proposition is that knowledge of that universal proposition must itself have a source. If they know it by inferring the unobserved from the observed, on the principle that the same judgment applies to a thing and to its like—as when we know that this fire burns, and therefore that an unobserved fire burns because it is like this one, and the same judgment applies to a thing and to its like—then the reply is: this is reasoning by analogy, which they claim yields not certainty but only conjecture. If, therefore, they have come to know the universal proposition only through analogy, they have based their certainty on what they themselves say yields only conjecture.

If they say:

“Rather, when particulars are perceived through the senses, universal knowledge arises in the soul from the Giver of Intellect—or, upon perceiving particulars through the senses, the soul becomes disposed to receive the universal emanating upon it from the Giver of Intellect.”

Or if they say that it comes from what they call the “Active Intellect,” or something similar, they are told: the question here is how it is known that the universal judgment in the soul constitutes knowledge, rather than conjecture or ignorance.

translated_text:
If they say, “This knowledge is self-evident or necessary,” this amounts to saying that these universal propositions are known self-evidently and necessarily, and that the soul cannot help knowing them. If this is true, then knowledge of particular entities and the various kinds of universals also arises in the soul self-evidently and necessarily—as indeed happens. For rational people are more certain about individual objects of sense perception than about universals, and more certain about universal propositions concerning species than those concerning genera. Knowledge of particulars reaches the natural disposition first, so its certainty about them is stronger.

As the intellect grows stronger, the scope of its universals broadens. Accordingly, one cannot say that knowledge of individuals depends on knowledge of species and genera, or that knowledge of species depends on knowledge of genera. Rather, a person may know that he himself is capable of sensation and voluntary movement before knowing that every human being is so; and he may know that human beings are so before knowing that every animal is so. Thus, his knowledge that other animals are capable of sensation and voluntary movement does not depend on demonstration.

When he knows that this judgment applies to all other people and animals, the soul arrives at that judgment through knowing that the unobserved is like the observed, or that it shares with it the cause that necessarily entails its capacity for sensation and voluntary movement, and through similar forms of analogical and causal reasoning used by jurists to establish rulings of Islamic law. Yet these people claim that such reasoning yields only conjecture, whereas their own syllogism yields certainty. translated_text:
analogical reasoning and syllogistic reasoning are equivalent, differing only in the particular material employed. If that material yields certainty in one, it yields certainty in the other; if it yields conjecture in one, it yields conjecture in the other. Syllogistic reasoning consists of three terms: the minor, the middle, and the major. Its middle term is what, in analogical reasoning, is called the effective cause, the basis of the ruling, and the common attribute.

Thus, concerning nabīdh, someone may say: “Every nabīdh is intoxicating, and every intoxicant is forbidden.” He must establish the major premise; only then is the demonstration complete. He can then say: “Nabīdh is intoxicating, so it is forbidden by analogy with grape wine, because both share the property of causing intoxication.” Intoxication is the basis of the prohibition in the original case, and it is also present in the case under consideration. The same evidence that establishes that every intoxicant is forbidden establishes, with even greater force, that intoxication is the basis of the prohibition. Indeed, making distinctions in analogical reasoning is easier for him, since the original case provides evidence for prohibition, and the ruling is therefore already known to hold in some particular instances.

In analogical reasoning, it is not enough to establish the ruling in one of the two cases on the grounds that it holds in the other merely because they share an attribute for which no evidence has established that it entails the ruling—as some mistakenly suppose. Rather, it must be known that their shared attribute entails the ruling; and this shared attribute is the middle term. Jurists and scholars of the principles of jurisprudence call this “the demand to establish the attribute’s effect on the ruling.” This is the most significant objection raised against an analogy, and answering it is generally what is needed

translated_text:
in assessing the validity of the analogy. An objector may deny that the attribute exists in the original case, deny the ruling in the original case, deny that the attribute exists in the case under consideration, or deny that the attribute is the effective cause of the ruling. He may say:

“We do not grant that the shared attribute you have mentioned is the effective cause or an indication of that cause.”

There must therefore be evidence establishing this: a text, consensus, enumeration and elimination, suitability, or concomitance—where such reasoning is accepted as evidence. Whatever establishes that the shared attribute entails the ruling, whether as its effective cause or as an indication of that cause, also establishes that the middle term entails the major term, and thus establishes the validity of the major premise. If it establishes the effective cause, it is a causal demonstration; if it establishes an indication of that cause, it is a demonstration from an indication. If it yields only conjecture rather than certain knowledge, then the major premise in that syllogism likewise remains merely conjectural. This is clear. Hence many jurists have come to employ syllogistic reasoning in jurisprudence, just as analogical reasoning is employed in rational inquiries. The essential nature of the one is the same as that of the other.

Some later proponents of speculative theology and reasoned opinion, such as Abū al-Maʿālī, Abū Hāmid, al-Rāzī, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and others, maintain that analogy has no place in rational matters, but applies only to matters of religious law; in rational matters, however, reliance is on evidence that establishes the conclusion, without restriction. Their position contradicts that of Muslim rational thinkers—indeed, that of all other people of reason. For analogy is used as evidence in rational matters just as it is in matters of religious law. وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فِي مُسَمَّى 
" الْقِيَاسِ "
.
 فَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْأُصُولِ:
 هُوَ حَقِيقَةٌ فِي قِيَاسِ التَّمْثِيلِ مَجَازٌ فِي قِيَاسِ الشُّمُولِ - كَأَبِي حَامِدٍ الْغَزَالِيِّ وَأَبِي حَامِدٍ المقدسي.
 وَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ:
 بَلْ هُوَ بِالْعَكْسِ حَقِيقَةٌ فِي الشُّمُولِ مَجَازٌ فِي التَّمْثِيلِ -
translated_text:
evidence in every field of knowledge. Likewise, if it is established that there is no relevant difference between the case under consideration and the original case, this constitutes evidence in every field of knowledge. Wherever analogical reasoning cannot serve as evidence, neither can syllogistic reasoning. Abū al-Ma'ālī and the speculative thinkers before him neither follow nor approve of the logicians’ method. Rather, they reason from evidence which, in their view, entails its conclusions.

Nevertheless, the logicians and most speculative thinkers draw analogies between the unobserved and the observed whenever the shared attribute entails the ruling. Their examples include linking the two through a common definition, cause, condition, or evidence. Their opponents say:

“The ruling is not established for the unobserved because it is established for the observed. Rather, the universal proposition itself suffices to establish the point, without any need for analogy.”

The answer to them is:

“The same applies in matters of religious law. Whenever evidence establishes that the ruling is tied to the shared attribute, there is no need for the original case. The evidence establishing that the ruling is tied to that attribute is itself sufficient. Yet because this is universal, and a universal exists only in particular instances, identifying the original case provides a means of knowing that this universal is actually instantiated. This is useful in both legal and rational matters.”

Thus you know that whenever evidence establishes that the shared attribute is the basis of the ruling, or that the difference between the original case and the case under consideration is irrelevant, the analogy is sound and constitutes valid evidence, whatever its subject.

People have differed over what the term “qiyās” denotes. One group of scholars of legal theory, including Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī and Abū Hāmid al-Maqdisī, maintains that it applies literally to analogical reasoning and figuratively to syllogistic reasoning. Another group maintains the reverse: it applies literally to syllogistic reasoning and figuratively to analogical reasoning—

translated_text:
as maintained by Ibn Hazm and others. The majority of scholars, however, hold that the term applies literally to both, and that rational inference encompasses them both. This is the position of most who have written on the foundations of religion, legal theory, and the various rational sciences. It is the correct view, for the essential nature of the two is the same; only the form of inference differs.

In its linguistic sense, “qiyās” means measuring one thing against another. This includes measuring a particular thing against another particular like it, and measuring it against a universal that encompasses both it and others like it. For a universal is a mental representation of its particulars; hence it corresponds to and agrees with the particular.

“Syllogistic reasoning” is the mind’s passage from a particular to the general, shared universal concept encompassing both it and other particulars, and its judging that particular according to what necessarily follows from the shared universal. It does so by passing from that necessarily entailed universal back to the original particular that entails it. Thus, it is a passage from the specific to the general, then from that general back to the specific: from a particular to a universal, then from that universal back to the original particular, of which that universal is then predicated.

For this reason, the evidence is more specific than what it establishes, namely the judgment. The existence of the evidence necessarily entails the existence of the judgment, and what is entailed cannot be more specific than what entails it. Rather, it must be either more general or coextensive with it. This is what is meant by its being more general.

" قِيَاسُ التَّمْثِيلِ "

translated_text:
As for what is indicated in the sense of the subject of the judgment—the thing judged, spoken of, described, or taken as the subject—it is either narrower in scope than the evidence or coextensive with it. It may thus be described as narrower than the evidence; it cannot be broader. For if it were broader, and the evidence did not necessarily follow from it, the judgment could not be known to apply to it, and the evidence would not constitute evidence. It constitutes evidence only when it necessarily follows from the thing judged, described, and spoken of—called the subject or grammatical subject—and itself entails the judgment, which is an attribute, a statement about the subject, and a judgment, and is called the predicate or grammatical predicate.

An example is intoxication, which is broader in scope than the disputed drink, nabīdh, but narrower than prohibition. The evidence may also be coextensive with the judgment while necessarily following from the subject of that judgment. This, then, is what gives it its evidentiary force, whether it is formulated as syllogistic or analogical reasoning or is not formulated in either way. This is something the mind understands even when the tongue does not express it. Hence human minds infer conclusions from evidence even when people do not express this in words that explain what is in their minds. They may also express their meanings clearly without adopting the terminology of any particular group of speculative theologians, logicians, or others. Knowledge of that which entails the conclusion must therefore be self-evident or established by further evidence.

As for “analogical reasoning,” it is the mind’s passage from one particular judgment to another because they share a common universal attribute, for that judgment necessarily follows from the shared universal. If this necessary connection is not self-evident, knowledge of it must have some basis, as explained earlier. The mind first conceives of the two particulars—the original case and the new case—and then proceeds to what both entail

It must be known that the judgment necessarily follows from the shared attribute; this is what is called the major premise in syllogistic reasoning. The mind then proceeds to establish this consequence for the original particular that entails it. The two forms of reasoning are thus essentially identical. They differ only in how the evidence is presented and arranged. Otherwise, the reality that makes it evidence—its necessarily entailing the conclusion—is one and the same.

Among the injustices and signs of ignorance of these people is that they illustrate analogical reasoning with the statement:

“The heavens are composite and must therefore have come into being, by analogy with a human being.”

They then raise objections specific to this particular argument. Yet if one were to say:

“The heavens are composite, and everything composite has come into being,”

the same objections, and others besides, would arise. But when syllogistic reasoning deals with evident subject matter, there is no difference between it and analogical reasoning. A universal is a mental exemplar of its particulars, and therefore corresponds and conforms to them. Indeed, analogical reasoning may be clearer. This is why rational people employ it in their reasoning.

Likewise, their assertion that a definition cannot be obtained through an example concerns only an example by which the thing defined is distinguished from everything else, so that one recognizes what invariably accompanies it in both directions—being present wherever it is present and absent wherever it is absent. For a definition that distinguishes the thing defined is one by which a concomitant exactly coextensive with it is known. Whenever this is achieved, the thing defined has been distinguished from everything else. This is what constitutes a definition according to the great majority of theoretical thinkers, who do not permit the inclusion of the general genus in a definition.

For this reason, the sciences are ‘three’: one concerns what cannot be abstracted from matter, either in the mind or in external reality. This is ‘physics’, whose subject is body. Another concerns what is abstracted from matter in the mind but not in external reality. This is ‘mathematics’, which discusses magnitude and number. The remaining science concerns what is abstracted from matter. This is ‘metaphysics’, whose subject is absolute existence and the attributes that belong to it insofar as it is existence, such as its division into necessary and contingent, and into substance and accident.

Substance is divided into that which inheres in something; that which serves as a substrate; that which neither inheres in something nor serves as a substrate, but is related to these through governance; and that which neither inheres in something nor serves as a substrate, nor has such a relation to them. (The first) is form. (The second) is matter—that is, hylē, which in their language means ‘substrate’. (The third) is the soul. (The fourth) is the intellect.

(The First) is classified by most of them under the category of substance. However, some of their later thinkers, such as Ibn Sīnā, refused to call it a substance. They said that substance is that which, if it exists, exists not in a subject—that is, not in a substrate independent of what inheres in it. This applies only to that whose existence differs from its essence. The First is not like this, and therefore is not a substance. This is one of the matters in which

Second: The noblest of existent beings is the “Necessary Existent,” whose existence is particular, not universal. Conceiving a universal does not preclude its being shared by many, whereas conceiving the Necessary Existent precludes such sharing. If, however, one does not know of Him that which, when conceived, precludes such sharing, but knows only a universal feature common to Him and others, then one has not known the Necessary Existent.

The same applies to what they call “intellectual substances”: the ten intellects—or more, according to those among them who hold that there are more, such as al-Suhrawardī, who was put to death, Abū al-Barakāt, and others. These are all particular substances, not universals. Thus, if we know only universals, we know none of them.

Likewise, the celestial spheres, which they maintain have neither beginning nor end, would remain unknown if we knew only universals. We would therefore know neither the Necessary Existent, nor the intellects, nor any of the souls, nor the celestial spheres, nor the elements, nor generated beings. Yet these comprise all existent things according to them. What knowledge is there here through which the soul attains perfection?

Third: Their division of the sciences into natural science, mathematics, and metaphysics, and their ranking of mathematics above natural science and metaphysics above mathematics, are among the ways in which they have turned realities upside down. For conceiving nothing but a circle, triangle, or square—even if one were to conceive everything in Euclid—or nothing but abstract numbers yields no knowledge of anything existing in external reality. This is not the perfection of the soul. Were it not intended to provide knowledge of external things that are counted and measured, namely bodies and accidents, it would not have been regarded as a science. They made geometry a preliminary to the study of astronomy only to assist them in astronomical demonstrations or to benefit from it in developing the material world. Yet their syllogistic demonstrations establish nothing with consistent certainty, free of error, except in these mathematical subjects.

For “arithmetic,” which is the science of discrete quantity, and “geometry,” which is the science of continuous quantity, constitute certain knowledge that admits no contrary whatsoever. Examples include adding, dividing, and multiplying numbers, and determining their ratios to one another. If you add one hundred to one hundred, you know that together they make two hundred. If you divide it by ten, each receives ten; and if you multiply it by ten, the product is one hundred.

Multiplication is the inverse of division. Multiplying whole numbers means repeating the units of one number as many times as there are units in the other. If the product is divided by either number, the other factor is obtained. If the quotient is multiplied by the divisor, the dividend is obtained. These matters, and others like them discussed in arithmetic, are intelligible matters shared by all rational people. Everyone knows something of them, for such knowledge is self-evident. Hence the example they give: “One is half of two.” There is no doubt that the propositions of arithmetic are universal, must be accepted, and admit no exceptions whatsoever.

This was the starting point of their philosophy, founded by Pythagoras, whose followers were called the adherents of number. They supposed that abstract numbers existed outside the mind. Then Plato and his followers recognized the error of this view. They supposed instead that abstract essences, such as man and horse considered without qualification, existed outside the mind and had neither beginning nor end. Then Aristotle and his followers recognized the error of that view and said: “Rather, these unqualified essences exist in external reality together with individual things.” Some of Aristotle’s later followers adopted this position, but it too is mistaken. For nothing in external reality is universal at all; everything that exists externally is a particular, determinate thing.

When it is said that the natural universal exists in external reality, this means that what is universal in the mind exists externally. But when it exists externally, it can only be a determinate particular, not a universal. Its being universal is therefore conditional upon its being in the mind. وَأَيْضًا فَفِي الْإِدْمَانِ عَلَى مَعْرِفَةِ ذَلِكَ تَعْتَادُ النَّفْسُ الْعِلْمَ الصَّحِيحَ وَالْقَضَايَا الصَّحِيحَةَ الصَّادِقَةَ وَالْقِيَاسَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ فَيَكُونُ فِي ذَلِكَ تَصْحِيحُ الذِّهْنِ وَالْإِدْرَاكِ وَتُعَوَّدُ النَّفْسُ أَنَّهَا تَعْلَمُ الْحَقَّ وَتَقُولُهُ لِتَسْتَعِينَ بِذَلِكَ عَلَى الْمَعْرِفَةِ الَّتِي هِيَ فَوْقَ ذَلِكَ؛
 وَلِهَذَا يُقَالُ:
 إنَّهُ كَانَ أَوَائِلُ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ أَوَّلَ مَا يُعَلِّمُونَ أَوْلَادَهُمْ الْعِلْمَ الرِّيَاضِيَّ وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ شُيُوخِهِمْ فِي آخِرِ أَمْرِهِ إنَّمَا يَشْتَغِلُ بِذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُ لَمَّا نَظَرَ فِي طُرُقِهِمْ وَطُرُقِ مَنْ عَارَضَهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ الْبَاطِلِ وَلَمْ
translated_text:
nor in external reality—his claim need only be fully understood for its falsity to become evident. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that this science admits of valid demonstrations, yet no soul attains perfection through it, escapes punishment by it, or achieves happiness through it. Hence Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī and others said of these men’s sciences:

“They consist either of true sciences that yield no benefit—and we seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that brings no benefit—or of false conjectures that cannot be trusted—and indeed, some suspicion is sinful.”

By the former, they mean the mathematical sciences; by the latter, what these men say about metaphysics, astrology, and the like. Nevertheless, the soul may take pleasure in this, just as it takes pleasure in other things. A person enjoys learning what he did not know and hearing what he had not heard, provided he is not preoccupied with something he considers more important. Likewise, he may enjoy various activities that fall under amusement and play.

Moreover, through sustained study of these matters, the soul becomes accustomed to sound knowledge, correct and true propositions, and sound inference. This serves to refine the mind and its understanding. The soul also becomes accustomed to knowing and speaking the truth, thereby gaining assistance in attaining knowledge of a higher order. Hence it is said that the early philosophers would begin their children’s education with mathematics. Many of their masters eventually devote themselves exclusively to this, because, when they examined their methods and those of their opponents among the proponents of false speculative theology, they did not

Likewise, many later scholars of our school spend their leisure studying inheritance shares, arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and similar subjects, because these refresh the soul and constitute sound knowledge free of error.

It is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said:

“When you seek recreation, practise archery; and when you converse, discuss inheritance shares.”

The calculation of inheritance shares is a rational discipline founded on a basis prescribed by the revealed law. It thus combines intellectual exercise with preservation of the revealed law. Yet it is not a science to be pursued for its own sake, nor does the soul attain perfection through it.

Those polytheists used to worship the celestial bodies, build temples for them, and invoke them with various supplications. This is well known from accounts of them and from books composed according to their methods on polytheism, magic, the invocation of celestial bodies, and the incantations and oaths through which Iblīs and his hosts are glorified. Through their polytheism and magic, Satan would entice them with things that themselves drew them into that polytheism and magic. They would observe the celestial bodies to learn their magnitudes, the measures of their motions, and the alignments between them, using this knowledge to assist them in what they considered appropriate to those bodies.

translated_text:
Since the celestial spheres are round, and their motions could not be calculated without knowledge of geometry and the properties of straight and curved lines, they studied “geometry” for this purpose and for worldly development. This is why they pursued it so extensively. Otherwise, if its only purpose had been the mere conception of numbers and magnitudes, that aim would not have warranted the effort described. Yet this may be an end in itself for some who take pleasure in it, for the pleasures of the soul are diverse. Some people take pleasure in chess, backgammon, and gambling until these distract them from what would benefit them more.

“Logic” originated in geometry. They called it “definitions,” drawing on the boundaries of those figures, so that they could pass from perceptible figures to intelligible ones. This was due to the weakness of their intellects and their inability to attain knowledge except by a circuitous route. Allah Most High has made knowledge, clear exposition, righteous deeds, and faith accessible to the Muslims, enabling them to surpass every other group of humankind. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

As for “metaphysics,” which they regard as independent of matter both in the mind and in external reality, it has already become clear to you that it has no object of knowledge in external reality. Rather, it is general in scope, concerning unrestricted universals that exist as universals only in the mind. None of this contributes to the perfection of the soul.

If they know the Necessary Existent specifically, this is knowledge of a particular whose very conception precludes its applying to more than one individual. This is something that the syllogism they call “demonstration” does not establish. Their demonstration does not establish any specific particular, whether the Necessary Existent or anything else

 هُوَ أَخَصُّ مِنْ مُسَمَّى الْوُجُودِ وَلَيْسَ فِي مُجَرَّدِ انْقِسَامِ الْأَمْرِ الْعَامِّ فِي الذِّهْنِ إلَى أَقْسَامٍ بِدُونِ مَعْرِفَةِ الْأَقْسَامِ مِمَّا يَقْتَضِي عِلْمًا كُلِّيًّا عَظِيمًا عَالِيًا عَلَى تَصَوُّرِ الْوُجُودِ. فَإِذَا عَرَفْت الْأَقْسَامَ فَلَيْسَ مَا هُوَ عِلْمٌ بِمَعْلُومِ لَا يَقْبَلُ التَّغْيِيرَ وَالِاسْتِحَالَةَ وَلَيْسَ مَعَهُمْ دَلِيلٌ أَصْلًا يَدُلُّهُمْ أَنَّ الْعَالَمَ لَمْ يَزَلْ وَلَا يَزَالُ هَكَذَا. وَجَمِيعُ
translated_text:
but establishes only a universal. The very conception of a universal does not preclude its applying to more than one individual, whereas knowledge of the Necessary Existent precludes this. Whoever has not conceived of that which cannot apply to more than one individual has not come to know Allah.

Anyone who attributes to the Lord knowledge of universals alone—as Ibn Sīnā and others like him claim—and regards this as a perfection of the Lord will, all the more, regard it as a perfection of the soul, especially if he says: “The soul perceives only universals; it is the body that perceives particulars.” This is ignorance in the extreme. These universals, through which existing particulars cannot be known, contain no perfection whatsoever. The soul desires knowledge of universals only to attain, through them, comprehensive knowledge of particulars. If this is not achieved, the soul finds no joy in that knowledge.

The fourth point:

It may be said: Suppose that the soul is perfected through abstract universals, as they claim. What they discuss in what they consider the highest science, which examines existence and its concomitants, does not meet this description.

Merely conceiving the meaning of existence is self-evident—so much so that, in their view, its obviousness dispenses with the need for a definition. This, then, is not what is sought; rather, what is sought is its divisions. Its very divisions into necessary and contingent, substance and accident, cause and effect, beginningless and temporally originated are more specific than what the term “existence” denotes. Merely dividing a general concept in the mind into categories, without knowing those categories, does not yield any great, lofty universal knowledge beyond the conception of existence. Once you know these categories, that knowledge is not knowledge of an object that admits of neither change nor transformation. They have no evidence whatsoever establishing that the world has always been, and will always remain, as it is. And all

 ثُمَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ الرُّسُلَ عَرَفَتْ مَا عَرَفْنَاهُ مِنْ نَفْيِ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ.

 بَلْ لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ هَذَا وَإِنَّمَا كَانَ كَمَالُهُمْ فِي الْقُوَّةِ الْعَمَلِيَّةِ لَا النَّظَرِيَّةُ.
translated_text:
the arguments they adduce for the perpetuity of the agent, agency, time, motion, and their concomitants establish only their beginninglessness and perpetuity in kind, not the beginninglessness or perpetuity of any particular thing. To assert categorically that those proofs establish this world or anything within it is sheer ignorance, with no basis beyond the lack of knowledge of anything existing other than this world. Yet the absence of knowledge is not knowledge of absence. Thus, these people have no faith in the unseen of which the prophets spoke: they believe neither in Allah, nor His angels, His Books, His messengers, nor resurrection after death.

If they say:

“We affirm the intellectual realm, or intelligible reality beyond what is perceptible to the senses, and that is the unseen,”

then this—even though some speculative theologians and philosophers have stated it—is error and misguidance. For, upon examination, the intelligible realities they affirm amount only to things postulated in the mind, not things existing in external reality. The messengers, by contrast, spoke of things that exist in external reality, whose existence is more perfect and greater than that of what we witness in this world.

What comparison can there be between the two? Since they denied what the messengers had conveyed, they said:

“The messengers intended to present the masses with imaginary representations, so that they might thereby benefit from the just order the messengers established for them.”

Some of them then say:

“The messengers knew, as we do, that these things do not exist.”

Others say:

“Rather, they did not know this; their perfection lay only in the practical faculty, not the theoretical.”

translated_text:
Even the least of the messengers’ followers, once he understands the true nature of their teachings, finds them unacceptable even to the least of those followers. When he knows through rational proofs that nothing in this world can be beginningless, and knows through the prophets’ reports, supported by reason, that another world preceded it, from which it was created, and that it will undergo transformation and the Resurrection will take place, and other such matters, he realizes that even their most far-reaching universal judgments do not correspond to reality: they are ignorance, not knowledge.

Even supposing that they do not know what the messengers conveyed, reason does not establish their claim that these universal kinds in this world are beginningless and everlasting, having always existed and continuing forever. Thus, purported knowledge of this is not knowledge of unchanging universals. Most of their “first philosophy” and “higher wisdom” is of this sort.

The same applies to those who wrote according to their method, such as the author of “Eastern Investigations,” the author of “The Wisdom of Illumination,” the author of “The Subtleties of Realities” and “Symbols of Treasures,” the author of “Unveiling the Realities,” and the author of “Hidden Secrets in the Rational Sciences,” and others like them. These writers neither devoted their discourse wholly to defending the philosophers’ doctrine nor escaped altogether from the entanglements of their error. Rather, they shared much of their error and many of their absurdities, while escaping some of their harmful consequences. Yet they also failed to do them justice in some matters in which they were correct, and erred either because they did not understand what they meant or because they did not recognize that what they said was correct.

These writers, moreover, merely follow the teachings of Ibn Sīnā.  وَغَيْرِهَا وَهُوَ آخِرُ مُنْتَهَى فَلْسَفَتِهِ وَبَيَّنْت بَعْضَ مَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْجَهْلِ فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي الطَّوَائِفِ الْمَعْرُوفِينَ الَّذِينَ يَتَكَلَّمُونَ فِي الْعِلْمِ الْإِلَهِيِّ مَعَ الْخَطَأِ وَالضَّلَالِ مِثْلَ عُلَمَاءِ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَأَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ أَجْهَلُ
translated_text:
the Muslims, although he acquired them only from heretics who claimed affiliation with the Muslims, such as the Ismāʿīliyyah. He, his household, and their followers were known among the Muslims for their heresy. The best they professed outwardly was the creed of the Rāfidah, while inwardly they concealed outright disbelief. Muslims wrote books, both large and small, exposing their secrets and tearing away their veils, and strove against them by word and deed, for they were more deserving of this than the Jews and Christians. One need only mention “Uncovering Secrets and Tearing Away Veils” by Judge Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Tayyib, the book of ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn Ahmad, the book of Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, and the writings of Abū Ishāq, Ibn Fūrak, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, and al-Shahrastānī, besides much else that would take too long to describe.

The point here is that Ibn Sīnā himself reported that his household, his father, and his brother belonged to these heretics, and that this was what led him to take up philosophy, for he used to hear them discussing the intellect and the soul.

These Muslims with whom he claimed affiliation, despite their outward heresy and inward disbelief, knew more about Allah than his philosophical predecessors, such as Aristotle and his followers. For whatever knowledge of Allah those philosophers possessed was surpassed by that of devout Arab polytheists.

I have cited Aristotle’s own statements in his “Metaphysics,” in “Book Lambda” and elsewhere, which represent the ultimate achievement of his philosophy, and have explained some of the ignorance they contain. For among the well-known groups who discuss divine knowledge, despite their error and misguidance—such as Jewish and Christian scholars, the innovators among the Muslims, and others—none are more ignorant

" الْعِلَّةَ الْأُولَى "

translated_text:
than these men, nor further removed from knowledge of Allah Most High. Admittedly, much of what they say about natural philosophy is sound. Their discussions of it are extensive, and they possess the intellectual faculties through which they acquired that knowledge. They may indeed seek the truth, without displaying obstinate resistance to it. Yet they are profoundly ignorant of divine matters, possessing only a little knowledge of them, riddled with errors.

When Ibn Sīnā acquired some knowledge of the Muslims’ religion—having received what he did from the heretics and from those better than them among the Muʿtazilah and the Rāfidah—he sought to reconcile what he had understood through reason from these men with what he had inherited from his philosophical predecessors. Among his innovations were his discussions of prophethood, the mysteries of signs and dreams, and even certain questions of natural philosophy, as well as his discussions of the Necessary Existent and similar matters. Aristotle and his followers, by contrast, make no mention in their writings of the Necessary Existent or of any properties belonging to the Necessary Existent. They speak only of “the First Cause,” establishing its existence as the final cause of celestial motion: the celestial sphere moves in order to resemble it.

Ibn Sīnā thus made some improvements to that corrupt philosophy, until it gained acceptance among students of rational inquiry who knew the religion of Islam. Some of its contradictions began to become apparent to them, and each addressed them according to the knowledge he possessed. Yet they conceded to the philosophers certain false premises in logic, natural philosophy, and metaphysics, without recognizing the falsehood embedded in them. This led them astray concerning lofty questions of faith and sublime Quranic aims, and thereby they departed

translated_text:
from true knowledge and faith. As a result, in many of these matters they neither listen nor reason; rather, they resort to sophistry in rational matters and Qarmatian esotericism in matters of revelation.

The point here is to emphasize that, even if we suppose that the soul is perfected through knowledge alone, as they claim—although this claim is false—the soul has two faculties: a theoretical faculty of knowledge and a practical faculty of will. Both faculties must therefore be perfected through knowing Allah and worshipping Him. Worshipping Him encompasses loving Him and humbling oneself before Him. No soul can ever attain perfection except by worshipping Allah alone, without partner. Worship encompasses knowing Him, loving Him and being His servant. For this Allah sent the messengers and revealed the divine Books, all of which call to the worship of Allah alone, without partner.

These men, however, hold that the acts of worship commanded by the messengers are intended to refine the soul’s character, preparing it for the knowledge which they claim constitutes its perfection, or to put the household and the city in order, which is practical wisdom. They thus make acts of worship mere means to what they claim to be knowledge. Consequently, they consider these obligations to lapse for anyone who has attained the goal. Such is the practice of the Ismā‘īlī heretics and of those who have embraced heresy, wholly or in part, while affiliating themselves with the Sufis, the speculative theologians, the Shī‘ah or others.

The Jahmiyyah said: “Faith is nothing more than knowledge of Allah.” Although this statement is better than theirs—for it defines faith as knowledge of Allah, together with the knowledge of His angels, His Books and His messengers that this entails—these men identify perfection with knowledge of absolute existence and its concomitants. Yet this is something that

translated_text:
even if it had any reality outside the mind, would not constitute perfection for the soul except through knowledge of its Creator, glorified and exalted is He. These Jahmiyyah are among the most extreme religious innovators. Indeed, several scholars have placed them outside the seventy-two sects, as is reported from ‘Abdullāh ibn al-Mubārak and Yūsuf ibn Asbāt. This is also the view of a group of later followers of Ahmad and others. Several leading scholars, including Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, have declared anyone who holds this view an unbeliever.

They said: “This would entail that Iblīs, Pharaoh and the Jews who recognize him as they recognize their own sons are believers.”

The Jahmiyyah’s position is therefore better than that of these men, for what the Jahmiyyah mention is the foundation upon which souls attain perfection. Yet they failed to combine the soul’s knowledge with its will, which is the source of its practical faculty. They located perfection in knowledge alone, even if neither speech nor action bears it out, and even if it is unaccompanied by reverent fear, love, veneration or any of the other foundations and necessary accompaniments of faith. These men, however, have strayed as far as possible from perfection. Our purpose here is solely to discuss their demonstration; we have mentioned only some of the consequences of their unsound principles.

Know that exposing the falsehood and logical flaws in their statements does not entail that they will be among the wretched in the Hereafter, unless Allah sent them a messenger whom they did not follow. Rather, it makes clear that anyone to whom the messengers brought the truth, but who turned away from their path to follow the path of these men, will be among the wretched in the Hereafter.

Were it not for the prophets, these men would have been more rational than others. But the prophets brought the truth, remnants of which remain among the nations, even though they disbelieve in some of it. Even the Arab polytheists retained remnants of Abraham’s religion and were therefore better than the polytheistic philosophers who agree with Aristotle and his like on their fundamental principles.

The fifth point:

If the aim of their demonstrative syllogism is knowledge of contingent beings, none of these necessarily remains in the same state from eternity past to eternity future. Rather, they are susceptible to change and transformation. Even when an attribute is assumed to be inseparable from its subject, the subject itself does not necessarily endure. Knowledge of it is therefore not knowledge of a necessarily existent being.

They have no sound proof that anything in the world has existed without a beginning, as has been explained at length elsewhere. At most, their arguments entail the perpetual existence of agency, matter and duration as kinds. This is possible through an endless succession of individual instances of those kinds, while affirming that every effect comes into being and is preceded by nonexistence, as sound reason and authentic revelation require. For sound reason judges it impossible for a particular effect to coexist with its agent from eternity past to eternity future, whatever its agent is assumed to be—especially if the agent acts by choice, as established by conclusive proofs, not those cited by men deficient in their knowledge of the foundations of knowledge and religion, such as al-Rāzī and his like. This has been explained at length elsewhere.

Since this is firmly rooted in people’s natural dispositions, the very acknowledgment that He is the Creator of everything entails that everything other than Him came into being and was preceded by nonexistence. Even if His creating one creature after another is assumed to have continued without beginning, this does not conflict with His being the Creator of everything, or with everything other than Him having come into being after nonexistence, with nothing else coeternal with Him. Rather, this is greater in perfection, generosity and bounty.

If, however, “cause” means something other than that which brings an effect into existence—as in their examples of a ring moving with the movement of the hand, or rays proceeding from the sun—this does not concern agency at all. Rather, it concerns something dependent on a condition, and a condition may coexist with what depends on it. As for an agent, its particular effect cannot coexist with it from eternity, although it is not impossible for it to produce one thing after another. Thus, the beginninglessness of action as a kind is like the beginninglessness of motion as a kind. This does not conflict with every individual instance of motion having a beginning; rather, it entails it, since no particular instance can be beginningless.

This is the position of the vast majority of rational people among all nations, including Aristotle and his followers. Although they held that the world is beginningless, they did not affirm that it has an originator or an efficient cause, but only a final cause that the celestial sphere moves to imitate, since the sphere’s movement is voluntary. This view—that the First does not bring the world into existence but is merely a final cause to be imitated—is one of the utmost ignorance and disbelief. Nevertheless, the point is that they agreed with all other rational people that a contingent being which is an effect cannot be coeternal with its cause, as Ibn Sīnā and those who agree with him claim. Aristotle and all other rational people on this matter. They explained that Ibn Sīnā’s position departed from that of his predecessors and the vast majority of rational people. His intention was to construct a doctrine combining the doctrines of the speculative theologians with that of his predecessors, making the contingent being an effect of the Necessary Being while nevertheless being beginningless and coeternal with Him. His followers, including al-Suhrawardī al-Halabī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, al-Tūsī and others, followed him in accepting this possibility. Al-Rāzī claimed in his Muhassal that the view that an effect brought about by a cause that acts by the necessity of its essence can be beginningless was agreed upon by the earlier philosophers whose statements have reached us, such as Aristotle and others like him. Yet this was only the view of Ibn Sīnā and those like him.

When the speculative theologians affirm the beginninglessness of the attributes and the like that subsist in the Beginningless One, they do not say that these are produced or are effects of an efficient cause. Rather, in their view, the beginningless essence possesses those attributes, which are inseparable from it. The Necessary Being cannot truly be necessary and beginningless without His inseparable attributes, as has been explained fully elsewhere. They also hold it impossible for a contingent being—which, considered apart from its agent, admits both existence and nonexistence—to be beginningless. Likewise, the leading philosophers hold it impossible for a beginningless being to admit nonexistence, and impossible for a contingent being to have always been necessary, whether it is said to be necessary in itself or through another.

But Ibn Sīnā’s and others’ claim that a contingent being may be beginningless, necessary through another, and eternal without beginning or end—as they maintain regarding the celestial sphere—is precisely what has exposed their account of “contingency” to objections that undermine their position and that they cannot answer, as has been explained fully elsewhere. As for the Necessary Being—blessed and exalted is He—syllogistic reasoning does not establish what is unique to Him, but only a universal notion shared by Him and others. Thus, through their demonstration, they have gained no knowledge of anything that must endure, whether concerning the Necessary Being or contingent beings. If the soul attains perfection only through knowledge that endures as long as its object endures, then their demonstration has provided them with no knowledge through which the soul attains perfection—let alone justify the claim that such knowledge can be attained only through their demonstration.

For this reason, the prophets—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them—followed the method of establishing knowledge of the Lord Most High by mentioning His signs. When they employed “inferential reasoning” in doing so, they used a fortiori reasoning, not a categorical syllogism whose instances stand on an equal footing, nor mere analogical reasoning. For the Lord Most High has no equal, nor can He and anything else fall under a universal whose instances stand on an equal footing. Rather, any perfection free of deficiency that is established for another belongs to Him all the more; and any deficiency from which another is free, He is all the more free from it. These constitute the noblest knowledge and the greatest means by which souls attain perfection through understanding. Yet their perfection necessarily requires perfection in both knowledge and intention. Worshipping Allah alone is therefore indispensable; it encompasses knowing Him, loving Him, and humbling oneself before Him. As for His use of signs as evidence, this is frequent in the Quran.

The distinction between signs and inferential reasoning is that a “sign” is a mark: evidence that entails the very thing it indicates. What it indicates is not a universal notion shared by the object sought and something else. Rather, knowledge of the sign itself entails knowledge of the very thing indicated, just as the sun is a sign of daytime.

Allah Most High says:

“We made the night and the day two signs. We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating.”

Thus, simply knowing that the sun has risen entails knowing that daytime has begun. Likewise, with the prophethood of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—knowledge of his prophethood specifically does not entail a notion shared by him and others. The same applies to the signs of the Lord Most High: knowledge of them itself entails knowledge of His own holy Self—exalted is He—not knowledge of a universal shared by Him and others.

covered by a universal proposition entails the conclusion. Such is the nature of universal propositions.

For unless the particular instances of universal propositions are known by means other than analogical reasoning, they can be known only through analogical reasoning. One must therefore know that what is indicated follows necessarily from the evidence, which is the middle term. If this is universal, one must know that every instance of the universal conclusion sought follows necessarily from every instance of the evidence. For example, when it is said:

“Every A is B, and every B is C; therefore every C is A.”

One must know that every instance of C follows necessarily from every instance of B, and that every instance of B follows necessarily from every instance of A. Clearly, knowing that a particular C follows necessarily from a particular B, and that a particular B follows necessarily from a particular A, is closer to our innate disposition than this.

If it is said, “That universal proposition arises in the mind as necessary or self-evident knowledge from the giver of reason,” the reply is: “It is even more natural for that particular proposition to arise in the mind from the giver of reason.”

It is known that every contingent thing other than Allah necessarily entails the very being of the Lord Most High. It cannot exist without the existence of the Lord’s very being—exalted and holy is He. If it also entails universal notions shared between it and other things, that is because its existence entails the existence of its necessary concomitants.

Those shared universals are among the necessary concomitants of the particular. I mean that what belongs specifically to it within that general universal necessarily accompanies it. The shared universal necessarily accompanies it on condition that it exists and that there exists a knower who conceives the common element. He—glory be to Him—knows things as they truly are: He knows His own holy Self in its distinctive reality, and He knows universals as universals. The existence of a particular also entails the existence of the corresponding unrestricted universal. Thus, when the Necessary Existent exists, so does the corresponding unrestricted existence; when the agent of all things exists, so does the corresponding unrestricted agent; when the One without beginning exists, so does the corresponding unrestricted being without beginning; when independence from all things is realized, so is the corresponding unrestricted independence; and when the Lord of all things exists, so does the corresponding Lord. As we have mentioned, when this human being and this animal exist, the corresponding unrestricted human being and unrestricted animal exist. Yet the unrestricted is unrestricted only in the mind, not in external reality.

If someone knows that an unrestricted human being and an unrestricted animal exist, he does not thereby know the particular individual itself. Likewise, if he knows an unrestricted necessary existent, an unrestricted agent, and an unrestricted self-sufficient being, he does not thereby know the Lord of the worlds Himself or what distinguishes Him from all others. That is what His signs—exalted is He—indicate. His signs entail His very being, the conception of which precludes its being shared by more than one.

Everything other than Him is evidence of His very being and a sign pointing to Him. For it is inseparably bound to His very being, and whatever is so bound is evidence of that to which it is bound. No contingent thing can exist unless His very being exists. Thus, all such things are necessarily bound to His own Self, evidence of Him, and signs pointing to Him. Through their method of analogical reasoning, however, these things indicate an unrestricted universal notion that exists only in the mind. Their demonstration therefore has not given them knowledge of what is distinctive to the Lord Most High.

As for “a fortiori reasoning,” which the early generations employed in following the Quran, it indicates that the attributes of perfection, free of all deficiency, belong to Him in a more perfect manner than anything they know to belong to others. The difference is beyond the intellect’s capacity to measure, just as it cannot measure the difference between the Creator and the created. Indeed, if the intellect recognizes differences in excellence between one creature and another whose extent cannot be encompassed, and knows that Allah’s superiority over every creature is greater than any creature’s superiority over another, this makes clear to it that what belongs to the Lord surpasses everything belonging to all others by an immeasurable degree.

Thus, it is as though “a fortiori reasoning” imparts knowledge of something distinctive to the Lord, while the general nature of that thing is known. For this reason, discerning scholars preferred the view that terms predicated of Him and of others are predicated in a graded manner: neither as mere homonyms nor as terms sharing a meaning whose instances are equal, but as terms sharing a meaning whose instances differ in degree. Thus, the terms whiteness and blackness apply both to an intense degree—such as the whiteness of snow—and to a lesser degree—such as the whiteness of ivory. Likewise, the term existence applies to both the Necessary Existent and contingent beings, but its greater perfection and excellence in the Necessary Existent exceed the difference between these two degrees of whiteness.

Yet this difference of degree in graded terms does not prevent their underlying meaning from being common and universal. Graded terms must therefore have a shared universal meaning, even though that universal exists only in the mind. This is the subject of “division”: the division of a universal into its particulars, as when one says that what exists is divided into the necessary and the contingent. The same applies to all other names and attributes predicated of the Creator and the created, such as “living,” “knowing,” “powerful,” “hearing,” and “seeing.” Likewise, this applies to His attributes, such as His knowledge, power, mercy, pleasure, anger, joy, and all the other names and attributes of His proclaimed by the messengers.

People have disagreed on this matter. One group—including Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāshiʾ, one of the Muʿtazilite masters who preceded Abū ʿAlī—held that these terms apply literally to the Creator and figuratively to the created. A group among the Jahmiyyah, Bātiniyyah, and philosophers held the reverse: they apply figuratively to the Creator and literally to the created.

The great majority across the various schools held that they apply literally to both. This is the position of groups of speculative thinkers among the Muʿtazilites, Ashʿaris, Karrāmiyyah, jurists, people of hadith, and Sufis. It is also the philosophers’ position. Many of these, however, contradict themselves: they acknowledge that some terms apply literally, such as “existent,” “self,” “essence,” “reality,” and the like, yet dispute this concerning others because of the specious arguments advanced by those who deny them all. Yet what applies to the terms someone denies is analogous to what applies to those he affirms. It is only his limited understanding that leads him to distinguish between equivalent cases. Denying them all rules out His existence.

Terms predicated in varying degrees are univocal with respect to their shared meaning. For this reason, earlier philosophical thinkers and others did not give such terms a separate designation; rather, “univocal” encompassed them all. Terms predicated in varying degrees therefore fall within univocal terms in the broad sense, while forming a separate category from univocal terms in the narrow sense.

Accordingly, a universal shared meaning must be affirmed: this is what univocal terms in the broad sense denote. It exists in an unrestricted form only in the mind, and this is what their demonstrative syllogism establishes. Differences in degree must also be affirmed: these are what terms predicated in varying degrees signify, as distinct from univocal terms in the narrow sense. This is what the Quran’s demonstrative arguments establish through a fortiori reasoning. One must also affirm the distinctive property of the Lord by which He is distinguished from everything else. This is what His signs—glorified be He—indicate, for their existence necessarily entails His own existence. No syllogism, whether demonstrative or otherwise, indicates this distinctive property.

It thus becomes clear that their demonstrative syllogism does not attain the objective through which the soul achieves perfection in its knowledge of existing things and their Creator, let alone justify saying that no objects of inquiry can be known except through it. This is an extensive subject, but the purpose here is to draw attention to the invalidity of their “negative proposition”: their claim that inferential knowledge can be attained only through their form of demonstration.

Yet they were not content with this sweeping negation, by which they restricted what was broad and confined knowledge to a narrow path yielding only a result of no value. They went so far as to claim that the knowledge of Allah Most High, and that of His prophets and close servants, is attained only through a syllogism containing a middle term, as Ibn Sīnā and his followers maintain. Still, in affirming such knowledge, they are better than those predecessors of theirs who denied His knowledge and that of His prophets—men among the most ignorant of the Lord of all worlds, His prophets, and His scriptures. Ibn Sīnā, distinguished from those men by greater knowledge and intelligence, followed their logical method in establishing this position.

Although those who follow this path are more knowledgeable and accomplished than their predecessors, they are nevertheless further astray and more ignorant than the Jews and Christians. For the latter attained a measure of faith in the Necessary Existent and His attributes that these misguided men have not attained, owing to the pride and vain imaginings within their hearts. They are followers of Pharaoh and his like. Hence you find them disparaging or hostile toward Moses and those who stand with him among the followers of revealed religions and laws.

Allah Most High says:

“Those who dispute Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them—there is nothing in their hearts but pride, aspiring to a greatness they will never attain.”

He Most High also says:

“Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah and those who believe. Thus does Allah seal the heart of every arrogant tyrant.”

And He says:

“When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in the knowledge they possessed, but the very thing they used to ridicule engulfed them.”

“When they saw Our punishment, they said, ‘We believe in Allah alone, and we reject whatever we used to associate with Him.’”

“But their faith did not benefit them once they had seen Our punishment. Such is Allah’s established way with His servants. And there the disbelievers lost everything.”

Pharaoh’s statements, these men’s following of him and Nimrod son of Canaan and other leaders of disbelief and misguidance like them, and their opposition to Moses, Abraham, and Allah’s other messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Allah made the house of Abraham leaders for the believers, the people of Paradise, and the house of Pharaoh leaders for the people of Hell. He Most High says:

“He and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land without right, thinking they would not be returned to Us.”

“So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. See, then, what was the end of the wrongdoers!”

“We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.”

“We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.”

“After destroying the earlier generations, We gave Moses the Scripture as a source of insight for mankind.”

And so on until His words:

“Say, ‘Then bring a scripture from Allah that offers better guidance than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful.’”

Concerning the house of Abraham, He says:

“We made leaders from among them, guiding by Our command, when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs.”

The point is that their later thinkers, who were more knowledgeable than their predecessors, held that the Lord’s knowledge is acquired through demonstrative syllogism, as is the knowledge of His prophets. We have refuted them at length elsewhere.

Section

Furthermore, they divide arguments into syllogism, induction, and analogy. They explain that inference proceeds either from the universal to the particular, from the particular to the universal, or from one particular to another. Sometimes they express this in terms of the specific and the general, saying that one infers the specific from the general, the general from the specific, or one specific case from another.

They call the first “qiyās,” meaning subsumptive syllogism, for they reserve the term qiyās for this form of reasoning. Many scholars of legal theory and dialectical theology, however, reserve the term qiyās for analogy. For most rational thinkers, the term encompasses both.

They say that inferring the universal from particulars is induction. If it is complete, it is complete induction and yields certainty; if it is incomplete, it does not yield certainty.

The former consists in examining all the particulars and judging the universal according to what is found in its particulars. The latter consists in examining most of them. An example is someone saying: “An animal moves its lower jaw when it eats, for we have surveyed animals and found this to be so.” One replies to him: “The crocodile moves its upper jaw.”

They then say that syllogisms are divided into “conjunctive” and “exceptive.” An exceptive syllogism explicitly contains either its conclusion or the contradictory of its conclusion, whereas a conjunctive syllogism contains it implicitly. An example of the latter is a syllogism composed of categorical propositions, such as: “All nabīdh (infused drink) is intoxicating, and everything intoxicating is forbidden.”

An exceptive syllogism is composed of conditional propositions and is of two types:

The first employs an “if–then” proposition, such as: “If the prayer is valid, then the person praying is ritually purified.” Affirming the antecedent yields the consequent, while denying the consequent yields the denial of the antecedent.

The second employs a disjunctive proposition. This may preclude both joint truth and joint falsity, as when we say: “A number is either even or odd.” These two cannot both apply, nor can a number be neither.

Alternatively, it may preclude joint truth alone, as when we say: “This is either black or white,” meaning that blackness and whiteness cannot coexist, although the subject may possess neither.

As for a proposition that precludes joint falsity, it is one in which both alternatives cannot be absent together, although they may coexist.

They sometimes call the proposition that precludes both joint truth and joint falsity the genuine conditional proposition. It is coextensive with a pair of contradictories. A proposition that precludes joint truth has a narrower scope than a pair of contradictories: two contraries cannot coexist, but both may be absent, and they are narrower in scope than a pair of contradictories. A proposition that precludes joint falsity, by contrast, has a broader scope than a pair of contradictories. They may find it difficult to give an example of this, unlike the first two types, for which examples abound.

translated_text:
one or the other, for he cannot drown unless he is at sea. Either he does not drown in it—in which case he has not gone to sea—or he has gone to sea. Going to sea and drowning may occur together.

Examples abound, such as our saying: “This is alive, or it lacks knowledge, power, hearing, sight, or speech.” If life is present, one of the two alternatives holds; if life is absent, these attributes are absent. Yet something may be alive without possessing these attributes. The same applies when one says: “This person is ritually purified, or he is not praying.” If prayer is absent, ritual purity is absent; if ritual purity is present, the other alternative holds. Thus, one or the other must hold.

The same applies to every instance involving the absence of a condition and the presence of that which depends upon it. When the alternatives are the presence of that which depends upon a condition and the absence of the condition, the proposition precludes joint falsity. For the condition must either be present or absent; when it is absent, the condition is absent. Thus, either that which depends upon the condition must be present, or the condition must be absent.

They then divide conjunctive syllogisms into the four figures. The middle term may be the predicate in the major premise and the subject in the minor premise—this is the natural figure, which yields all four types of conclusion: particular and universal, affirmative and negative. Alternatively, the middle term may be the predicate in both premises: this is the second figure, which yields only negative conclusions. Or it may be the subject in both, yielding only particular conclusions. The fourth figure yields particular conclusions and universal negative conclusions, but it is far removed from natural reasoning.

Then, when they wish to demonstrate how the second and third figures yield conclusions, or to establish other conclusions, they need to reason by means of contradictories, converses, and contrapositives. For the truth of

We say: What they have proposed is either false or an unnecessarily lengthy procedure that makes the reasoner’s path longer. It therefore involves either an error that obstructs the truth or a long path that exhausts the person following it before he reaches the truth, although he could reach it by a shorter route. Some of our predecessors illustrated this by comparing it to someone who, when asked, “Where is your ear?” raised [his hand] (*) very high and then swung it around to his left ear, although he could have pointed directly to either his right or his left ear.

How beautifully Allah describes His Book when He says:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.”

The most upright path to the noblest goals is therefore what Allah sent His Messenger with. As for these people’s method, besides their going astray in some matters and taking a crooked, lengthy path in others, it leads them only to something that cannot save them from Allah’s punishment, let alone secure felicity for them, much less enable human souls to attain perfection through their method.

To explain: Their restriction of proof to syllogism, induction, and analogy is unsupported by any proof; indeed, it is false. Likewise, their assertion that the knowledge sought can be attained only through two premises—neither more nor fewer—is unsupported by any proof; indeed, it is false.

Their argument for this restriction is their statement: “One reasons either from the universal to the particular, or from the particular to the universal

translated_text:
or from one of the two parts to the other. The first is syllogism, the second induction, and the third analogy.”

The reply is:

You have offered no proof that inference is confined to these three forms. If, by inference from one particular to another, you mean analogical reasoning, then your classification is not exhaustive. It leaves out inference from one universal to another necessarily connected with it and matching it in generality and particularity. Likewise, it leaves out inference from one particular to another necessarily connected with it, such that the existence of either entails the existence of the other, and its absence entails the other’s absence. This is none of what you have called syllogism, induction, or analogy. These are signs.

An example is inferring daytime from sunrise, or sunrise from daytime. This is not inference from a universal to a particular. Rather, inferring a particular daytime from a particular sunrise is inference from one particular to another, while inferring sunrise in general from daytime in general is inference from one universal to another.

Likewise, using the stars to determine the direction of the Kaaba is inference from one particular to another—for example, using al-Jady, Banāt Na‘sh, and the small star near the pole which some people call “the Pole.” The same applies to inferring the appearance of a star from the appearance of its counterpart in latitude, or inferring from one star’s rising that another is setting or that another is culminating, and other such indications upon which people agree.

The Most High says:

“And by the stars they are guided.”
