translated_text:
Using places to determine times and other places is accepted by Arabs and non-Arabs, adherents of religions and philosophers alike. If the appearance of the Pleiades is used to infer the appearance of nearby stars to their east and west, right and left, this is inference from one particular to another because they are necessarily connected. It is not analogical reasoning. If this is expressed as a universal judgment, it is inference from one universal to another, not from a universal to a particular. Rather, one of two necessarily connected universals is used to infer the other.

Someone who knows the distances between the stars and knows which of them accompany the break of dawn can infer, from the stars he sees, how much of the night has passed and how much remains. This is inference from one of two necessarily connected things to the other. Likewise, someone familiar with mountains, rivers, and winds can use them to infer the places associated with them.

If this connection is permanent, with no known beginning, but has existed since Allah created the earth—as with mountains, the great rivers (the Nile, the Euphrates, Sayhān, and Jayhān), and the sea—then the inference holds consistently.

If the connection has endured for a shorter period, as in the case of the Kaaba—may Allah Most High honour it—then inferences drawn from it apply accordingly. Abraham, Allah’s close friend, built it, and it has remained venerated; no tyrant has ever prevailed over it. Thus, it can be used to infer other things, and other things can be used to infer its location. The corners of the Kaaba face the earth’s four cardinal directions: the Black Stone faces east; the western corner opposite it, also called the Syrian corner, faces west; the Yemeni corner faces south; and the corner opposite it is called the Iraqi corner—if one calls

This Syrian–Iraqi corner faces north, towards the celestial pole. Thus, the Kaaba can be used to determine directions, and directions can be used to locate it. Things whose duration is shorter than that of the Kaaba, such as buildings in towns and trees, can serve as indications for a correspondingly shorter period. One might say, for example, that a particular house can be identified by a tree at its entrance with such-and-such characteristics. The two remain connected for a certain period. This and similar cases involve inferring one of two necessarily connected things from the other, both being specific particulars. This is not analogical reasoning.

For this reason, Muslim scholars of rational inquiry departed from their method and said:

Evidence is that which guides one to what is sought and leads one to the intended conclusion. It is something knowledge of which entails knowledge of what is sought, or something whose sound examination leads to knowledge or to a belief judged more likely to be true. They have a terminological disagreement over whether this second kind should be called evidence or given the distinct designation of a sign. The majority call both kinds evidence, while some speculative theologians apply the term only to the first.

The criterion for evidence is that it entails what it indicates. Anything that entails something else can therefore be used as evidence for it. If the entailment runs in both directions, either can be used as evidence for the other: one reasons from whichever of the two one knows to the other, which one does not know. An example of the first kind is the way created things indicate their Creator—glorified and exalted is He—and His knowledge, power, will, mercy, and wisdom. Their existence necessarily entails His existence and these attributes; their existence without these is impossible. Thus, they cannot exist without indicating them. Another example is the way the Messenger’s report establishes the truth of what he reports from Allah. He speaks only the truth concerning Him, for he is divinely safeguarded in what he reports from Allah: no error whatsoever is allowed to stand in his reports from Him. Such evidence necessarily entails what it indicates, with an entailment that cannot be severed under any circumstances.

This holds whether the evidence that entails the conclusion consists in existence or nonexistence. Evidence may consist in either existence or nonexistence, and either may be used to infer existence or nonexistence. The presence of something is used to infer the absence of its contradictory and its contrary; the absence of its contradictory is used to infer its presence. The presence of that which entails something is used to infer the presence of what it entails, while the absence of what is entailed is used to infer the absence of that which entails it. Indeed, anything used as evidence entails what it indicates. This encompasses everything they have mentioned, as well as what they have not mentioned.

What they call a connected conditional amounts to inferring the presence of the consequent from the presence of the antecedent, and the absence of the antecedent from the absence of the consequent, whether this is expressed in conditional or categorical form. Differences in the wording of evidence do not change its essential nature when its meaning remains the same. The discussion concerns intelligible meanings, not words.

Thus, someone might say:

“If the prayer is valid, then the person praying is in a state of ritual purity”; “If the sun is up, then it is daytime”; “If an agent possesses knowledge and power, then he is alive”; and similar statements.

 وَكَذَلِكَ تَكَلُّفَاتُهُمْ فِي حُدُودِهِمْ:
 مِثْلَ حَدِّهِمْ لِلْإِنْسَانِ وَلِلشَّمْسِ بِأَنَّهَا كَوْكَبٌ يَطْلُعُ نَهَارًا وَهَلْ مَنْ يَجِدُ الشَّمْسَ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْحَدِّ وَنَحْوَهُ إلَّا مِنْ أَجْهَلِ النَّاسِ. وَهَلْ عِنْدَ النَّاسِ شَيْءٌ أَظْهَرُ مِنْ الشَّمْسِ وَمَنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ الشَّمْسَ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَجْهَلَ اللَّفْظَ فَيُتَرْجِمَ لَهُ. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مِنْ الْحَدِّ الَّذِي ذَكَرُوهُ وَإِمَّا أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ رَآهَا لِعَمَاهُ فَهَذَا لَا يَرَى النَّهَارَ وَلَا الْكَوَاكِبَ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى
translated_text:
This has the same meaning as saying: “The validity of the prayer entails the validity of the ritual purification”; or: “The validity of the prayer entails the presence of ritual purity”; or: “A person cannot be praying unless he is ritually pure”; or: “Ritual purity is a condition for the validity of prayer, and when the condition is absent, that which depends upon it is absent”; or: “Everyone who prays is ritually pure; therefore, whoever is not ritually pure is not praying.” There are similar ways of combining words and meanings that convey this inference, rather than confining people to a single formulation.

As minds and their conceptions expand, so do their forms of expression. When minds, expressions, and conceptions become narrow, a person’s intellect and tongue remain as though imprisoned. This is what happens to the adherents of Greek logic: you find them among the narrowest of people in knowledge and exposition, and among the least capable of conceiving and expressing ideas.

Thus, even an intelligent person, when engaging with the various disciplines and following the logicians’ approach, becomes long-winded and restrictive, laboured and strained. At best, he explains the evident and clarifies the obvious—an instance of inarticulacy. This may also lead him into various forms of sophistry from which Allah has spared those who have not followed their path.

The same applies to their laboured definitions, such as their definition of man, and their definition of the sun as “a celestial body that rises by day.” Is anyone who recognizes the sun through such a definition or the like anything but among the most ignorant of people? Is anything more apparent to people than the sun?

Someone who does not know the sun is either unfamiliar with the word, in which case it can be translated for him—but this is not the kind of definition they describe—or he has never seen it because he is blind, in which case he cannot see daylight, let alone the stars

although he is bound to hear from people enough to make this known to him without recourse to their method. They themselves acknowledge that the first figure of categorical syllogisms suffices in place of all other syllogistic forms. Its form is grasped naturally and need not be learned from them. Moreover, inference does not require conceiving it in the manner they claim.

Section

As for their statement, “Inference must consist of two premises, neither more nor less,” this claim is false in both directions. The premises needed by someone drawing an inference vary from person to person. Some people need only one premise because they already know the rest, just as some need no inference at all to know the matter, but may know it directly. Others need two premises; others three; and others four or more.

Suppose someone wishes to know whether this particular intoxicant is prohibited. If he knows that every intoxicant is prohibited, but does not know whether this particular intoxicant causes intoxication, he needs only one premise: to know that it is intoxicating. If he is told, “This is prohibited,” and asks, “What is the evidence for that?” and the person presenting the argument replies, “The evidence is that it is intoxicating,” the desired conclusion has been established.

The same applies if two people disagree about a particular kind of drink: is it intoxicating or not?

translated_text:
as people frequently ask about particular drinks without knowing whether or not they intoxicate, although they already know that every intoxicant is prohibited. Once it is established for the questioner, through the report of someone he trusts or through other evidence, that the drink is intoxicating, he knows that it is prohibited. The same applies to any category or particular instance whose inclusion under a universal proposition is in doubt, while the ruling expressed by that proposition is already known. Examples include people’s disagreement over backgammon and chess: do they constitute gambling or not? Likewise, their disagreement over the disputed nabīdh: does it fall under the category of wine or not?

Another example is their disagreement over oaths involving vows, divorce, and manumission: do these fall within His words,

“Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths,”

or not? Likewise, their disagreement concerning His words,

“or the one in whose hand is the marriage contract waives it”:

is this the husband or the guardian with independent authority? There are many similar examples.

An inference may require two premises for someone who does not know that the disputed intoxicating nabīdh is prohibited and does not know that this particular drink is intoxicating. He cannot know that it is prohibited until he knows both that it is intoxicating and that every intoxicant is prohibited.

He may know that this drink is intoxicating and that every intoxicant is wine, yet not know that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited wine—because he has only recently embraced Islam, or because he grew up among ignorant people or heretics who question this.

Or he may know that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said,

“Every intoxicant is prohibited.”

Or he may know that this is wine and that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited wine, yet not know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Alternatively, he may not know that he prohibited it for all believers, but suppose instead that he permitted it for some people and consider himself one of them—as someone might suppose that he permitted drinking it for medical treatment or some other purpose. For such a person, nothing suffices for knowing

 وَلَمْ نَقُلْ مُؤَلَّفٌ مِنْ مُقَدِّمَاتٍ لِأَنَّا لَا يُمْكِنُنَا تَعْرِيفُ الْمُقَدِّمَةِ مِنْ حَيْثُ هِيَ مُقَدِّمَةٌ إلَّا بِكَوْنِهَا جُزْءَ الْقِيَاسِ فَلَوْ أَخَذْنَاهَا فِي حَدِّ الْقِيَاسِ كَانَ دَوْرًا. وَالْقَضِيَّةُ الْخَبَرِيَّةُ إذَا كَانَتْ جُزْءَ الْقِيَاسِ سَمَّوْهَا مُقَدِّمَةً وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مُسْتَفَادَةً بِالْقِيَاسِ سَمَّوْهَا نَتِيجَةً وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مُجَرَّدَةً عَنْ ذَلِكَ سَمَّوْهَا قَضِيَّةً وَتُسَمَّى أَيْضًا قَضِيَّةٌ مَعَ تَسْمِيَتِهَا نَتِيجَةً وَمُقَدِّمَةً. وَهِيَ الْخَبَرُ وَلَيْسَتْ هِيَ الْمُبْتَدَأَ وَالْخَبَرَ فِي اصْطِلَاحِ النُّحَاةِ. بَلْ أَعَمُّ مِنْهُ. فَإِنَّ الْمُبْتَدَأَ وَالْخَبَرَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا جُمْلَةً اسْمِيَّةً وَالْقَضِيَّةُ تَكُونُ جُمْلَةً اسْمِيَّةً وَفِعْلِيَّةً كَمَا لَوْ قِيلَ قَدْ كَذَبَ زَيْدٌ وَمَنْ كَذَبَ اسْتَحَقَّ التَّعْزِيرَ. وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّهُمْ أَرَادُوا بِالْقَوْلِ - فِي قَوْلِهِمْ الْقِيَاسُ قَوْلٌ مُؤَلَّفٌ مِنْ أَقْوَالٍ - الْقَضِيَّةُ الَّتِي هِيَ جُمْلَةٌ تَامَّةٌ خَبَرِيَّةٌ لَمْ يُرِيدُوا بِذَلِكَ الْمُفْرَدَ الَّذِي هُوَ

Another indication that restricting inference to two premises is invalid is their definition of the syllogism, encompassing demonstrative, rhetorical, dialectical, poetic, and sophistical syllogisms:

“It is a statement composed of statements, or an expression of a composition of statements, such that, if these are conceded, another statement necessarily follows from them by virtue of those statements alone.”

They say:

“By saying ‘of statements,’ we exclude a single proposition which, by itself, entails the truth of its converse and its contrapositive, and the falsity of its contradictory, yet is not a syllogism.”

They say:

“We did not say ‘composed of premises,’ because we cannot define a premise, insofar as it is a premise, except as a component of a syllogism. Were we to include it in the definition of the syllogism, the definition would be circular.”

When a declarative proposition forms part of a syllogism, they call it a premise. When it is derived through a syllogism, they call it a conclusion. When considered apart from either role, they call it a proposition. It is also called a proposition even when designated a conclusion or a premise. It is a declarative statement, not a subject–predicate construction in the grammarians’ terminology; rather, it is broader than that. A subject–predicate construction can only be a nominal sentence, whereas a proposition may be either a nominal or a verbal sentence, as when one says, “Zayd has lied, and anyone who lies deserves discretionary punishment.”

The point here is that by ‘statement’ in their definition, ‘A syllogism is a statement composed of statements,’ they mean a proposition constituting a complete declarative sentence. They do not mean a simple expression, which is

a term. A syllogism comprises three terms: the minor, the middle, and the major. For example, one might say, “The disputed nabīdh is intoxicating, and every intoxicant is prohibited.” Here, “nabīdh,” “intoxicating,” and “prohibited” are each simple expressions, constituting the terms of the syllogism. This, then, is not what they mean by “statement”; rather, they mean that each proposition is a statement, as they themselves have explained.

Hence they say:

“A syllogism is a statement composed of statements such that, if these are conceded, another statement necessarily follows from them by virtue of those statements alone.”

What necessarily follows is the conclusion, which is a proposition, a declarative statement, and a complete sentence—not a simple expression.

Likewise, they say, “A syllogism is a composite statement,” thus calling the two propositions taken together a statement. Since they describe a syllogism as composed of statements, meaning propositions, this need not mean precisely two statements. For a plural expression either encompasses two or more, as in His words:

“If he has siblings, his mother receives a sixth.”

Or it means three or more, which, according to the majority, is its primary meaning. It may, however, denote numerical plurality in general, thus encompassing two or more; the plural is not restricted to two.

Thus, when they say, “It is composed of statements,” if they mean numerical plurality in general, this means two or more. A syllogism may therefore be composed of three or four premises and is not restricted to two. If, however, they intend the plural in its strict sense, it could only be composed of three or more. They certainly do not intend this, so only the first interpretation remains.

The reply is:

“This contradicts what is in your books, for you allow only two premises.”

They have expressly stated that a syllogism yielding the desired conclusion, whether conjunctive or exceptive, consists of neither fewer nor more than two premises. They justify this by saying that a single conclusion has no more than two parts: a subject and a predicate.

If the syllogism is conjunctive, each of the two parts of the conclusion must correspond to one of its premises—that is, it must occur within that premise as either its subject or its predicate, without itself constituting the entire premise.

They say:

“The conclusion has no more than two parts and therefore requires no more than two premises. If the syllogism is exceptive, it must contain a conditional premise, either implicative or disjunctive, corresponding to the whole conclusion or its contradictory. It must also contain an exceptive premise, so there is no need for a third.”

They say:

“However, a statement additional to the syllogism’s two premises may sometimes be incorporated into it. This is either unrelated to the syllogism or related to it. If related, it serves either to make the discourse more persuasive and polished or to explain both premises or one of them.”

They call this a compound syllogism.

They say:

They illustrate the connected form with the statement:

“Every human being is an animal, every animal is a body, and every body is a substance. Therefore, every human being is a substance.”

They illustrate the separated form with the statement:

“Every human being is an animal, and every animal is a body. Therefore, every human being is a body.” Then one says: “Every animal is a body, and every body is a substance. Therefore, every human being is an animal.” From these two it follows that every human being is a substance.

The reply to them is:

As for the desired conclusion having no more than two parts, that concerns its verbal formulation. In the mind, however, what is sought is only one thing, not two: whether the relation expressed in the judgment holds or does not hold.

Alternatively, one may describe it as the affirmation or denial of an attribute of its subject. Or one may speak of the relation of predicate to subject, or of grammatical predicate to grammatical subject, by way of denial or affirmation. These and similar expressions indicate the single meaning intended by the proposition.

Thus, if the conclusion is that nabīdh is forbidden or is not forbidden, or that a human being is capable of sensation or is not capable of sensation, and so forth, what is sought is to establish or deny that prohibition applies to nabīdh, and likewise to establish or deny that human beings possess sensation. This pointless verbosity in their syllogisms resembles their verbosity in their definitions, as when they define the sun as “a celestial body that rises by day.” Such discourse serves only to waste time, weary minds, and multiply nonsense. Moreover, those who follow them in their definitions and demonstrations continually disagree over how to define things already known without their definitions, and dispute demonstrations of matters that have no need of their demonstrations.

Their claim, “The desired conclusion has no more than two parts and therefore requires no more than two premises,” may be answered as follows:

If you mean that it contains only two simple terms, that is not so. Rather, it may be expressed using several terms. Consider someone who is uncertain whether nabīdh is forbidden by a scriptural text or is not forbidden by either a text or analogy. If the respondent says, “Nabīdh is forbidden by a scriptural text,” the desired conclusion has three parts. Likewise, if someone asks, “Is consensus conclusive evidence?” and the respondent says, “Consensus is conclusive evidence,” the desired conclusion has three parts.

If someone asks, “Is a human being a body endowed with sensation, growth, voluntary movement, and reason, or not?” the desired conclusion here has six parts. The reply is:

If you accept this approach—treating one thing as equivalent to several—then a single expression may convey an entire proposition. If someone says, “Intoxicating nabīdh is forbidden,” and the respondent says, “Yes,” the word “yes” is equivalent to saying, “It is forbidden.”

If he asks, “What is the proof for this?” and the reply is, “The prohibition of every intoxicant,” or “That every intoxicant is forbidden,” or “The words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden,’” or some similar expression, then the proof has been expressed as a single nominal expression, constituting one element. It has not been formulated as a proposition composed of two nominal elements—a subject and a predicate. For “the prohibition of every intoxicant” is a noun in a possessive construction.

Likewise, “that every intoxicant is forbidden,” with anna pronounced with an a-vowel, is a single nominal expression. This is because anna and its complement are equivalent to a single verbal noun, whereas inna, pronounced with an i-vowel, together with its complement, forms a complete sentence.

The same applies when you say, “The proof for this is the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,” or “The proof for this is the explicit text,” or “the consensus of the Companions,” or “The proof for this is such-and-such verse,” or “such-and-such hadith”; or “The proof for this is the presence of a ground for prohibition unopposed by any countervailing consideration of equal force”; or “The proof for this is that it shares with grape wine a characteristic that entails prohibition.” These and similar formulations express the proof through a single nominal expression, rather than through a proposition constituting a complete sentence. Yet when this proof, expressed through a single nominal expression, is set out in detail, it is expressed in multiple terms.

The point is this: you say that a proof—that is, a syllogism—consists of exactly two parts. If you mean only two expressions, and that anything beyond two expressions constitutes several proofs rather than one, on the grounds that each attribute qualifying an expression requires its own proof, then the reply is:

The same could be said of the two expressions: they constitute two proofs, not one, since each premise requires a proof. Restricting the number to two, rather than allowing more, is therefore an arbitrary stipulation without any meaningful basis. For the intended point may be conveyed by a single expression, or it may require two, three, four, or more. To insist that two expressions are the required norm, to the exclusion of both more and fewer, and to treat anything additional as multiple propositions if it concerns what is to be established, or as equivalent to multiple syllogisms if it consists of premises stated in the proof, is sheer arbitrariness. It is no more justified than saying:

“Rather, the norm is that there should be one proposition to establish, with a proof consisting of a single part. If what is to be established exceeds this, it is treated as two, three, or four propositions, according to its import.”

If this were said, it would be better than their position, because the term “proof” is singular, so what it denotes should likewise be single; and a syllogism is a proof.

The word “qiyās” (syllogism) implies measurement, as when one says, “I measured this against that.” Measurement can be made against one thing. If something is measured against two or three things, however, there are two or three measurements, not one. Those measurements would therefore constitute several syllogisms, not a single syllogism. It thus becomes clear that, in what they call “definition” and “demonstration,” these people have relied neither on an existing reality nor on anything rationally intelligible, but merely on convention. This resembles the dispute over the term “cause”: does it designate that which necessarily entails its effect, such that the effect never fails to follow under any circumstances, admitting neither a contrary instance nor exceptions? Or does it designate that which tends to produce the effect, although the effect may fail to follow because a condition is absent or an impediment is present?

Likewise, some practitioners of rational inquiry and disputation use the term “proof” for that which unconditionally entails its conclusion, so that the absence of countervailing evidence is included within it. Others use “proof” for that which is such as to entail its conclusion, its failure to do so arising only because a condition is absent or an impediment is present.

Practitioners of disputation have also disagreed over whether someone presenting an argument must, when stating the proof, clarify countervailing evidence in general or in detail wherever detail is possible; whether he need address it neither in general nor in detail; or whether he must clarify it in general but not in detail. These are stipulated conventions, comparable to the words people agree upon to express what is in their minds. They are not independently established truths concerning intelligible matters on which nations agree, as these people claim for their logic.

translated_text:
took account of actual properties of causes and proofs: complete sufficiency or the mere capacity to produce a result. Their considerations were therefore closer to truth and reason than those of these others, who relied on nothing but arbitrary stipulation. For this reason, knowledgeable people of sound judgment described their logic as a conventional system devised by a Greek man, which rational people do not need.

Nor does rational people’s pursuit of knowledge depend on it, any more than it depends on using their vocabulary, such as fīlāsūfiyā (philosophy), sūfistīqā (sophistics), anūlūtīqā (analytics), athūlūjiyā (theology), qātīghūriyās (categories), and other terms with which they express their meanings. No one claims that all other rational people need this language—especially those whom Allah has honoured with the noblest of languages, one that combines the highest degrees of eloquence and conveys what minds conceive in the fewest words and with the fullest clarity.

This was among the arguments Abū Saʿīd al-Sīrāfī advanced in his celebrated debate with the philosopher Mattā, when Mattā began praising logic and claiming that rational people needed it. Abū Saʿīd replied that there was no need for it, and that what was needed was to learn Arabic. Meanings are naturally accessible to reason and require no special convention, unlike the language just mentioned, which is needed to understand the meanings one is required to know and must therefore be learned. Hence, learning the Arabic upon which understanding the Quran and hadith depends is a collective obligation, unlike logic.

translated_text:
Any later scholar who claims that learning logic is a collective obligation, or that it is a prerequisite for independent juristic reasoning, thereby demonstrates his ignorance of both the revealed law and the usefulness of logic. The falsity of this claim is necessarily known in the religion of Islam. The best of this community—the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the leading scholars of the Muslims—knew what was required of them and what would perfect their knowledge and faith before Greek logic became known.

How, then, can it be said that knowledge cannot be trusted unless weighed by logic, or that human beings’ natural faculties generally become sound only through it? If they say, “We do not maintain that people need the logicians’ terminology, but rather the concepts by which knowledge is weighed,” the answer is: There is no doubt that the unknown can be understood only through what is known. People need to weigh what they do not know against what they know. This is among the balances Allah has sent down, as He says:

“It is Allah who has sent down the Book in truth and the balance.”

And He says:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the balance.”

This is found both in our community and in other communities among people who have never even heard of Greek logic. It is therefore clear that peoples have no need of the logical concepts that the logicians expressed in their own language, namely, their discourse on secondary intelligibles.

For the “subject matter of logic” is intelligibles insofar as they serve to attain knowledge of what is not yet known. It examines the properties of secondary intelligibles: the secondary relations that attach to essences considered without qualification, if these lead to the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired or assist in doing so—not in a particular instance, but according to a universal rule. the scholar of legal theory examines evidence in Islamic law and its relative authority, distinguishing what constitutes legal evidence from what does not. He also examines the relative ranks of proofs, so that when they conflict, he gives precedence to the stronger over the weaker. They claim that the logician examines evidence as such, which is broader than legal evidence, and distinguishes what constitutes evidence from what does not. They claim that their logic stands in relation to meanings as prosody does to poetry, scales to goods, measures of time to time, and the cubit to the objects measured by it.

This is precisely what the majority of Muslim scholars and other rational people have declared false. Their logic does not distinguish evidence from what is not evidence, whether in its form or its content. Nor is there any need to weigh meanings by it; indeed, meanings cannot validly be weighed by it. Rather, this claim is among the most false of all claims.

Our dispute with them concerns the concepts they incorporated into logic, claiming that the conceptions and judgments sought cannot be attained except through them. They thus advanced “four claims” for their logic: two negative and two affirmative. They claimed that conceptions cannot be attained by any method other than the one they set out in it, and that judgments cannot be attained by any method other than the one they set out in it. These two claims are among the most manifestly false of all claims. They also claimed that their stated method yields a conception of realities not previously conceived. This too is false. translated_text:
a discussion of their fourth claim, which is more plausible than the others: that their demonstrative proof yields knowledge through judgment.

And if they say, “Knowledge through judgment—or through conception—cannot be attained without it,” then they are claiming that all avenues to knowledge are closed to rational human beings except the two methods they have described: definition and syllogism. They also claim that these two methods lead to the knowledge that human beings attain through reason, meaning that any method which leads to knowledge must follow the procedure they have described, and no other. Thus, what they have set out is a rule-based instrument by which methods of acquiring knowledge are weighed, and sound methods distinguished from unsound ones. Observing this set of rules therefore safeguards the mind against error in the reasoning through which a conception or judgment is attained. This summarizes what they have said.

All these claims are false, both in what they deny and in what they affirm. Not all the methods of others that they reject are invalid, nor are all the methods of their own that they endorse sound in the manner they claim. Some of their methods are indeed sound, just as some methods used by others are invalid. No one, whether among them or others, composes a work without its necessarily containing some truth.

Our discussion now concerns the argument they advanced to establish that a proof must contain two premises, neither more nor fewer. Its weakness has already become clear.

Then, when they recognized that a proof may require several premises, while a single premise may sometimes suffice, they said that an additional proposition—that is, a third premise beyond the two—may sometimes be inserted into a syllogism for an unsound or sound purpose, such as establishing the two premises. They call this a compound syllogism.

They said that it comprises several syllogisms presented to establish more than one proposition, although only one of these is sought in its own right.

They also said that one of the premises may sometimes be omitted, either because it is already known or for an unsound purpose. They divided compound syllogisms into disconnected and connected forms.

You may then be told:

If you claim that what is indispensable is just one syllogism comprising two premises, and that anything beyond this amounts to further syllogisms, each establishing one of the premises, then say instead that what is indispensable is one premise, and that any additional premises serve only to establish that premise. This is more reasonable. For if an attribute’s belonging to its bearer—that is, a judgment’s applying to its subject, a grammatical predicate’s applying to its subject, or a logical predicate’s applying to its subject—can be known only through an intermediary between the two, namely the evidence, then what is indispensable is one premise. Anything beyond that may or may not be needed.

As for claiming that a syllogism consisting of two premises is needed because some questions require it, this is like claiming that three, four, or five premises are needed in some questions because some questions require them. There is no more reason to prescribe one number than another. What they say about omitting one of the two premises because it is obvious, or in order to mislead, applies equally to omitting a third or fourth premise. Anyone who argues for a conclusion using one premise that is insufficient on its own to establish it—or two or three premises that are insufficient—is asked to supply whatever further premises are needed to make the argument sufficient.

Once the premises have been stated, those open to denial are denied, and those open to counterargument are countered, until the reasoning is complete. premise is sufficient if the listener knows that every intoxicant is forbidden, provided he accepts that premise. If he challenges it, saying, “We do not accept that this is intoxicating,” it must be established through the testimony of someone trustworthy or through experience with something similar. This is reasoning by analogy, and it yields certainty. For when someone tests a portion of a large quantity of drink and knows that it is intoxicating, he knows that the remainder is intoxicating, since the same judgment applies to each portion.

Likewise, all other empirical propositions—such as knowing that bread satisfies hunger and water quenches thirst—are based on reasoning by analogy. Indeed, the same applies to all sensory judgments known to hold universally: their universality is known only through reasoning by analogy.

If, however, his interlocutor disputes that intoxicating fermented drink is forbidden, he needs two premises: to establish that this drink is intoxicating and that every intoxicant is forbidden. He establishes the second through various proofs, such as the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

And:

“Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.”

And the report that:

“He was asked about a drink made from honey called bitʿ and a drink made from sorghum called mizr. He had been granted the gift of expressing much in few words, and he said: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

These hadiths are recorded in the Sahīh. They, and many times as many other reports, are well known from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and show that he prohibited every intoxicating drink.

If the interlocutor says, “I know that it is intoxicating liquor, but I do not accept that intoxicating liquor is forbidden,” or, “I do not accept that it is forbidden without qualification,” then this third premise must be established, and so on. translated_text:
a proof is that which entails the judgment it establishes, as explained earlier. Since the first term entails the middle term, and the middle term entails the third, it follows that the first entails the third.

For an antecedent of an antecedent is itself an antecedent, and a consequence of a consequence is itself a consequence. The judgment is thus a necessary consequence of the proof, but this necessary connection is known only through a middle term between them. The middle term is what follows the words “because.” This is something the logicians themselves have mentioned. Ibn Sīnā and others discussed the inseparable attributes of a subject, explaining that some are self-evidently inseparable. On this basis, they refuted those among their own school who distinguished an essential attribute from a necessary concomitant of the essence by saying that the latter requires a middle term, whereas the former does not. They replied that many inseparable attributes require no middle term: namely, those whose necessary connection is self-evident. For these logicians, the middle term is the proof.

Some people, however, have supposed that the middle term is something that actually stands between an immediate consequence and a remote consequence. This is mistaken. Nevertheless, it becomes clear that the intended conclusion follows on either understanding. We say: if some necessary consequences are so self-evidently connected to their antecedents that no intervening proof is needed, then merely conceiving such a consequence and its antecedent suffices to know that it holds of that antecedent. If there is a middle term between them, and both its necessary connection to the first antecedent and the second term’s necessary connection to it are self-evident, no further middle term is required. If either of the two antecedents is not self-evident, a middle term is needed; if neither is self-evident, two middle terms are needed. This middle term is a term for which a single premise suffices. Thus, if someone asks for proof that intoxicating fermented drink is forbidden, he is told that it is because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is authentically reported to have said:

“Every intoxicant is wine,” or “Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

For the believer, no further middle term is needed to establish that the prohibition of intoxicants follows from this middle term—namely, the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Nor is a middle term needed to establish that the prohibition of the disputed fermented drink follows from the prohibition of intoxicants. Everyone knows that if he forbids every intoxicant, he thereby forbids the intoxicating fermented drink under dispute; and every believer knows that whatever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbids is forbidden.

If someone says, “The proof that it is forbidden is that it is intoxicating,” then, if his interlocutor knows that it is intoxicating and that intoxicants are forbidden, he will concede its prohibition. But he may be overlooking the fact that it is intoxicating, or he may not know that it is intoxicating. The same applies if someone says, “Because it is wine.” If the interlocutor acknowledges that it is wine, its prohibition is established. If he acknowledges this after denying it, he may previously have been ignorant and then learned, or heedless and then remembered. Not everyone who knows something has it in mind.

For this reason, these logicians disagreed over whether knowledge of the two premises suffices for knowledge of the conclusion, or whether one must also become aware of a third matter. The latter is the position of Ibn Sīnā and others. They argued that a person may know that a female mule does not give birth, then lose sight of that fact. He sees a female mule with a swollen belly and asks, “Is this one pregnant or not?”

He is asked, “Do you not know that it is a female mule?”

He replies, “Yes.”

He is asked, “Do you not know that a female mule does not give birth?”

He replies, “Yes.”

It is then, he said, that the person becomes aware that it does not give birth.

I say:

“The truth of the matter” is that this dispute arose from their assumption that two premises are necessary, not from the inferential process itself, since a condition is distinct from what it conditions. But that is not how matters stand. Rather, what is needed is whatever establishes the conclusion sought, whether one premise, two, or three. What one has lost sight of is not known while one remains heedless of it; once one recalls it, it becomes actual knowledge.

Here, the proof is the knowledge that a female mule does not give birth. He had lost sight of this premise, so he did not know it in the manner required for it to serve as proof. Something overlooked does not serve as proof while it remains overlooked; it does so only when recalled, for only then is it knowledge present to the mind.

The Lord, Most High, is free of heedlessness and forgetfulness, because these contradict the very reality of knowledge. Likewise, He is free of drowsiness and sleep, because these contradict the perfection of His life and His being the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all. Sleep is the brother of death; hence the people of Paradise do not sleep, just as they do not die. They are inspired to glorify Allah just as we are inspired to breathe.

The point here is that the inferential force of a proof lies in knowing that what it establishes follows necessarily from it, whether this is called bringing it to mind, becoming aware of it, or something else. Whenever a person brings this necessary connection to mind, he knows that the proof establishes its conclusion. If this connection is evident to him, that suffices; otherwise, explaining it may require one, two, three, or more premises.

Middle terms vary from person to person. The middle term that entails a judgment for one person need not be the middle term for another; the latter may arrive at a different middle term. The middle term is the proof: it mediates, in knowledge, between what is entailed and what entails it, namely the predicate and the subject. For the predicate necessarily belongs to the subject so long as it is predicated of it. These middle terms—which are proofs—vary and multiply according to the guidance Allah opens up to people. When the middle term is a truthful report, for example, the report received by one person may differ from that received by another.

When the crescent moon is sighted and its sighting confirmed at the ruler’s court, and people disperse and spread the news throughout the town, each group acquires knowledge through reports from informants other than those who informed the other groups. Likewise, the Quran and Sunnah transmitted to people from the Messenger reached each group through intermediaries different from those through whom they reached others, especially in the second and third centuries. One group had its Quran instructors and teachers, and another had its own Quran instructors and teachers. All these were intermediaries: they were the middle terms between those people and knowledge of what the Messenger said and did. They were the ones who directed them to that knowledge through their reports and teaching.

The same applies to things known through reason or sensory perception when someone draws attention to them or guides others to them. As for those who take the middle term concerning necessary attributes to be the intermediary in their actual inherence

Even supposing it to be correct, the middle term in thought has a wider scope than its counterpart in external reality, just as a proof has a wider scope than a cause. Every cause can be used to infer its effect, but not every proof is actually a cause. Likewise, whatever serves as an intermediary in reality can be made an intermediary in thought, thus serving as a proof, but the converse does not hold. For a proof is that which entails what it establishes. A cause that entails its effect can therefore be used to infer it. Similarly, a middle term that necessarily follows from what entails it, and itself entails a more remote consequence, entails that consequence and can therefore be used to infer it.

Thus, on any account, the desired conclusion can be established through a single premise if no other premise is needed. Sometimes, however, it can be established only through several premises, which must therefore be known. Insisting that exactly two premises are needed—neither more nor fewer—is entirely arbitrary. Hence, among all the various groups of rational people and authors in the sciences, you find no one who insists on demonstrating his arguments through two premises, no more and no fewer, striving to reduce any excess to two and to make up any shortfall so as to produce two premises, except the adherents of Greek logic and those who follow their path. This is not the practice of those who have retained their sound natural disposition or followed a path other than theirs, such as the Emigrants, the Helpers, those who followed them in righteousness, the other leading Muslim authorities, scholars and thinkers, and the various religious communities.

Likewise, among grammarians, physicians and geometers, none engages in this practice except those who follow these logicians in this respect, just as they followed them uncritically in adopting definitions composed of genus and differentia. Its use became widespread only from the time of Abū Hāmid. He placed an introduction to Greek logic at the beginning of his book al-Mustasfā and claimed that only someone acquainted with this logic could have confidence in his own knowledge. He also wrote Mi‘yār al-‘Ilm (The Criterion of Knowledge) and Mihakk al-Nazar (The Touchstone of Reasoning) on the subject. He wrote another book, which he called al-Qistās al-Mustaqīm (The Just Balance), in which he presented five balances: the three categorical forms, the conjunctive conditional form, and the disjunctive conditional form. is not true. They call a syllogism in which one premise has been omitted an enthymeme, and say that the premise may be omitted because it is already known, by mistake, or to mislead. The response is this: if it is known, it is like any other known premise. In that case, there is no greater justification for leaving one premise implicit than for leaving two, three, or four implicit. If, in an argument requiring only one premise, one may claim that another premise has been left implicit and omitted, then, in an argument requiring two, one may claim that a third has been omitted; the same applies to an argument requiring three. There is no limit to this. Anyone who reflects on this will find it to be so.

This is why eloquent masters of expression, who establish demonstrations and conclusive arguments in the clearest terms, do not employ two premises in their discourse as frequently as logicians do. Rather, anyone who follows the logicians’ method becomes one of those who constrict the path to knowledge in both thought and expression. Their meanings are of a piece with their wording: one finds in them a feebleness and clumsiness that no rational person would accept.

Ya‘qūb ibn Ishāq al-Kindī was the philosopher of Islam in his day. I mean a philosopher living within the Islamic world; otherwise, the philosophers are not Muslims. Thus, people once asked one of the eminent judges of our time, “Is Ibn Sīnā one of the philosophers of Islam?” He replied, “Islam has no philosophers.”

We have explained elsewhere that analogical reasoning and syllogistic reasoning necessarily entail one another: whatever either yields, whether knowledge or probable judgment, the other yields likewise, provided the content is the same. What matters is the content of the knowledge, not the form of the proposition. Indeed, when the content is certain, it remains the same whether expressed through analogy or through syllogism, and whether the syllogism is conjunctive or exceptive—in their terminology or in whatever wording you choose, especially wording that is better than theirs, clearer to the mind, and more concise. The meaning remains the same.

This can be seen in the most obvious examples. You may say: “This is a human being, and every human being is a created being, or an animal, or sentient, or capable of voluntary motion, or rational,” or mention whatever other necessary attribute of a human being you choose. You may formulate the argument in this way, or you may say: “He is a human being; therefore, he is a created being, or sentient, or an animal, or capable of motion, like other human beings, since they share the human nature that entails these attributes.” Alternatively, you may say: “This is a human being, and human nature entails these properties; therefore, they necessarily belong to him.” Or you may say: “If he is a human being, then he possesses these attributes that necessarily belong to human beings.”

You may also say: “Either he possesses these attributes or he does not. The second alternative is false, so the first must hold, because these attributes necessarily belong to a human being, whose existence without them is inconceivable.”

is not an inference from a particular to a universal, or from the specific to the general. Rather, it is an inference from one of two mutually entailing things to the other. For if that judgment holds for every individual instance of a general universal, it must necessarily hold for that universal.

Their claim that this is an inference from what is specific and particular to what is general and universal is therefore untrue. How could that be so, when the evidence must entail what it proves? For if the evidence could exist without what it proves, and what it proves did not necessarily follow from it, then knowing that the evidence was present would not enable us to know that what it proves was also present—if we knew that the latter sometimes accompanied it and sometimes did not. If we knew this and then said that it always accompanied it, we would be affirming two contradictories simultaneously.

The necessary connection we are discussing here makes inference possible, whatever form that connection takes. The stronger, more complete and more evident the connection, the stronger, more complete and more evident its indication. This is the case with created things, which point to the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. Every created thing necessarily entails its Creator: it cannot exist without its Creator’s existence, nor indeed without His knowledge, power, will, wisdom and mercy. Every created thing points to all of these.

If what is proved necessarily follows from the evidence, then it is evident that a necessary consequent must be either coextensive with that which entails it or broader in scope. Thus, the evidence can only be broader in scope than what it proves.

When they say that in syllogistic reasoning one infers the particular from the universal, the particular is not the judgment being proved. Rather, it is the subject being described and spoken of as the locus of the judgment. This may be narrower in scope than the evidence or coextensive with it. The judgment, by contrast—which is the formulation concerning that subject and the ruling asserted of it—can only be broader in scope than the evidence or coextensive with it. For this is what is proved and necessarily follows from the evidence, while the evidence itself necessarily follows from the subject being spoken of and described.

 النَّبِيذُ حَرَامٌ لِأَنَّهُ خَمْرٌ فَكَوْنُهُ خَمْرًا هُوَ الدَّلِيلُ وَهُوَ لَازِمٌ لِلنَّبِيذِ وَالتَّحْرِيمُ لَازِمٌ لِلْخَمْرِ وَالْقِيَاس الْمُؤَلَّفُ مِنْ الْمُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ إذَا قُلْت كُلُّ النَّبِيذِ الْمُتَنَازَعِ فِيهِ مُسْكِرٌ أَوْ خَمْرٌ وَكُلُّ خَمْرٍ حَرَامٌ فَأَنْتَ لَمْ تَسْتَدِلّ بِالْمُسْكِرِ أَوْ الْخَمْرِ الَّذِي هُوَ كُلِّيٌّ عَلَى نَفْسِ مَحَلِّ النِّزَاعِ الَّذِي هُوَ أَخَصُّ مِنْ الْخَمْرِ وَالنَّبِيذِ فَلَيْسَ هُوَ اسْتِدْلَالًا بِذَلِكَ الْكُلِّيِّ عَلَى الْجُزْئِيِّ بَلْ اسْتَدْلَلْت بِهِ عَلَى تَحْرِيمِ هَذَا النَّبِيذِ فَلَمَّا كَانَ تَحْرِيمُ هَذَا النَّبِيذِ مُنْدَرِجًا فِي تَحْرِيمِ كُلِّ مُسْكِرٍ قَالَ: مَنْ قَالَ إنَّهُ اسْتِدْلَالٌ بِالْكُلِّيِّ عَلَى الْجُزْئِيِّ. وَ 
" التَّحْقِيقُ "
 أَنَّ مَا ثَبَتَ لِلْكُلِّيِّ فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ جُزْئِيَّاتِهِ وَالتَّحْرِيمُ هُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنْ الْخَمْرِ وَهُوَ ثَابِتٌ لَهَا فَهُوَ ثَابِتٌ لِكُلِّ فَرْدٍ مِنْ جُزْئِيَّاتِهَا فَهُوَ اسْتِدْلَالٌ بِكُلِّيٍّ عَلَى ثُبُوتِ كُلِّيٍّ آخَرَ لِجُزْئِيَّاتِ ذَلِكَ الْكُلِّيِّ. وَذَلِكَ الدَّلِيلُ هُوَ كَالْجُزْئِيِّ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى ذَلِكَ الْكُلِّيِّ وَهُوَ كُلِّيٌّ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى تِلْكَ الْجُزْئِيَّاتِ وَهَذَا مِمَّا مَا لَا يُنَازِعُونَ فِيهِ؛ فَإِنَّ الدَّلِيلَ هُوَ الْحَدُّ الْأَوْسَطُ وَهُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنْ الْأَصْغَرِ أَوْ مُسَاوٍ لَهُ وَالْأَكْبَرُ أَعَمُّ مِنْهُ أَوْ مُسَاوٍ لَهُ؛ وَالْأَكْبَرُ هُوَ الْحُكْمُ وَالصِّفَةُ وَالْخَبَرُ. وَهُوَ مَحْمُولُ النَّتِيجَةِ. وَالْأَصْغَرُ هُوَ الْمَحْكُومُ عَلَيْهِ الْمَوْصُوفُ الْمُبْتَدَأُ. وَهُوَ مَوْضُوعُ النَّتِيجَةِ.

 إنَّهُ اسْتِدْلَالٌ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْجُزْئِيِّ عَلَى الْجُزْئِيِّ. فَهَذَا غَلَطٌ. فَإِنَّ 
" قِيَاسَ التَّمْثِيلِ "
 إنَّمَا يَدُلُّ بِحَدِّ أَوْسَطَ: وَهُوَ اشْتِرَاكُهُمَا فِي عِلَّةِ الْحُكْمِ أَوْ دَلِيلِ الْحُكْمِ مَعَ الْعِلَّةِ. فَإِنَّهُ قِيَاسُ عِلَّةٍ أَوْ قِيَاسُ دَلَالَةٍ.
translated_text:
Thus, if one says, “Nabīdh (a drink prepared by steeping ingredients in water) is forbidden because it is khamr (intoxicating liquor),” its being khamr is the evidence, and this is a necessary attribute of the nabīdh, while prohibition necessarily applies to khamr. In a syllogism consisting of the two premises, “All the nabīdh under dispute is intoxicating or is khamr,” and “All khamr is forbidden,” you have not used the universal—“intoxicant” or “khamr”—to establish the very subject under dispute, which is narrower in scope than either khamr or nabīdh. This is therefore not an inference from that universal to the particular. Rather, you have used it to establish that this nabīdh is forbidden. Since the prohibition of this nabīdh falls within the prohibition of every intoxicant, some have described this as an inference from the universal to the particular.

The precise account, however, is that whatever holds for a universal holds for each of its particular instances. Prohibition is broader in scope than khamr, and since it applies to khamr, it applies to every particular instance of it. This is therefore an inference from one universal establishing that another universal applies to the particular instances of the former. The evidence is like a particular in relation to that other universal, while itself being a universal in relation to those particular instances. This is something they do not dispute: the evidence is the middle term, which is broader in scope than the minor term or coextensive with it, while the major term is broader in scope than the middle term or coextensive with it. The major term is the judgment, the attribute, and the predicate; it is the predicate of the conclusion. The minor term is that about which the judgment is made, the thing described, and the grammatical subject; it is the subject of the conclusion.

As for their statement that analogy is an inference from one particular to another: if this is stated without qualification and taken to mean an inference from one particular to another merely on the basis of their being particulars, it is mistaken. Analogical reasoning establishes its conclusion only through a middle term: the two cases share the cause of the ruling, or an indication of the ruling together with the cause. It is thus either an analogy based on a cause or an analogy based on an indication.

translated_text:
As for “analogy based on resemblance,” if it is accepted, it falls within one of these two categories. The shared feature connecting the original case and the new case must be either the cause itself or something that entails the cause. Yet sharing something that entails the cause does not entail sharing the ruling; rather, the shared feature may or may not be accompanied by the cause. We therefore cannot know that the analogy is valid; indeed, it is valid only if both cases share the cause. We cannot know that they share it unless we know that they share either the cause itself or something that entails it, since the presence of what entails something necessitates the presence of what it entails. If we suppose that they share neither something that entails the cause nor the cause itself, the analogy is certainly invalid, since the cause would then be confined to the original case. If that is not known, the validity of the analogy is not known.

The validity of an analogy may also be known through the absence of any relevant difference between the original case and the new case, even when neither the specific cause nor its indication is known. The absence of any relevant difference necessarily means that they share the ruling. Since analogical reasoning is complete only through establishing the absence of a relevant difference or identifying a shared feature—a universal encompassing both cases that entails the ruling—and since either procedure can be cast in syllogistic form, this is not an inference that a ruling applies to one particular merely because it applies to another. Rather, it involves the ruling necessarily applying to the universal, and the universal necessarily applying to its particular instances. This is the very essence of syllogistic reasoning.

If it is asked, “How is it known that the shared feature entails the ruling?” the answer is: “By the same means through which the major premise of a syllogism is known.” Identifying the middle term amounts to identifying the shared connecting feature, while the major term necessarily applying to it amounts to the ruling necessarily applying to that shared connecting feature, as previously pointed out. As for their division into three types, all of them reduce to what has been stated about evidence necessarily entailing what it establishes. What they describe as a “conjunctive syllogism” can be cast in the form of an “exceptive syllogism”; likewise, an “exceptive syllogism” can be cast in the form of a “conjunctive syllogism.” The matter therefore comes down to a single consideration: the material content of the argument. This content is not learned from the syllogistic form they describe. Rather, whoever understands the content sufficiently to know that this necessarily entails that understands the inference, whether or not it is cast in syllogistic form, and whether it is expressed in their terminology or otherwise. Indeed, the expressions refined by Muslim minds and tongues are far, far better than theirs.

The “conjunctive syllogism” reduces entirely to one necessary entailment followed by another, as explained. This is precisely what the “exceptive syllogism,” constructed from implicative and disjunctive conditionals, amounts to. An implicative conditional is an inference through necessary entailment: from affirming the entailing proposition—the antecedent, or condition—to affirming the entailed proposition—the consequent, or result; or from negating the entailed proposition—the consequent, or result—to negating the entailing proposition—the antecedent, or condition.

A disjunction that precludes joint truth involves inferring the negation of one of two contraries from the affirmation of the other, since the two are mutually incompatible. A disjunction that precludes joint falsity involves both contradiction and necessary entailment. Two contradictories cannot both be false, so it precludes their both being absent. However, it concerns the existence of one thing and the nonexistence of another, not the existence and nonexistence of the same thing. The existence of one thing and the nonexistence of another may stand in a relation whereby one necessarily follows from the other, even though they cannot both be absent: their simultaneous absence would entail the simultaneous absence of both the existence and the nonexistence of a thing.

In short, everything has something it necessarily entails, without which it cannot exist, and something incompatible with and opposed to its existence. Its existence can therefore be inferred from the existence of something that necessarily entails it, and its nonexistence from the absence of something it necessarily entails. Its nonexistence can also be inferred from the existence of something incompatible with it, and its existence from the absence of that incompatible thing, provided the possibilities are confined to these two, so that they can neither both be absent nor both exist.

Such inference yields knowledge of a thing’s states, what necessarily entails them, and what they necessarily entail. Once the natural disposition conceives of this, it expresses it in various ways and casts it into various forms of argument. None of this is confined to the form they describe for syllogism, let alone what they call demonstration. For demonstration, they stipulate particular material content: the propositions they have specified. They exclude from self-evident first principles what they call “estimative propositions” and what they call “commonly accepted propositions,” although the natural disposition assents to both—especially what they call estimative propositions—more strongly than it assents to many of the certainties they have made the material content of demonstration.

translated_text:
I have discussed this at length, explaining their statements on the matter and their contradictions, and showing that their exclusions also exclude the means of attaining the noblest branches of theoretical and practical knowledge. They are left with nothing but things conceived in the mind that have no reality outside it. Were there room here to quote their own words on this subject and the objections I have raised against them, I would do so. I have already set all this out in its appropriate places in the universal and theological sciences, for these are the sciences ultimately sought.

The discussion of “logic” arose only because they claimed that it is a rule-governed instrument whose observance protects the mind from error in thought. We therefore needed to examine this instrument: is it as they claim, or is it not?

Some of their leading authorities, when shown flaws in their statements that expose their misguidance, and unable to rebut this, say: “These are sciences that minds have refined for more than a thousand years and that learned men have accepted.”

There are several answers to this.

First: this is not the case. Men of reason superior to these have always criticized them and exposed their errors and misguidance. As for the ancients, their numerous disagreements are well known. The books recording their histories and doctrines contain accounts of these that this is not the place to recount. As for the Islamic era, Muslim speculative thinkers have written extensively to expose the unsound elements in their logical and theological principles—indeed, even their physical and mathematical principles. Every school of Muslim speculative thinkers has composed works on this, even the Rāfidah.

translated_text:
And as for the testimony of all the other communities of believers and scholars that they are misguided and guilty of disbelief, this is a widespread judgment that only an obstinate opponent would deny. The believers are Allah’s witnesses on earth. Since the foremost intelligent and distinguished figures of the various schools, together with the rest of the people of knowledge and faith, openly declare them mistaken and misguided, whether in general or on particular points, it cannot be true that all people of reason have accepted their teachings.

(Second response)

This is not a valid argument. Aristotle criticized much of the philosophy that preceded him and had been accepted by his predecessors, exposing their errors. Ibn Sīnā and his followers disagreed with the ancients on a number of their doctrines and demonstrated their errors. Philosophers refute one another more than the members of any other school refute one another. Abū al-Barakāt and others like him have refuted Aristotle extensively, as Allah has willed, for they say: “We seek only the truth; our aim is not partisan allegiance to any particular thinker or doctrine.”

(Third)

The religion of the idol-worshippers is older than their philosophy, and the communities that have embraced it are more numerous than those that have embraced their philosophy. Likewise, the altered religion of the Jews is older than Aristotle’s philosophy, while the altered religion of the Christians arose close to Aristotle’s time. Aristotle lived approximately three hundred years before the Messiah, during the time of Alexander son of Philip, from whom the Roman era used by the Jews and Christians is reckoned.

 وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ الِاسْتِقْرَاءَ هُوَ الْحُكْمُ عَلَى كُلِّيٍّ بِمَا تَحَقَّقَ فِي جُزْئِيَّاتِهِ فَإِنْ كَانَ فِي جَمِيعِ الْجُزْئِيَّاتِ كَانَ الِاسْتِقْرَاءُ تَامًّا كَالْحُكْمِ عَلَى الْمُتَحَرِّكِ بِالْجِسْمِيَّةِ لِكَوْنِهَا مَحْكُومًا بِهَا عَلَى جَمِيعِ جُزْئِيَّاتِ الْمُتَحَرِّكِ مِنْ الْجَمَادِ وَالْحَيَوَانِ وَالنَّبَاتِ وَالنَّاقِصِ كَالْحُكْمِ عَلَى الْحَيَوَانِ بِأَنَّهُ إذَا أَكَلَ تَحَرَّكَ فَكُّهُ الْأَسْفَلُ عِنْدَ الْمَضْغِ لِوُجُودِ ذَلِكَ فِي أَكْثَرِ جُزْئِيَّاتِهِ. وَلَعَلَّهُ فِيمَا لَمْ يُسْتَقْرَأْ عَلَى خِلَافِهِ
translated_text:
(Fourth)

It may be said: Grant that this is so. These disciplines are purely rational: they do not rest on following anyone’s authority, but are known through reason alone. They therefore cannot be validated by transmitted reports; indeed, they must be discussed solely on rational grounds. When clear reason demonstrates the falsity of their erroneous elements, its judgment cannot be rejected. Their adherents have not claimed that these disciplines derive from any source that must be believed, but rather from pure reason. They must therefore be judged according to what clear reason requires.

Section

They have argued, as mentioned, that induction is inferior to syllogistic reasoning—specifically, subsumptive syllogism—and that reasoning by analogy is inferior to induction. They say:

“Reasoning by analogy yields only probability, and the subject of its judgment may be a particular. Induction, by contrast, may yield certainty, and the subject of its judgment can only be a universal.”

They say:

“This is because induction consists in judging a universal on the basis of what has been established in its particular instances. If this has been established in all its instances, the induction is complete. An example is judging that everything that moves is corporeal, since corporeality is predicated of all the particular instances of moving things: inanimate objects, animals, and plants. Incomplete induction is exemplified by judging that an animal, when eating, moves its lower jaw as it chews, because this is found in most instances. Yet the opposite may be true of those instances that have not been examined

This is especially so because the cause of the judgment in the primary case may consist of shared attributes together with other attributes, all actually present in that case. When the shared feature is present in the primary case, the judgment holds because its cause is complete; when it is absent, the judgment ceases to hold because the cause is incomplete. It therefore does not follow that the presence of the shared feature in the secondary case establishes the judgment, since the remaining attributes, or some of them, may be absent.

“As for ‘division and elimination,’ it amounts to claiming that the attributes of the primary case are confined to a specified set, then ruling out all but the one retained. This, too, does not yield certainty. The judgment may hold in the primary case because of the very nature of that case, rather than because of something extrinsic; otherwise, an infinite regress would follow. Even if it holds because of something extrinsic, it always remains possible that this is something other than the enumerated attributes, even though inquiry has failed to uncover it. Matters of ordinary experience are different: when our sight is sound and nothing obstructs it, we have no doubt that there is no sea of mercury or mountain of gold before us if we do not see one.

“Even if the possible causes are confined to the enumerated attributes, the judgment may be explained by all of them together, or by some that are not present in the secondary case. The presence of the judgment alongside the shared feature in a particular case, despite the absence of other attributes accompanying it in the primary case, does not establish that this feature alone accounts for the judgment. In that particular case, the judgment may have another cause, and there is nothing impossible about this. Even if it has no cause other than the shared feature, that feature may be a cause by virtue of its particular character rather than its general nature. If it is demonstrated that the attribute entails the judgment by virtue of its general nature, then—quite apart from the difficulty of establishing this—reasoning by analogy becomes unnecessary.”

translated_text:
They say:

“Physiognomy based on bodily features is itself reasoning by analogy, except that the common feature linking the primary and secondary cases is an indication of the cause, not the cause itself. This is what jurists call ‘analogy based on an indication’: one infers the existence of a cause from one of its effects, then infers its other effect from the existence of that cause. This rests on the premise that bodily temperament causes both an inward disposition and an outward feature. The outward feature thus indicates the temperament, which in turn indicates the inward disposition. An example is inferring courage from breadth of the upper body, on the grounds that both result from the same temperament, as is found in the lion.

“Establishing the cause in the primary case necessarily requires covariation or division, as explained above. Even if we assume that the two judgments in the primary case have a single cause, nothing prevents one of them from holding in the secondary case through a cause other than that operative in the primary case. In that event, the other judgment does not necessarily follow.”

The response is:

Their distinction between syllogistic reasoning and reasoning by analogy—that the former may yield certainty, whereas the latter yields only probability—is invalid. Rather, whenever either yields certainty, the other does too; and whenever either yields only probability, the other likewise yields only probability. Whether an argument yields certainty or probability does not depend on its taking one of these two forms rather than the other. It depends instead on whether it contains something that yields certainty. If either contains something that entails the judgment with certainty, certainty is attained through it. If it contains only something that establishes the judgment as probable, it yields only probability.

If the analogy proceeds by eliminating any relevant difference, a specific primary case is indispensable, for the shared attribute is the equality and equivalence of the two cases. If the analogy proceeds by identifying the cause, mentioning the primary case may be unnecessary when establishing the attribute’s causal character does not depend on it. Those who distinguish between analogical and syllogistic reasoning have sought to show that one of them is conjectural in particular subject matters. Yet those subject matters that yield only conjecture in analogical reasoning likewise yield only conjecture in syllogistic reasoning. Conversely, when they employ it in matters in which syllogistic reasoning yields certainty, analogical reasoning also yields certainty. Indeed, the certainty it yields is even more evident there.

Thus, if the following syllogism is stated:

“Every human is an animal, and every animal is a body; therefore, every human is a body,”

If the causal basis of the judgment in the primary case is disputed, and someone objects, “We do not concede that being an animal necessarily entails being a body,” this is a dispute over the statement, “Every animal is a body.” For when the attribute shared by the primary and secondary cases is called a cause, what is meant is simply that which necessarily entails the judgment, whether it is the cause that necessitates the judgment’s existence in external reality or something that necessarily entails it.

The same is also evident in the case of sound assertions. Syllogistic reasoning must include a universal affirmative proposition, for they agree that no conclusion follows from two negative premises or from two particular premises. A universal is universal only in the mind. Knowing that some of its instances exist in external reality helps establish knowledge of the universal affirmative proposition. When a person perceives particular external instances, he abstracts a universal attribute from them, especially when those instances are numerous. Knowledge that the shared attribute is present in an original case in external reality is the foundation of knowledge of the universal proposition. Thus, analogical reasoning is foundational to syllogistic reasoning: either it causes such reasoning to arise, or it must be said that syllogistic reasoning cannot exist without it. How, then, can syllogistic reasoning alone be stronger than analogical reasoning?

These thinkers illustrate universals with statements such as: “The whole is greater than the part”; “Two contradictories cannot both be true or both be false”; and “Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.” Many external instances of every one of these universals are already known. When one wishes to establish such a universal proposition firmly in the mind, one illustrates it with a particular instance and demonstrates either that there is no relevant difference between it and the other instances, or that a common attribute is present. The intellect then judges that the ruling applies to that shared universal attribute. This is the very essence of analogical reasoning.

Knowledge of the particular only makes that knowledge more complete. Thus, the form of inference they reject is more complete than the one they affirm.

Know that in “metaphysical logic”—indeed, even in “natural logic”—they altered some of what Aristotle had stated. Yet their additions in metaphysics are better than Aristotle’s own statements, for I have examined both accounts. In metaphysics, Aristotle and his followers are far, far more ignorant than the Jews and Christians. In natural philosophy, however, most of what he says is sound. As for logic, his statements on it are better than his statements on metaphysics.

Their disparagement of “analogical reasoning” comes only from their later thinkers, who observed that jurists commonly employed it. Jurists frequently use it with content that yields only probable knowledge. Here, however, the probability arises from the content, not from the form of the inference. Had they cast that content in syllogistic form, it would likewise have yielded only probable knowledge. These thinkers, however, supposed that the weakness lay in the form. They therefore deemed their own form of inference productive of certainty, and the jurists’ form productive only of probability. For the arguments advanced by the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah, and those among the Ashʿariyyah and others who agree with them to establish that bodies originated in time are weak because of their content, not because their form yields only probability. Hence, it makes no difference whether they cast them in analogical or syllogistic form.

Section

As for (the fourth point)—their claim that syllogism or demonstration yields propositional knowledge—it is the most subtle of these points.

[For the logicians’ error concerning the three points—namely, denying that conception is possible except through definition, attaining conception through definition, denying that judgment is attained through definition, and denying that judgment is attained through syllogism—is clear upon the slightest reflection. The grounds for recognizing it are readily accessible, and knowledge of it is evident] (*).

They merely confuse people through intimidating displays and prolixity. Their most obviously erroneous claim is that the conceptions sought can be attained only through the definitions they prescribe. Next comes their assertion that none of the judgments sought can be attained except through the syllogisms they prescribe. There is no way to know that such a sweeping denial is true, nor is there any evidence whatsoever to support it. Indeed, its falsity is known from the judgments sought that are attained without their prescribed syllogisms, just as conceptions sought are attained without their prescribed definitions—unlike the present point
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 79):
“For the error in the three premises—namely, denying that conception (tasawwur) is possible except through definition (hadd), asserting that definition yields conception, and denying that judgment (tasdīq) can be attained except through syllogism (qiyās)—is clear upon the slightest reflection. The grounds for recognizing it are readily accessible, and knowledge of it is evident.”

The three preceding positions mentioned by the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, are:
The first: Conception can be attained only through definition (8/83).
The second: Definition yields a conception of things (8/88).
The third: No judgment can be known except through syllogism (8/103).
