their terminology, which becomes ambiguous, encompassing both truth and falsehood. This gives rise to misguidance contrary to the very purpose of balances. These balances thus become unjust rather than just. In using them, they become defrauders:

“Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full,”

“But when they give by measure or weight to them, they give less.”

Yet how can defrauding people of wealth compare with defrauding them in matters of reason and religion? Most of them, however, do not intend to defraud. Rather, they are like someone who inherited scales from his father and uses them to weigh, sometimes to his advantage and sometimes to his disadvantage, without knowing whether they are just or unjust. The balance that Allah sent down with the Book is a just balance. It involves comparing a thing with what resembles it and what differs from it, treating like things alike and distinguishing between unlike things, through the recognition of similarities and differences that Allah has instilled in His servants’ natural dispositions and minds.

If it is asked, “If this can be known through reason, why did Allah include it among the things with which He sent the Messengers?”

The answer is: Because the Messengers set forth rational comparisons for people through which they could recognize similarities and differences. The Messengers directed and guided people to the means of recognizing justice and sound rational inferences by which religious truths are established. Prophetic knowledge is therefore not confined to reports. Rather, the Messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—explained the rational knowledge through which Allah’s religion is perfected in knowledge and practice. They set forth parables, thereby perfecting the natural disposition through what they brought to its attention and guided it toward when it had been heedless of it

or had been corrupted by the false opinions and desires that affected it, a corruption they then removed. The Quran and hadith are full of examples of this: Allah explains truths through rational comparisons and illustrative parables. He explains how to treat like things alike and distinguish between unlike things. He condemns those who depart from this, as when He says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds”—to the end of the verse.

And He says:

“Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

That is, this is an unjust judgment, not a just one, because it treats unlike things alike.

An example of treating like things alike is His saying:

“Are your disbelievers better than those?”

And His saying:

“Or do you think you will enter Paradise without facing trials like those who passed away before you?”—to the end of the verse.

The point is to draw attention to the fact that the rational balance is sound, as Allah has stated in His Book. It is not confined to Greek logic; rather, it consists of sound inferences that treat like things alike and distinguish between unlike things, whether formulated as syllogistic deduction or analogical inference. Analogical formulations are primary; they involve assimilating one case to another. The balance is the common element—the attribute linking the two.

(The eighth argument): Just as they restricted certainty to the syllogistic form, they also restricted it to the material they specified: propositions based on sense perception, self-evident first principles, mass-transmitted reports, experience, and intuition. Yet it is well known that there is no proof for excluding propositions other than these. As for smell, taste, and touch, there is no particular object that all people share in perceiving through these senses. What one group smells, tastes, and touches is not the very same thing another group smells, tastes, and touches. The objects may, however, be alike in kind without being individually identical. The same applies to what is known through mass transmission, experience, and intuition: reports may reach one group through mass transmission without reaching others in that way, and one group may experience what others have not experienced. Nevertheless, their knowledge may concern things of the same kind. For example, one group may try certain medicines, while others try medicines of the same kind. They thus share knowledge of the kind, not knowledge of the particular thing tested.

Yet, despite this, they say in logic:

 فَإِنْ أَدْخَلُوا ذَلِكَ فِيمَا ذَكَرُوهُ مِنْ الْحِسِّيَّاتِ وَالْعَقْلِيَّاتِ لَمْ يُمْكِنْهُمْ نَفْيُ مَا لَمْ يَذْكُرُوهُ وَلَمْ يَبْقَ لَهُمْ ضَابِطٌ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ ابْنُ سِينَا وَأَتْبَاعُهُ:
 أَنَّ الْقَضَايَا الْوَاجِبَ قَبُولُهَا الَّتِي هِيَ مَادَّةُ الْبُرْهَانُ: الْأَوَّلِيَّاتُ وَالْحِسِّيَّاتُ وَالْمُجَرَّبَاتُ وَالْحَدْسِيَّاتُ وَالمُتَواتِراتِ وَرُبَّمَا ضَمُّوا إلَى ذَلِكَ قَضَايَا مَعَهَا حُدُودُهَا وَلَمْ يَذْكُرُوا دَلِيلًا عَلَى هَذَا الْحَصْرِ وَلِهَذَا اعْتَرَفَ الْمُنْتَصِرُونَ لَهُمْ أَنَّ هَذَا التَّقْسِيمَ مُنْتَشِرٌ غَيْرُ مُنْحَصِرٍ يَتَعَذَّرُ إقَامَةُ دَلِيلٍ عَلَيْهِ. وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ لَمْ يَلْزَمْ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا لَمْ يَدْخُلْ فِي قِيَاسِهِمْ لَا يَكُونُ مَعْلُومًا. وَحِينَئِذٍ فَلَا يَكُونُ الْمَنْطِقُ آلَةً قَانُونِيَّةً تَعْصِمُ مُرَاعَاتُهَا مِنْ الْخَطَأِ فَإِنَّهُ
translated_text:
learned. Even if they mention a group who made astronomical observations, this amounts, at most, to mass transmission confined to a particular group. How can someone who claims that reports mass-transmitted from the prophets cannot establish a demonstration binding upon him then establish a demonstration binding upon others through mass transmission of this kind, extol astronomy and philosophy, and claim that they constitute rational knowledge established by demonstration? Such is the state of what they regard as the foremost subject of rational demonstration. What, then, should one think of their metaphysics? When a discerning, rational person examines and reflects upon what their First Teacher, Aristotle, said about it, he learns only that they were among the most ignorant of all people concerning the Lord of the worlds, and that the unbelievers among the Jews and Christians knew more about these matters than they did.

The ninth point:

The prophets and the close servants of Allah possess knowledge through revelation and inspiration that lies beyond the syllogistic reasoning these men have described. Indeed, discernment and similar faculties also lie beyond it.

If they include such knowledge within the sensory and rational categories they have mentioned, they cannot exclude what they have not mentioned, and they are left with no defining criterion. Ibn Sīnā and his followers have stated that the propositions which must be accepted, and which constitute the material of demonstration, are self-evident first principles, sensory propositions, propositions based on experience, propositions based on intuition, and mass-transmitted propositions. Sometimes they add propositions accompanied by their terms. Yet they have offered no proof that these categories are exhaustive. Their defenders have therefore acknowledged that this classification is open-ended rather than exhaustive, and that no proof can be established for it.

Since this is so, it does not follow that everything outside their syllogistic reasoning cannot be known. Logic, then, cannot be an instrument providing rules whose observance safeguards against error. For

translated_text:
if propositions that can be known by some other method are presented, they cannot be assessed by these forms of proof. Most of these logicians deny whatever has not been established through their syllogistic reasoning. This is the height of ignorance, especially when what they deny consists of reports conveyed by the prophets.

If, then, the noblest knowledge cannot be attained by their method, two consequences follow:

First, they have no grounds for denying anything for which their syllogistic reasoning provides no proof.

Second, what they know is paltry compared with what they do not know. How much more so when it is known that their knowledge brings neither salvation nor happiness!

The tenth point:

They treat genuine knowledge, which must be accepted as true, as though it were not knowledge, while treating what is false and is not knowledge as knowledge. They claim that what the prophets taught concerning knowledge of Allah, His attributes, and the Hereafter has no corresponding reality. They claim that the prophets merely presented the masses with imagined representations of these matters, so that these would help them secure their worldly welfare, not so that they might thereby know the truth; and that this amounts to lying for people’s benefit.

They say that a prophet is well versed in the practical teachings of religion, but not its doctrinal teachings. Some of them regard the philosopher as superior to every prophet, including our Prophet—may the finest blessings and peace be upon him. They do not consider it obligatory to follow any particular prophet, neither Muhammad nor

Thus, when the Tatars emerged and some of them wished to embrace Islam, it is reported that one of the philosophers accompanying Hulagu advised him not to do so, saying: “His language is Arabic, and you have no need of his religious law.” Those among them who follow the Prophet in practical religious laws do not follow him in the foundations of religion and belief. Rather, they regard the Prophet as the speculative theologians regard one of the four imams. When the leading speculative theologians adhere to one of the four schools, they confine their adherence to matters of jurisprudence and do not consider themselves bound to agree with its imam on doctrinal foundations and questions of divine oneness. Indeed, they may regard their own teachers in speculative theology as superior to those imams in these matters.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has told us about Allah, His specific names and attributes, and about the angels, the Throne, the Footstool, Paradise, and Hell. None of this can be known through their syllogistic reasoning. Likewise, he has told us about particular matters, past and future, none of which can be known through their syllogistic reasoning, whether demonstrative or otherwise. Their syllogisms yield only universals, whereas these are particular matters.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold specific events, even telling of the Tatars who appeared six hundred years after his prediction. Likewise, he foretold the fire that broke out before the Tatars arrived, in 655 AH. Could their syllogistic reasoning and demonstration conceivably point to a particular individual or a particular nation, let alone one possessing the characteristics he described?

 مَعْنَاهُ كَوْنُهَا مَشْهُورَةً أَوْ مَقْبُولَةً أَوْ مَظْنُونَةً. وَجَمِيعُ هَذِهِ الْفُرُوقِ هِيَ نِسَبٌ وَإِضَافَاتٌ عَارِضَةٌ لِلْقَضِيَّةِ لَيْسَ فِيهَا مَا هُوَ صِفَةٌ مُلَازِمَةٌ لَهَا فَضْلًا
translated_text:
Another of their grievous errors and statements of unbelief is their claim that the Creator—exalted is He—does not know particulars, does not know Moses, Jesus, or anyone else as individuals, and knows nothing of the details of events. This claim and its refutation are discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is to recognize that they make statements of ignorance and unbelief that represent the utmost misguidance, seeking to evade an implication for whose denial they have never had any evidence.

The eleventh point:

They acknowledge things perceived through the external and internal senses, such as hunger, pain, and pleasure. Yet they deny the existence of things that some people alone may see, such as angels, jinn, and what the soul sees at death. The Quran and Sunnah explicitly affirm these things. A detailed discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere. The point here is that the unsound logical principles they have adopted—denying what has not been established to be nonexistent—have led them into ignorance and unbelief that have become a barrier to them, leaving them worse off than the disbelievers among the Jews and Christians.

The twelfth point:

It may be said that, according to them, a proposition’s being “demonstrative” means that it is known to the person reasoning from it; its being “dialectical” means that it is conceded; and its being “rhetorical” means that it is widely held, accepted, or considered probable. All these distinctions are relations and attributions incidental to the proposition. None is an inseparable attribute of it, let alone

translated_text:
an essential attribute of it according to their own principles. Indeed, none of these is an attribute of the proposition in itself; rather, they are relative attributes depending on someone’s awareness of it. It is well known that a proposition may be true without a person even being aware of it, let alone considering it probable or knowing it to be true. Likewise, a proposition may be rhetorical or dialectical while being true in itself; indeed, it may also be demonstrative, as they themselves have acknowledged.

Since this is so, the Messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—conveyed propositions that are true in themselves and can never be false or erroneous. They also explained generally accessible methods of knowing by which the truth of propositions can be established, thus benefiting humankind. This is knowledge that benefits people.

These would-be philosophers, however, did not follow this path. Instead, they approached propositions in relative terms: they classified as demonstrative whatever the person reasoning knew, and did not classify anything else as demonstrative, even if another person reasoning knew it. Accordingly, propositions considered demonstrative by one person or group may not be considered demonstrative by others. Propositions known to be true therefore cannot be encompassed by a comprehensive definition; rather, they vary according to the circumstances of those who know them and those who do not. Indeed, practitioners of each discipline know propositions that others do not.

Consequently, their method cannot distinguish truth from error or true statements from false ones on the basis of how matters actually stand—what is true or erroneous, truthful or false—within each discipline. Nor can its benefit be shared by all human beings. This is unlike the method of the Prophets, who conveyed true propositions that distinguish truth from error

and true statements from false ones. Whatever contradicts a true statement is false, and whatever contradicts the truth is erroneous. For this reason, Allah made the Scripture He revealed a judge between people concerning their disagreements. He also sent down the balance and that by which things are weighed and truth is distinguished from error. Every truth has a balance by which it is weighed. This is unlike what the philosopher-logicians devised: it cannot guide to the truth or distinguish truth from error, nor is it a balance by which truth can be distinguished from error. As for the speculative theologians, whatever in their discourse agrees with what the Prophets brought derives from it; whatever contradicts it belongs to the innovations that are invalid according to both revelation and reason.

If it is said:
“We regard demonstrative propositions as relative. Whatever a person knows through its premises is demonstrative for him, even if it is not demonstrative for someone else.”

The reply is:
“They have not done so. Anyone who followed this path would not find the material of demonstration confined to particular things, when many people may know other matters without those particular materials they have specified.”

If they say, “We do not specify the materials,” then one of the constituent parts of logic has been invalidated—which is precisely the point.

through reason or truthful reports, about many matters that cannot be known by the methods they have described, including the knowledge possessed by the Prophets, may Allah bless them—they sought to subject all this to their flawed framework.

They said:
“A prophet possesses a faculty stronger than that of others, enabling him to arrive at the middle term without a teacher’s instruction. Once he forms a conception, he apprehends through that faculty the term which others may find difficult or impossible to apprehend without instruction, for the souls’ capacities for apprehension have no fixed limit.”

Thus, they maintained that the Prophets’ reports of the unseen came only through logical syllogism. This is utterly unsound. Logical syllogism yields knowledge only of universals, as explained earlier, and they themselves concede this. Yet the Messengers reported specific, individual, particular matters—past, present, and future. This establishes that the Messengers’ knowledge did not come through logical syllogism. Indeed, Ibn Sīnā even placed the Lord’s knowledge of what He brings into existence in this category. Exalted is Allah far above what he says!

What has been established demonstrates the falsity of their attempt, in logic, to restrict the means of acquiring knowledge in respect of both matter and form. It also shows that they excluded bodies of true knowledge far greater in dignity, importance, and extent than those they acknowledged. The method they described yields only a little knowledge of a lowly kind, neither abundant nor noble. Such is the standing of these people: they are among the basest of people in knowledge and deeds. The unbelievers among the Jews and Christians are superior to them in knowledge and deeds in many respects. All of philosophy cannot bring its adherent to the level of the Jews and Christians after the abrogation and alteration of their religions

translated_text:
let alone their level before that. Ibn al-Qushayrī recited these verses in refutation of Ibn Sīnā’s al-Shifā’ (The Healing):

We severed the bonds of brotherhood with a people
Whom The Healing had afflicted with disease.
How often I said, “My people, you stand
On a precipice’s edge because of The Healing!”
When they dismissed our warning,
We turned to Allah until He sufficed us.
They died following the religion of Aristotle,
While we lived following the faith of the Chosen One.

If it is said:

“Something similar to the logicians’ restriction of the means of acquiring knowledge appears in the writings of Muslim speculative theologians. Indeed, some state precisely the same thing, either in the logicians’ own terms or in different wording.”

The answer is:

Not everything the speculative theologians say is true. Rather, everything the Messengers brought is true. Whatever the speculative theologians and others say that agrees with it is true, and whatever they say that contradicts it is false. The condemnation of newly introduced speculative theology by the early generations and the leading scholars is well known.

He said:

What is astonishing is that some people sought, as they claimed, to defend the revealed Law through their deficient reasoning and unsound syllogisms. Yet what they did emboldened the heretics, the enemies of religion

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section: On setting out the general principles of “logic” and its flaws

They constructed it on the premise that the means of acquiring knowledge are confined to “definition” and related forms, such as descriptive definition and the like, and to syllogism and related forms, such as induction and analogy. For knowledge is either “conception,” which is knowledge of individual concepts, or “assent,” which is knowledge of the relations between them through negation or affirmation. Each of these two kinds of knowledge is either “self-evident,” requiring no method of acquisition, or “inferential,” requiring such a method. The method for acquiring conceptions is “definition,” while the method for attaining assent is “syllogism,” which they call demonstration if its premises are certain.

They then said: “Definition” is an expression indicating the essence of a thing, although it may also refer to the thing defined itself, just as a name is an expression indicating the thing named and may also refer to the thing named itself,

since what is understood from a definition and a name is the thing defined and the thing named, just as “essence” is what is stated in answer to “What is it?” It is also described as the answer to a question formulated as “What is it?” Thus, essence is the definition, and it is also the thing itself. These verbal nouns derived from interrogative expressions are later coinages, such as māhiyya and mā’iyya (whatness), kayfiyya (howness), haythiyya (respect or aspect), ayniyya (whereness), and limmiyya (whyness). They are comparable to verbal nouns derived from declarative expressions, such as hawqala (saying “There is no power nor strength except through Allah”), qalhada, basmala (saying “In the name of Allah”), hamdala (saying “Praise be to Allah”), and the like.

They then said that “essence” is composed of essential attributes. They explained the distinction between essential and accidental attributes by saying that “essential” attributes are those without conceiving which it is impossible to conceive the thing possessing them. The thing therefore depends on them both in existence and in conception, as an animal depends on corporeality. Whatever is not of this kind is “accidental.”

An accidental attribute is then divided into an inseparable attribute and a separable accident. An inseparable attribute is either inseparable from the essence, as evenness is from four and oddness from three, or inseparable from its existence rather than its essence, as blackness is from pitch and coming into existence is from an animal. A separable accident either passes away slowly, like youth and greying hair, or quickly, like the redness of embarrassment and the pallor of fear.

The difficulty lies in distinguishing an essential attribute from an attribute inseparable from the essence, since neither is separable from the thing itself, whether in external existence or in the mind.

translated_text:
They therefore distinguished between them by saying that an essential attribute is conceived before the essence is conceived, so that the thing itself cannot be understood without it, unlike an attribute inseparable from the essence.

Both essential and accidental attributes may be shared throughout a genus, yielding the general genus and the common accident; or exclusive to a species, yielding the differentia and the distinctive property; or combine what is shared with what distinguishes, yielding the species. These, then, are the “five universals”: genus, differentia, species, distinctive property, and common accident. Discussing these attributes and their divisions is chiefly useful for definitions and the essential realities of things.

As for the syllogism, it is a statement composed of statements which, if conceded, necessarily entail another statement by virtue of themselves. It must contain two premises. A “premise” is a proposition—that is, a declarative sentence—and must contain two simple terms. The discussion thus proceeds on three levels:

(First) The discussion of simple terms, their expressions and meanings: signification by correspondence, inclusion, and necessary implication; synonymous, distinct, equivocal, and univocal names; simple and compound expressions; and the universal and the particular.

The “second level” concerns propositions and their divisions: particular, universal, and unqualified propositions; affirmation and negation; and the modalities of propositions. It also concerns the rules governing propositions, such as the falsity of the contradictory and the truth of the converse and the contrapositive.

translated_text:
And the “third level” concerns the syllogism, its moods, and the conditions under which it yields a conclusion: it must contain a universal affirmative proposition; no conclusion follows from two negative premises, two particular premises, or a negative minor premise and a particular major premise. Rather, there must be either two affirmative premises, one of which is universal, or a negative minor premise and a particular major premise. It also concerns other rules governing the forms and types of syllogism, established through proof by contradiction—which is reduced to the rule governing the contradictory of a proposition—or through reduction to the proposition’s converse or contrapositive.

They then explained the material content of syllogisms, dividing them into:

“Demonstrative”: those whose premises are certain. They restricted certainties to the categories they mentioned: inward and outward sense perceptions, self-evident truths, mass-transmitted reports, and propositions established by experience. Some also added propositions established by intuition.

“Rhetorical”: those whose premises are widely accepted, whether certain or uncertain.

“Dialectical”: those whose premises are conceded by the opponent, whether certain, widely accepted, or otherwise.

“Poetic”: those whose premises are felt rather than believed, such as those that evoke joy, sorrow, or laughter.

“Fallacious, sophistical”: those whose premises are disguised with semblances of truth.

translated_text:
Section

There are three views concerning what the term qiyās denotes:

The first is that it literally denotes analogical reasoning and figuratively denotes syllogistic reasoning. This is the view of al-Ghazālī and Abū Muhammad.

The second is the reverse. This is the view of Ibn Hazm.

The third is that it literally denotes both. This is the more correct view, held by the majority.

According to our scholars and the majority, qiyās is divided into rational reasoning, for which reason alone suffices, and reasoning based on revelation, which necessarily requires a foundation known through revelation.

Both rational reasoning and reasoning based on revelation—and everything termed qiyās—are divided into analogical reasoning and syllogistic reasoning. The former consists in treating something like its counterpart; the latter consists in bringing something under the rule of a general concept that encompasses it.

Each is connected to the other: two similar things must share a common feature that encompasses them both, while a concept encompassing two or more things necessarily entails treating any two of them alike with respect to that concept. Thus, qiyās is present in both: it consists in measuring, comparing, and reckoning.

translated_text:
Section

The flaws in logic lie in demonstration and definition.

As for “demonstration,” its logical form is valid, and when its premises are sound, it undoubtedly yields sound knowledge. The error, however, lies in two things:

First: There is absolutely no evidence for restricting its premises to the categories they have mentioned. They are correct in what they affirm, but not in what they deny. On what grounds can one judge that certainty can arise only from these particular sources? If someone bases this on what he finds within himself, how can he know that the rest of humanity—even the prophets and the friends of Allah—cannot attain certainty by other means? Indeed, reality shows otherwise.

Second: This demonstration does yield knowledge. But how is it known that no human heart can acquire knowledge except through demonstration of the kind described? We have, in fact, seen many things that some people know immediately or through sense perception, while others know them through reflection and syllogistic reasoning. Thus, they denied what they did not fully comprehend: knowledge acquired through premises outside these restricted categories, or without any analogical or syllogistic reasoning at all. Indeed, the most accomplished of their later thinkers claimed that the knowledge of the prophets and the friends of Allah can be acquired only

through syllogistic reasoning. Their statements imply that the same holds for the Lord’s knowledge. Yet he has no evidence whatsoever for this, beyond simply drawing an analogy between the prophets and friends of Allah and himself, and between the Lord and the angels and human beings.

This is a point of which the believer should be certain. He should know that these people and others have generally gone astray because of what they denied and rejected, not because of what they affirmed and knew. This is why logic can lead to heresy in someone whose heart lacks firm faith: he believes that knowledge can be attained only through these particular kinds of premises and this logical form, yet he finds these lacking in most of what the prophets have conveyed. He therefore doubts it, rejects it, or turns away from believing and accepting it as true. His lack of faith and knowledge thus stems from his mistaken belief that knowledge can arise only from these particular kinds of premises—a belief for which there is absolutely no evidence. Although these premises do yield knowledge, there is an obvious difference between saying that they yield it and saying that they yield it and that it cannot be attained otherwise.

A further clarification is that syllogistic reasoning establishes only universal knowledge, as they themselves acknowledge, since it must contain a universal affirmative premise. A universal indicates only what is shared in common, which is itself universal. Thus, syllogistic reasoning does not establish any particular realities in their individuality. All that can be known through it—if anything is known—is an attribute that they share with other things. Through it, therefore, nothing whatsoever can be known of the distinctive attributes of Lordship, nor of what is distinctive to any angel, prophet, or friend of Allah, nor even to any king or any being in the higher or lower realms. Thus, knowledge of these things must either be absent or be acquired

by means other than syllogistic reasoning. Both cases occur: such knowledge is absent among them, since they have no method other than syllogistic reasoning, whereas the prophets and their followers possess it. Indeed, such knowledge is possessed, in general, by all those endowed with knowledge among the angels, the prophets, and other human beings.

Furthermore, since syllogistic reasoning must contain a universal premise, if that premise requires reasoning, it will require another premise. If it is self-evident, then, if all the individual cases it covers can be known self-evidently, what prevents some of those cases from being known in this way—an easier task?

As for definition, it calls for discussion on several points.

First: their claim that concepts acquired through reasoning can be known only through the kind of definition they describe. The same applies here as to their claim that judgments acquired through reasoning can be attained only through the demonstrative proof whose premises they have restricted to certain kinds. There is no evidence for this.

The weakness of this claim is shown by the following: if the person giving a definition knows the thing being defined through someone else’s definition, circular reasoning or an infinite regress necessarily follows. If he knows it without a definition, the claim is disproved.

If it is said, “Rather, he knows it through the definition formed in his own mind, just as he attains propositional knowledge through the demonstrative proof formed in his mind before expressing it in words,” the reply is that a demonstrative proof is distinct from its conclusion: knowledge of the two premises is not itself knowledge of the conclusion. The definition formed in the mind, however, is itself knowledge of the thing being defined—and that is precisely what is sought. Where, then, is the definition that imparts knowledge of the thing being defined? This is one of the points that makes the matter clear.

translated_text:
Second point:

It may be argued that a definition cannot, under any circumstances, make known the essence of what it defines, unlike a demonstrative proof, which provides evidence for the conclusion sought. As regards the person giving the definition, this is because he knew the thing before defining it; otherwise, his definition could not be valid. A definition must correspond exactly to what it defines, being neither broader nor narrower in scope. Without knowing the thing beforehand, he could not know that this correspondence holds.

As regards the listener, if this is not self-evident to him and the person giving the definition offers no proof of it, he cannot acquire knowledge merely from that person’s assertion. Hence, you find the listener challenging a definition and producing counterexamples showing that it includes what it should exclude or excludes what it should include. Had he not conceived the thing independently of the definition, such challenges and counterexamples would have been impossible.

The benefit of a definition is only to distinguish what is defined from other things, not to furnish a conception of it. This accords with the linguistic meaning of hadd—a boundary separating one thing from another. A person may conceive the essence of something without qualification. For example, someone may conceive a command, a statement, or knowledge without qualification, rather than as a universal. A definition then distinguishes the universal concept encompassing every statement, every instance of knowledge, or every command.

From this, it becomes clear that what is conceived self-evidently of the things denoted by these names—the unqualified reality—is different from what is sought through definition—the universal reality. Furthermore, the distinction sometimes concerns names and sometimes attributes. A definition may therefore concern the name: this is a verbal definition, needed when reasoning from the Quran, the Sunnah, or the words of any scholar. Alternatively, it may concern the description: this conveys an understanding of a reality whose description is known, and can be achieved through a descriptive definition, distinctive properties, and other means.

Moreover, if identifying an essential attribute depends on conceiving the essence, while conceiving the essence depends on identifying its essential attributes, the reasoning is circular. For we know the essence only through its essential attributes, yet we cannot identify those attributes until we conceive the essence. Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

I have already written a summary of “logic” as translated into Arabic, which the Arabs transmitted from the Greeks and rendered into Arabic in both wording and meaning. They refined its wording and made its meanings precise. It is attributed to Aristotle the Greek, whom his followers among the Sabaean philosophers who introduced religious innovations call “the First Teacher,” because he established the disciplines they study: logic, natural philosophy, and metaphysics.

When these disciplines reached the Muslims and their books were translated into Arabic, alongside works on medicine, arithmetic, astronomy, and other subjects—with these translations becoming widespread during the reign of the Caliph Abū al-ʿAbbās, known as al-Maʾmūn—the Muslims took them up and refined both their wording and meaning. Yet they contain much falsehood and misguidance.

(فَالْأَوَّلُ)

(الثَّانِي)

translated_text:
Some followed these disciplines while professing Islam. These are the Sabaeans among the Muslims, known as philosophers. They thus came to believe in some of the Scripture but not the rest, like the religious innovators among the Jews and Christians prior to abrogation, when they altered some of the scriptures in their possession.

Others did not intend to follow these disciplines, but adopted ideas from their adherents, supposing that all of them agreed with Islam and supported it, whereas many contradicted and undermined it. Such is the condition of many Muʿtazilī practitioners of speculative theology. Hence they have been called “the effeminates of the philosophers.”

Others turned away from these disciplines in a general, undifferentiated manner, yet did not follow those teachings of the Quran and Islam that would suffice in place of all the truth these disciplines contain and repel their falsehood. Nor did they strive against their adherents in the prescribed manner. Such is the condition of many scholars of hadith and jurisprudence, and others. I have previously written about aspects of this in various discussions of foundational principles. In my summary of the main principles of logic, I also mentioned the ignorance and misguidance it has caused, as well as some of its defects.

Here I summarize that discussion, saying:

The discussion concerns the methods of acquiring knowledge in the form of conceptions and assents. (The first) includes definition and description; (the second) includes syllogism in its various forms, demonstrative and otherwise, as well as analogy and induction. They may claim that the conceptions sought can be attained only through definition in the broad sense

وَأَمَّا الثَّانِي وَهُوَ النَّفْيُ فَإِنَّ إدْرَاكَ الْحَقَائِقِ الْمُتَصَوَّرَةِ الْمُطْلَقَةِ لَيْسَ مَوْقُوفًا عَلَى الْحَدِّ لَوْ فُرِضَ أَنَّهَا تُعْرَفُ بِالْحَدِّ بَلْ تَحْصُلُ بِأَسْبَابِ الْإِدْرَاكِ الْمَعْرُوفَةِ
translated_text:
and that the assents sought can be attained only through syllogism in the broad sense. The general category of syllogism may be called “relation,” just as the general category of explanatory discourse is called “definition.” What is self-evident in either category requires neither definition nor demonstration. This account thus maintains that definitions enable us to conceive realities, and that this cannot be achieved otherwise; and that syllogism yields assent concerning realities, and that this cannot be achieved otherwise. Error has occurred in both matters. As regards definition, the error lies in both propositions, negative and affirmative—in what they affirm and what they deny.

As for the first:

A definition does not convey a conception of realities; it merely distinguishes what is defined from other things. A conception of realities cannot be acquired merely through a definition, which consists of the definer’s words. Rather, those realities must be apprehended through inward and outward perception. If they are not apprehended, an illustrative example is given of them. Through that example—an analogy serving to form a conception, not to establish assent—a kind of apprehension is attained, such as our apprehension of the reward and punishment Allah has promised in the Hereafter. The parables set forth in the Quran sometimes serve to form conceptions and sometimes to establish assent. This point has been established in several ways; the purpose here is merely to summarize the matter.

As for the second, namely the negative claim, apprehending realities conceived in the abstract does not depend on definition, even if it were granted that they could be known through definition. Rather, such conceptions are attained through the recognized means of apprehension.

(الثَّانِي)
 أَنَّ الْقِيَاسَ الْبُرْهَانِيَّ لَيْسَتْ مَوَادُّهُ مُنْحَصِرَةً فِيمَا ذَكَرُوهُ فِي الْحِسِّيَّاتِ والوجديات وَالْبَدِيهِيَّاتِ وَالنَّظَرِيَّاتِ والمتواترات والتجريبيات وَالْحَدْسِيَّاتِ كَمَا بَيَّنْت هَذَا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ؛ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
and they may also be attained through the use of single terms, just as through definition. Indeed, a term may sometimes be more useful in this respect than a definition. This too has been established.

As for syllogism, there is no doubt that it yields assent when its premises and their arrangement are sound. Here, however, the error lies in the negative claims, again in two respects.

(First)
The acquisition of knowledge involving assent in the mind does not depend on syllogism; rather, it can be attained by other means.

(Second)
The premises of demonstrative syllogism are not confined to the categories they have listed: propositions based on sensory perception, inward experience, self-evidence, reasoning, mass transmission, experimentation, and intuition. I have explained this elsewhere. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked about “books on logic.”

He replied:

As for “books on logic,” they contain no knowledge whose study is required by Islamic law, although some people, through their independent judgment, have concluded that studying it is a collective obligation. Others have said that the sciences cannot be established without it, as Abū Hāmid stated. This is a grave error, both rationally and according to Islamic law.

As for “reason,” rational people from every group engaged in scholarly discourse have developed their disciplines with precision without Greek logic. As for “Islamic law,” it is necessarily known in the religion of Islam that Allah has not obliged people of knowledge and faith to learn this Greek logic.

As for logic itself, some of it is true and some false. Much—or most—of the truth it contains is unnecessary. As for whatever is needed, most people of sound natural disposition can grasp it unaided. The dull-witted derive no benefit from it, while the intelligent have no need of it, and its harm to

The claim that it is all true is false. Rather, their discussions of definition, essential and accidental attributes, the categories of syllogism, and demonstration and its premises contain errors that we have explained elsewhere. Muslim scholars have also explained this. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām, the imam and eminent scholar Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halīm ibn Abd al-Salām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

Is the human “intellect” an accident? What is the “spirit” that governs the body? Is it the soul? Does it have a mode of being that can be known? Is it an accident or a substance? Is it known where it resides within the body, and where the intellect resides?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. In the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the words of the Companions, the Successors, and all the other leading Muslim scholars, the “intellect” is something that inheres in the rational person, whether it is called an accident or an attribute. It is not a self-subsisting entity, whether called a substance, a body, or anything else.

The term “intellect” is used to denote a rational entity that is a self-subsisting substance only in the discourse of certain philosophical thinkers who discuss the intellect and the soul and claim that ten intellects exist. This is mentioned by some followers of Aristotle and other Peripatetic philosophers, and by those affiliated with religious communities who adopted it from them. These thinkers have been discussed at length elsewhere, and it has been shown that what they speak of

translated_text:

Their designation of these things as “separate entities” derives originally from the soul’s separation from the body at death. This is correct: the deceased person’s soul does indeed separate from the body at death. This rests upon the fact that the soul subsists in its own right and remains after leaving the body at death, experiencing either bliss or punishment. This is the position of the religious communities, Muslim and otherwise, and the view of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and all the other leading Muslim scholars, although many speculative theologians claim that the soul is the life that inheres in the body.

Some of them say that it is a constituent part of the body, like the air circulating within it or the vapour issuing from the heart. In short, according to the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars, the soul that separates from the body at death is neither a constituent part of the body nor one of its attributes. These two views are held only by certain adherents of newly invented speculative theology among the followers of the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and others like them. The Peripatetic philosophers acknowledge that the soul remains after separating from the body, but they ascribe false attributes to it, claiming that once it separates from the body, it becomes an intellect.

For them, the intellect is that which is free of matter and material attachments, and by matter they mean body. They may also say: “It is that which is free of attachment to hayūlā,” with hayūlā in their terminology meaning a substratum. They also speak of “matter and form.”

translated_text:
For them, the intellect is a substance that subsists in its own right, is described as neither moving nor at rest, and undergoes no new states whatsoever. What their position actually entails is that, once the soul separates from the body, no new state arises in it: no knowledge or conceptions, no hearing or sight, no volitions, no joy or delight, nor anything else that might newly arise or occur. Rather, according to them, it remains in a single state from eternity to eternity, as they claim concerning the intellect and the soul.

Some of them say that souls are numerically one, while others say that they are multiple. Their discourse contains falsehoods that this is not the place to discuss at length. The purpose here is only to draw attention to what is relevant to the present discussion.

They call whatever is associated with matter—that is, hayūlā, which here means body—a soul, such as the human soul that governs the body. They claim that the celestial sphere has a soul that moves it, just as human beings have souls. Their earlier thinkers, however, used to say that the soul of the celestial sphere is an accident inhering in the sphere, like the souls of beasts, and just as desire and anger inhere in a human being. But some of them, such as Ibn Sīnā and others, claimed that the soul of the celestial sphere is a substance subsisting in its own right, like the human soul.

As long as the human soul governs the body, they call it a soul; once it separates from the body, they call it an intellect. This is because, for them, the intellect is that which is free of matter and material attachments, whereas the soul is attached to the body by governing and directing it.

translated_text:
Their designation of these as immaterial entities originally derives from the fact that a person abstracts universal intelligible notions from particular objects of sense perception. When he sees individual human beings, such as Zayd and ʿAmr, he apprehends an element common to human beings and to the universal, shared humanity conceived in his heart. When he sees horses, mules, donkeys, livestock, and other individual animals, he apprehends a universal element common to these individuals: universal animality as conceived by the intellect. When, alongside these, he considers animals, trees, and plants, he apprehends a common universal element: a body that grows and takes nourishment. They sometimes call this the vegetative soul.

When, alongside these, he considers all the other bodies—the celestial bodies above and the elemental bodies below—he apprehends a common universal element: body in its general, unrestricted sense. When he considers the other things that exist, he apprehends a common universal element: general, universal existence, which is divided into substance and accident. According to them, this existence is the subject matter of the “highest science,” which examines existence and its concomitants. This is what they call “first philosophy” and “supreme wisdom.”

They divide existence into substance and accident, and classify accidents into “nine kinds.” This is what Aristotle set forth. His followers include this within logic because it deals with the simple terms to which composite definitions ultimately reduce. The same is true of those who followed their approach in writing on this subject, such as Ibn Hazm and others.

Ibn Sīnā and his followers, however, said: “Discussion of this subject is not confined to logic.”

so they excluded these categories from logic, as did those who followed Ibn Sīnā’s approach, such as Abū Hāmid, al-Suhrawardī who was executed, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others. These are the “ten categories,” which they designate as substance, quantity, quality, place, time, relation, position, possession, acting, and being acted upon. They have been brought together in two lines of verse:

Zayd, tall and black, the son of Mālik, … was reclining in his house yesterday;
In his hand a sword—he drew it, and it was drawn: … these are ten categories in full.

Most people, both his followers and others, rejected the restriction of accidents to nine genera, saying: “There is no proof for this.” They maintain that these can be reduced to three genera or to other numbers.

They classified substances into “five kinds”: body, intellect, soul, matter, and form. Body is a substance perceived by the senses, while the remaining kinds are intelligible substances. Yet the evidence they offer to establish intelligible substances establishes their existence only in minds, not in external reality. These are what they call “immaterial intelligibles.”

They say that substances are divided into material and immaterial substances. Material substances are those that subsist in matter—that is, prime matter, which is body—while immaterial substances are those abstracted from matter. What they call immaterial entities have their origin in these notions

translated_text:
—universals apprehended in the human soul—just as the notion of separate entities originates in the soul’s separation from the body. Both of these are undeniable.

However, they make false claims about the soul’s attributes and states. They also assert the existence of intelligible substances subsisting in themselves, concerning which they say: “The one who understands, what is understood, and understanding itself are one and the same.” They say the same concerning the Lord of the worlds:

“He is the one who understands, what is understood, and understanding itself; the lover, the beloved, and love itself; that which gives delight, the one who experiences delight, and delight itself.”

They identify the attribute with the subject possessing it, and each attribute with every other attribute. Thus, they identify understanding itself—which is knowledge—with the one who understands and knows, and passionate love itself—which is love—with the passionate lover, the one who loves. They identify delight itself with knowledge itself and love itself. They also identify power and will with knowledge itself, making knowledge identical with power, will, love, and delight. They identify the one who knows, wills, loves, and experiences delight with knowledge itself, which they identify with will itself, love itself, and delight itself. Thus, they make distinct realities one and the same, and identify the various attributes themselves with the very essence that possesses them.

Then they contradict themselves by affirming that He has knowledge that is not identical with His essence, as Ibn Sīnā contradicted himself in his Ishārāt, as did other leading thinkers among them. A detailed refutation of them is given elsewhere.

The point is that they use the term “intellect” to designate a substance subsisting in itself, and affirm intelligible substances that they call “immaterial entities” and “entities separate from matter.” Yet when their position is rigorously examined, they have nothing beyond the human soul, which they call “rational,” and the quality subsisting in it that is called intellect.

translated_text:
Aristotle and his followers called “the Lord” an intellect and a substance. According to them, He knows nothing other than Himself, wills nothing, and does nothing. They call Him “the Principle” and “the First Cause,” because, in their view, the celestial sphere moves in order to resemble Him, or to resemble the intellect. Thus, according to them, the celestial sphere needs the First Cause only insofar as it seeks to resemble it, just as someone following an imam in prayer emulates him, or a pupil emulates his teacher.

He may also say that He moves the sphere as the beloved moves his lover. They do not hold that He has brought anything into existence or done anything. Nor did they call Him the Necessary Existent, or divide existence into necessary and contingent while regarding the contingent as something eternal and beginningless, like the celestial sphere in their view. Rather, this was the work of Ibn Sīnā and his followers. In this, they opposed their predecessors and all rational people; they also contradicted themselves. For they explicitly affirmed what their predecessors and all other rational people had affirmed: that what is contingent—capable of existing or not existing—must have come into being after not existing. As for that which is beginningless, which has always existed and will always exist, they and all other rational people consider it impossible for it to be contingent, admitting either existence or nonexistence. Rather, whatever admits existence and nonexistence must have come into being. This is among the arguments used to establish that everything other than Allah has come into being, preceded by nonexistence, existing after it did not exist, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

Yet Ibn Sīnā and his followers contradicted themselves, stating elsewhere that existence is divided into necessary and contingent, and that a contingent being may be eternal and beginningless, having always existed and continuing forever, such that it is impossible

they thought that revelation had to be believed where it differed from the conclusions of rational thinkers. They did not realize that clear rational proof does not contradict authentic scriptural proof. Indeed, valid proofs cannot conflict, whether they are rational, derived from revelation, or a combination of the two. If two proofs conflict, this indicates that one or both are unsound.

Many of them came to accept that events could continue perpetually into the future, but not into the past. They advanced subsidiary arguments whose weakness their most discerning scholars recognized, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Their position commits them to holding that the Lord was once without power and then became possessed of power, without any new cause arising that would account for His becoming capable; and that He could not act or speak by His will, but then action became possible for Him without any cause arising to account for this new possibility.

When this is pointed out to them, they say, “He possessed power in pre-eternity, as He always had.” They are answered: “One cannot possess power over something while that very thing is impossible. Rather, having power over the impossible is itself impossible. One can have power only to do what is possible. Thus, if He has always possessed power, it has always been possible for Him to act.”

Since this was their foundational premise, they divided into three positions concerning Allah’s speech.

One group said: “Speech does not subsist in the Lord Himself; rather, His speech can only be created. Yet originated events cannot subsist in Him, because if they did, He would never be free of them, and whatever is never free of originated events is itself originated.”

They said: “For it is through this principle that we established that bodies have a beginning, and through it that the world was established to have a beginning.”

They said: “It is known that whatever does not precede an originated event cannot exist before it: it must exist either alongside it or after it. Whatever exists alongside an originated event or after it is itself originated.”

Many of them failed to recognize the distinction between events as a kind and a particular event. A particular event, or a finite set of events, cannot have existed perpetually without beginning. Whatever did not exist before them must exist either alongside them or after them, and whatever is of this description is certainly originated. This is plain to everyone. The question requiring examination and giving rise to dispute, however, concerns “events as a kind”: can the kind be perpetual, such that the Lord continually speaks or acts by His will and power, or is that impossible?

When a group recognized this distinction, they said: “This too is impossible, because a beginningless succession of events is impossible.” They advanced arguments for this, such as the argument from correspondence, the argument that what is infinite cannot come to an end, and similar arguments. Most of what has been stated on this subject and related matters has already been discussed elsewhere; every occasion calls for its own discourse.

 وَاعْتَقَدَ هَؤُلَاءِ أَنَّ الْمَفْعُولَ الْمَصْنُوعَ الْمُبْتَدَعَ الْمُعَيَّنَ كَالْفَلَكِ يُقَارِنُ فَاعِلَهُ أَزَلًا وَأَبَدًا لَا يَتَقَدَّمُ الْفَاعِلُ عَلَيْهِ تَقَدُّمًا زَمَانِيًّا وَأُولَئِكَ قَالُوا:
 بَلْ الْمُؤَثِّرُ التَّامُّ يَتَرَاخَى عَنْهُ أَثَرُهُ ثُمَّ يَحْدُثُ الْأَثَرُ مِنْ غَيْرِ سَبَبٍ اقْتَضَى حُدُوثَهُ فَأَقَامَ الْأَوَّلُونَ الْأَدِلَّةَ الْعَقْلِيَّةَ الصَّرِيحَةَ عَلَى بُطْلَانِ هَذَا كَمَا أَقَامَ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأَدِلَّةَ الْعَقْلِيَّةَ الصَّرِيحَةَ
translated_text:
not having been one, and that the effect of a complete cause cannot lag behind it—they supposed that, by refuting this position, they had secured their claim concerning “the beginninglessness of the world,” including the celestial spheres, generated things as a kind, and the matter of the elements. They fell into profound error, contradicting clear reason and rejecting the testimony of every messenger. For the messengers unanimously affirm that everything other than Allah is originated and created, coming into existence after not having existed; that nothing alongside Allah is beginningless as He is; and that He created the heavens, the earth, and everything between them in six days.

Sound reason recognizes that originated events must have an originator. If there were nothing but an eternal, beginningless cause necessarily entailing its effect, no originated events would exist in the world. For it is impossible for an originated event to arise from an eternal, beginningless cause necessarily entailing its effect. If its effect were inseparable from it, that effect would be beginningless along with it, never coming after it. Thus, none of these events would have a cause necessitating its occurrence, and all originated events would have arisen without an originator. These men fled from the notion that an agent endowed with power should originate them without a newly arising cause, only to hold that they arise without any originator whatsoever, whether endowed with power or not. What they fled to was therefore worse than what they fled from, and they were worse than someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in fire.

These men believed that a particular thing brought about, fashioned, and originated—such as a celestial sphere—coexists with its agent without beginning or end: the agent does not precede it in time. The others said: “Rather, the effect of a complete cause is delayed, then comes into existence without any cause necessitating its occurrence.” The former established clear rational proofs refuting this, just as the latter established clear rational proofs

عَلَى بُطْلَانِ قَوْلِ الْآخَرِينَ وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ قَوْلَ هَؤُلَاءِ أَهْلِ الْمُقَارَنَةِ أَشَدُّ فَسَادًا وَمُنَاقَضَةً لِصَرِيحِ الْمَعْقُولِ. وَصَحِيحِ الْمَنْقُولِ مِنْ قَوْلِ أُولَئِكَ أَهْلِ التَّرَاخِي.
 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّالِثُ الَّذِي يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ الْمَعْقُولُ الصَّرِيحُ وَيُقِرُّ بِهِ عَامَّةُ الْعُقَلَاءِ وَدَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَأَقْوَالُ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ لَمْ يَهْتَدِ لَهُ الْفَرِيقَانِ:
 وَهُوَ أَنَّ الْمُؤَثِّرَ التَّامَّ يَسْتَلْزِمُ وُقُوعَ أَثَرِهِ عَقِبَ تَأَثُّرِهِ التَّامِّ لَا يَقْتَرِنُ بِهِ وَلَا يَتَرَاخَى كَمَا إذَا طَلَّقْت الْمَرْأَةَ فَطَلَقَتْ. وَأَعْتَقْت الْعَبْدَ فَعَتَقَ. وَكَسَرْت الْإِنَاءَ فَانْكَسَرَ وَقَطَعْت الْحَبْلَ فَانْقَطَعَ فَوُقُوعُ الْعِتْقِ وَالطَّلَاقِ لَيْسَ مُقَارِنًا لِنَفْسِ التَّطْلِيقِ وَالْإِعْتَاقِ بِحَيْثُ يَكُونُ مَعَهُ وَلَا هُوَ أَيْضًا مُتَرَاخٍ عَنْهُ بَلْ يَكُونُ عَقِبَهُ مُتَّصِلًا بِهِ.
 وَقَدْ يُقَالُ هُوَ مَعَهُ وَمُفَارِقٌ لَهُ بِاعْتِبَارِ أَنَّهُ يَكُونُ عَقِبَهُ مُتَّصِلًا بِهِ كَمَا يُقَالُ:
 هُوَ بَعْدَهُ مُتَأَخِّرٌ عَنْهُ بِاعْتِبَارِ أَنَّهُ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ عَقِبَ التَّأْثِيرِ التَّامِّ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{إنَّمَا أَمْرُهُ إذَا أَرَادَ شَيْئًا أَنْ يَقُولَ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ}
 فَهُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ يَكُونُ مَا يَشَاءُ تَكْوِينَهُ فَإِذَا كَوَّنَهُ كَانَ عَقِبَ تَكْوِينِهِ مُتَّصِلًا بِهِ لَا يَكُونُ مَعَ تَكْوِينِهِ فِي الزَّمَانِ وَلَا يَكُونُ مُتَرَاخِيًا عَنْ تَكْوِينِهِ بَيْنَهُمَا فَصْلٌ فِي الزَّمَانِ؛ بَلْ يَكُونُ مُتَّصِلًا بِتَكْوِينِهِ كَاتِّصَالِ أَجْزَاءِ الْحَرَكَةِ وَالزَّمَانِ بَعْضِهَا بِبَعْضِ. وَهَذَا مِمَّا يُسْتَدَلُّ بِهِ عَلَى أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا سِوَى اللَّهِ حَادِثٌ كَائِنٌ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ وَإِنْ قِيلَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ بِدَوَامِ فَاعِلِيَّتِهِ ومتكلميته وَهَذِهِ الْأُمُورُ مَبْسُوطَةٌ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
translated_text:
refuting the position of the other group. Undoubtedly, the position of these proponents of simultaneity is far more unsound, and more contrary to clear reason and authentic revelation, than that of the proponents of delay.

Neither group arrived at the third position, which is supported by clear reason, acknowledged by rational people generally, and attested by the Book, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations and the imams.

This position is that a fully operative cause necessarily entails its effect occurring immediately after it becomes fully operative, neither simultaneously with it nor after a delay. This is as when you divorce a woman and she becomes divorced, free a slave and he becomes free, break a vessel and it breaks, or cut a rope and it parts. The resulting emancipation and divorce are not simultaneous with the actual acts of divorcing and emancipating, such that they coexist with them; nor are they delayed after them. Rather, they follow immediately upon them, without a gap.

The effect may be said to be with its cause yet distinct from it, insofar as it follows immediately upon it without a gap. Likewise, it may be said to be after it and subsequent to it, insofar as it occurs only after the full causal act. Hence Allah, Most High, says:

“His command, when He wills something, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

He, glorified be He, brings into being whatever He wills to bring into being. When He brings it into being, it exists immediately after His act of bringing it into being, without a gap. It does not exist simultaneously in time with that act, nor is it delayed after it with a temporal interval between them. Rather, it follows His act without a gap, just as the parts of motion and time adjoin one another. This is among the arguments establishing that everything other than Allah is originated, coming into existence after not having existed, even while affirming that He has always been acting and speaking. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ هَذَا هُوَ أَصْلُ مَنْ قَالَ الْقُرْآنُ مُحْدَثٌ وَمَنْ قَالَ إنَّ الرَّبَّ لَمْ يَقُمْ بِهِ كَلَامٌ وَلَا إرَادَةٌ بَلْ وَلَا عِلْمٌ بَلْ وَلَا حَيَاةٌ وَلَا قُدْرَةٌ وَلَا شَيْءٌ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ.
 فَلَمَّا ظَهَرَ فَسَادُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ شَرْعًا وَعَقْلًا قَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ مِمَّنْ وَافَقَتْهُمْ عَلَى أَصْلِ مَذْهَبِهِمْ:

 وَقَالُوا:
 إنَّ الْأَمْرَ وَالنَّهْيَ صِفَاتٌ لِلْكَلَامِ لَا أَنْوَاعٌ لَهُ. فَإِنَّ مَعْنَى 
" آيَةِ الْكُرْسِيِّ "
 وَ 
" آيَةِ الدَّيْنِ "
 وَ 
{قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ}
 وَ 
{تَبَّتْ يَدَا أَبِي لَهَبٍ}
 مَعْنًى وَاحِدٌ.
 فَقَالَ جُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ لَهُمْ:
 تَصَوُّرُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ يُوجِبُ الْعِلْمَ بِفَسَادِهِ وَقَالُوا لَهُمْ: مُوسَى سَمِعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ كُلَّهُ أَوْ بَعْضَهُ. إنْ قُلْتُمْ كُلَّهُ لَزِمَ أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدْ عَلِمَ عِلْمَ اللَّهِ. وَإِنْ قُلْتُمْ بَعْضَهُ فَقَدْ تَبَعَّضَ.

 إذَا جَوَّزْتُمْ أَنْ تَكُونَ حَقِيقَةُ الْخَبَرِ هِيَ حَقِيقَةَ الْأَمْرِ وَحَقِيقَةُ النَّهْيِ عَنْ كُلِّ مَنْهِيٍّ عَنْهُ. وَالْأَمْرِ بِكُلِّ مَأْمُورٍ بِهِ هُوَ حَقِيقَةُ الْخَبَرِ عَنْ كُلِّ مُخْبَرٍ عَنْهُ فَجَوَّزُوا أَنْ تَكُونَ حَقِيقَةُ الْعِلْمِ هِيَ حَقِيقَةَ الْقُدْرَةِ وَحَقِيقَةُ الْقُدْرَةِ هِيَ حَقِيقَةَ الْإِرَادَةِ.
 فَاعْتَرَفَ حُذَّاقُهُمْ بِأَنَّ هَذَا لَازِمٌ لَهُمْ لَا مَحِيدَ لَهُمْ عَنْهُ وَلَزِمَهُمْ إمْكَانُ أَنْ تَكُونَ حَقِيقَةُ الذَّاتِ هِيَ حَقِيقَةَ الصِّفَاتِ وَحَقِيقَةُ الْوُجُودِ الْوَاجِبِ هِيَ حَقِيقَةَ الْوُجُوبِ الْمُمْكِنِ وَالْتَزَمَ ذَلِكَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ فَقَالُوا:
translated_text:
The point here is that this is the underlying premise of those who say that the Quran is originated, and of those who say that no speech or will subsists in the Lord—indeed, neither knowledge, life, power, nor any attribute whatsoever.

When the unsoundness of this position became evident in light of revelation and reason, a group who shared their fundamental premise said: “He does not speak by His will and power. Rather, His speech is inseparable from His essence, just as life is inseparable from His essence.” Some of them then said that His speech is a single meaning, because an infinite number of meanings cannot coexist at a single instant, and because it cannot be restricted to one number rather than another. They said: “That meaning is the command enjoining everything commanded and the information concerning everything spoken of. If expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel.”

They also said: “Commands and prohibitions are attributes of speech, not types of it. Thus, the meaning of the ‘Verse of the Throne,’ the ‘Verse of Debt,’ ‘Say: He is Allah, One,’ and ‘May the hands of Abu Lahab perish’ is one and the same.”

The vast majority of rational people replied: “Merely conceiving this position is enough to recognize its unsoundness.” They also asked them: “Did Moses hear all of Allah’s speech, or only some of it? If you say all of it, it follows that he knew all that Allah knows. If you say some of it, then His speech admits of division.”

They further said to them: “If you allow that the reality of a declaration is the reality of a command, and that the reality of prohibiting everything prohibited and commanding everything commanded is the reality of information concerning everything spoken of, then allow that the reality of knowledge is the reality of power, and that the reality of power is the reality of will.”

Their most accomplished thinkers acknowledged that this consequence was inescapable for them. Their position also entailed the possibility that the reality of the essence is the reality of the attributes, and that the reality of necessary existence is the reality of contingent necessity. A group of them accepted this consequence and said:

الْوُجُودُ وَاحِدٌ وَعَيْنُ الْوُجُودِ الْوَاجِبِ الْقَدِيمِ الْخَالِقِ هُوَ عَيْنُ الْوُجُودِ الْمُمْكِنِ الْمَخْلُوقِ الْمُحْدَثِ. وَهَذَا أَصْلُ قَوْلِ الْقَائِلِينَ بِوَحْدَةِ الْوُجُودِ كَابْنِ عَرَبِيٍّ الطَّائِيِّ وَابْنِ سَبْعِينَ وَأَتْبَاعِهِمَا كَمَا بُسِطَ فِي مَوَاضِعَ.
 وَمِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الْقَائِلِينَ بِأَنَّهُ لَا يَتَكَلَّمُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ مَعَ قِيَامِ الْكَلَامِ بِهِ مَنْ قَالَ:

 وَزَعَمُوا أَنَّ كُلًّا مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ وَالتَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنْجِيلِ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ قَدِيمَةٌ أَزَلِيَّةٌ لَمْ تَزَلْ وَلَا تَزَالُ فَقَالَ لَهُمْ جُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ:

 إنَّهُ يَتَكَلَّمُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ بِالْقُرْآنِ الْعَرَبِيِّ وَأَنَّهُ نَادَى مُوسَى بِصَوْتِ سَمِعَهُ مُوسَى كَمَا دَلَّتْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ النُّصُوصُ وَأَقْوَالُ السَّلَفِ لَكِنْ نَقُولُ إنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي الْأَزَلِ مُتَكَلِّمًا وَيَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ
translated_text:
“Existence is one, and necessary, eternal existence—the Creator—is identical with contingent, created, originated existence.” This is the foundation of the position of those who profess the unity of existence, such as Ibn ‘Arabī al-Tā’ī, Ibn Sab‘īn, and their followers, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Among those who maintain that He does not speak by His will and power, while affirming that speech subsists in Him, some said:

“His individual utterances consist of particular letters and sounds that are eternal and beginningless, have always existed, and will always exist.”

They claimed that the Quran, the Torah, and the Gospel each consist of eternal, beginningless letters and sounds that have always existed and will always exist. The vast majority of rational people replied:

“It is self-evident that the letter bā’ precedes sīn, and that sīn precedes mīm. How, then, can they coexist from eternity and forever? It is also known that a particular sound does not endure for two successive moments. How, then, can it be beginningless, having always existed and continuing forever?”

Then the third group—among those who followed the approach of those speculative theologians—said:

“Rather, we say that He speaks by His will and power, with speech that subsists in His essence, as indicated by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations and the leading scholars. Even if this entails that temporal occurrences subsist in Him, there is nothing objectionable in that, whether according to revelation or reason. Indeed, this consequence is inescapable for all groups of rational people, and it is indicated by numerous scriptural texts and statements of the early generations and the leading scholars.

“We also say that He speaks the Arabic Quran by His will and power, and that He called to Moses with a voice that Moses heard, as indicated by the scriptural texts and the statements of the early generations. But we say that He was not speaking in the beginningless past, and that it is impossible for Him to

They were answered:

“It is well known that speech is an attribute of perfection, not deficiency, and that one who speaks by his will and power is more perfect than one who is unable to do so. They were also told:

“If you say that He spoke after speech had been impossible for Him, without any cause bringing about His ability to speak or making speech possible for Him, then you are saying that He had always been unable to speak, and speech had always been impossible for Him, but then He became able to speak by His will without anything having occurred. The early generations and the leading scholars explicitly stated that the Lord, Most High, has always spoken whenever He wills and however He wills. This was expressly stated by ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other leading religious scholars and early Muslims. These are the very people who affirmed that the Quran is the speech of Allah, sent down and uncreated. None of them said that He does not speak by His will and power. The point is that these doctrines—advanced by the speculative theologians among the Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah, Kullābiyyah, Karrāmiyyah, and Sālimiyyah, and by those later scholars who agreed with them while affiliating themselves with some of the four imams—contradicted the consensus of the early generations and the leading scholars, what the Quran and Sunnah brought, and the clear rational understanding that Allah has made innate in His servants. It was these doctrines that enabled those eternalist philosophers to gain the upper hand over them. Nevertheless, the philosophers’ position is even more unsound in terms of both rational and transmitted evidence.

Section

The point here is that, among Muslims and most rational people, the term “reason” denotes an attribute, what is called an accident inhering in the rational being. This is what the Quran indicates in the words of the Most High:

“So that you may understand.”

And His words:

“Have they not travelled through the land so that they may have hearts with which to reason?”

And His words:

“We have made the signs clear to you so that you may understand.”

These and similar passages indicate that ‘aql (reason) is the verbal noun of ‘aqala–ya‘qilu (to reason). Accordingly, the term “reason” does not apply to mere knowledge upon which its possessor does not act, nor to action without knowledge. Rather, it applies only to knowledge
